organizations.name: BurnBot
organizations.description: Remote-operated prescribed burn machines for fuels reduction without smoke/escape risk

paragraphs: BurnBot sells wildfire fuels management, equipping infrastructure operators, communities, agencies and ecological partners with tools and services. The work runs from fire mitigation and fuels management to timber operations.

The equipment is remote-controlled masticators and blackline machines. Crews pair the machines with real-time telemetry and monitoring. Because operators work remotely, treatments can be made in steep, remote or hazardous areas. The company says the machines run around the clock in most weather conditions. Prescribed burning uses controlled ignition systems on land and in the air. Projects are documented with dynamic treatment maps and fuel load models.

Government customers are described as federal, state, tribal and local land managers. On the community side, the site names WUI neighborhoods, fire safe councils and cooperatives. The company says it is a qualified contractor for both personnel and equipment, supporting state and federal agencies. It says it was built by fire practitioners, scientists and foresters. Its headquarters is in South San Francisco, California.

quote.text: BurnBot is a qualified contractor for both personnel and equipment, supporting state and federal agencies with safe, effective wildfire operations.

organizations.name: First Due
organizations.description: Cloud fire department suite: pre-incident planning, RMS, scheduling, and response

paragraphs: First Due sells cloud software that fire and EMS agencies use to run records and daily operations in one place. The suite pulls incident reporting, prevention, pre-incident planning, scheduling, assets, hydrants, training and mobile response behind a single login.

Incident documentation is built around the national fire reporting standard, with dynamic forms and error checking at submission. The patient care record is written to the NEMSIS data standard. It reads from cardiac monitors so crews do not key the same values twice. Pre-incident plans hold hazardous materials detail down to chemical location and quantity. Those plans can layer in GIS data through an Esri partnership.

The site describes CAL FIRE moving from a December decision to a July go-live. A county fire department is described using it to coordinate inspections and share preplan information with response crews. The company claims it accounts for nearly half of all NERIS submissions nationwide.

quote.text: Born in the cloud and built to run your entire operation in one place.

organizations.name: Technosylva
organizations.description: Wildfire spread modeling and risk analytics used by CAL FIRE and major utilities

paragraphs: Technosylva sells wildfire and extreme weather risk software to electric utilities and fire agencies. The point of it is turning complicated weather data into something a planning or response team can act on.

For planning, the company combines large numbers of validated fire simulations with historical weather and a customer's own asset data. Its models estimate what an ignition would mean in acres burned, buildings destroyed and people affected. For operations, simulations run nightly to produce the wildfire risk metrics crews plan around. Utilities use the output to target power shutoffs instead of cutting service broadly. Feeds from computer-aided dispatch and IRWIN bring in incidents from federal and state agencies. Flooding, high wind, extreme temperature and winter storms sit in the same view as fire.
The homepage points readers toward Xcel Energy, CAL FIRE and CORE. Bryan Spear is named as chief executive. The company has also announced modeling of urban conflagration in the built environment.

quote.text: One platform for comprehensive, multi-hazard risk intelligence

organizations.name: Dryad Networks
organizations.description: Solar-powered gas sensors under the forest canopy for ultra-early fire detection

paragraphs: Dryad provides ultra-early wildfire detection and autonomous drone systems for public and private forests. The sensors are meant to detect fires within minutes from ignition so firefighters can put them out before they spread out of control.

The fourth generation sensor combines VOC, CO and PM2.5 sensing to catch a fire as early as the smoldering phase. The units form a wireless environmental sensor network based on LoRaWAN. A patented distributed architecture is meant to allow large-scale deployments in areas without existing network coverage. A cloud platform handles deployment planning, operation, analytics and alerting for those networks. An observation drone is dispatched when a sensor detects a fire, and a second drone applies fire suppressant liquids to extinguish fires autonomously.

Beyond forest owners, the company pitches utility and grid operators on protection against liabilities. Published case studies include a fire in Lebanon stopped by early detection. The founders say they came to this work after several startups and exits in IT, electronics and telecommunications.

quote.text: When it comes to fighting wildfires, speed is everything.

organizations.name: Frontline Wildfire Defense
organizations.description: Exterior retardant/foam systems and app-based wildfire defense for homes and HOAs

paragraphs: Frontline Wildfire Defense sells exterior sprinkler systems and companion software that defend homes and businesses against wildfire. The company describes its mission as providing faster, safer and more precise ways to protect homes, families, businesses and communities from wildfire.

The second-generation defense system is tied to fire tracking software and turns on automatically when fire comes within seven miles of a home. Once running, it saturates the property with water and biodegradable firefighting foam to create conditions the company calls too wet to burn. A commercial version is aimed at businesses, campuses and critical infrastructure, meant to cut risk before a fire reaches the property. A companion app carries wildfire alerts, maps, fire danger indexes, emergency contact groups and evacuation checklists.

Homeowners, businesses and new housing developments are the audience, and the company says its system will safeguard 151 homes at a Woodside Homes community. Installation is handled by licensed contractors in each state rather than by the company itself. Financing options, including zero-down wildfire protection, are offered to buyers. The company points to embers as the central danger, saying they cause up to 90% of structure loss during a wildfire.

quote.text: Draw the line against Wildfire.

paragraphs: Axon sells public safety agencies a connected set of hardware and software: Axon Body 4 cameras, Axon Fleet 3 cameras, TASER 10 energy weapons and drones, unified on a real-time crime center platform with an open ecosystem of integrated partners. The company describes itself as an operating system for public safety. TASER 10, its current less-lethal weapon, can deploy up to 10 individually targeted probes without reloading when de-escalation fails.

Axon Fusus puts officer location, alerts, dispatch data, ALPR overlays and video feeds on a single live map so command, field and real-time crime center teams work from the same picture. Residents and businesses can opt in through Community Connect to share their camera video, and those cameras then appear on the Fusus map. The Axon AI Era Plan bundles current and future Axon AI products for a fixed annual cost. Among them is Draft One, which generates first-draft report narratives from audio transcripts of digital evidence and details the officer narrates. Axon Assistant, a voice assistant on the Body 4 camera, translates conversations when no human interpreter is available.

Chief Gary Berg of Campbell PD is quoted saying Fusus lets him see live location, alerts and video from body cams, drones and public safety cameras in one platform. Axon says it is on a mission to cut gun-related deaths between police and the public in half by 2033 through technology, training and trust.

quote.text: We are on a mission to cut gun-related deaths between police and public in half by 2033 through technology, training and trust.

paragraphs: Motorola Solutions builds and connects technologies to protect people, property and places, supporting the collaboration between public safety agencies and enterprises. Its public safety lineup includes APX portable and mobile radios and ASTRO radio systems. On the command center side it sells NG911 call routing and call handling and Computer-Aided Dispatch. The company also designs video security and access control systems.

For police users the APX NEXT smart radio comes in single-band and multi-band configurations. The APX 8500 all-band mobile radio adds interoperability, Wi-Fi connectivity and Bluetooth in the vehicle. Vehicle routers keep first responders connected to broadband so they can reach real-time intelligence on the road. Its broadband products can run on FirstNET or on commercial carrier LTE networks. Managed, support and professional services are sold alongside to keep those systems secure and current.

Customer stories on the site include the Ouachita Parish Sheriff's Office, Peel Police, Nampa PD and York Regional Police, which serves 1.2 million residents. Hutto Independent School District uses the VB400 body camera to capture evidence in its schools. The home page announces the completed acquisition of D-Fend Solutions, which the company describes as a counter-drone technology firm.

paragraphs: Flock Safety sells license plate readers, video cameras, gunshot detection and response drones to law enforcement agencies, schools, businesses and neighborhoods to help them deter crime, respond to emergencies and investigate safety incidents. Its license plate recognition cameras capture plates and vehicle characteristics such as make, color and body type to generate investigative leads. Responders get an instant alert when a vehicle matches a customer-defined or NCIC hot list. Users include law enforcement agencies, businesses, neighborhoods, apartment complexes, houses of worship and schools.

Beyond plate readers, Flock sells PTZ video cameras for open areas such as parking lots, intersections and parks, and fixed cameras for buildings and city streets. A gunshot and audio detection product verifies gunfire and links each alert with nearby LPR reads and video. Flock DFR, its drone as first responder system, launches a docked drone to the coordinates of a 911 call, LPR hit or gunshot alert and streams live video to officers before they arrive. Solar-powered mobile trailers cover parking lots, retail centers and construction sites, and an optional Alert Response Service puts trained agents on live alerts.

Flock sells on an annual subscription that covers hardware, software, maintenance and support. The company has reduced its recommended default data retention from 30 days to 7 days, which it says applies to new law enforcement customers. Customers control their data and how it is shared, and every search is logged.

paragraphs: Skydio makes autonomous drones, along with the docks and software to run them, and sells drone programs to customers from energy networks to neighborhood precincts to battlefields. Those programs cover Drone as First Responder, automated inspection and site security. Dock for X10 positions Skydio X10 drones at a site so that missions launch remotely without anyone present. The smaller Skydio R10 puts eyes indoors before officers enter.

Skydio states that more than 1,500 public safety agencies use its drones. In a Drone as First Responder program, Skydio says its drones launch in under 20 seconds and reach incidents autonomously in under 90 seconds. DFR Command is the software from which remote operators launch and manage drones, respond to multiple calls and stream live video to patrol and command. It integrates with RapidSOS and CAD at dispatch, Axon Fusus for live operations, and automatic evidence upload into Axon Evidence. Skydio's customer stories include Brookhaven PD, which it says reached 30 second response times after deploying 8 Docks.

Skydio Site Security uses the same dock-based drones to verify alarms, patrol perimeters and deliver live visibility across a site. Video streams into Genetec or Milestone, and flights launch automatically when triggered by alarms or access control events. Skydio says its data is encrypted in transit and at rest and that it aligns to SOC 2, ISO 27001 and NIST frameworks.

quote.text: Skydio drone programs help even the most dangerous work get done safer, smarter, and faster through remote autonomous flight.

paragraphs: BRINC sells drone hardware, software and services built exclusively for public safety agencies and supported by one partner. The company was founded in response to the 2017 Las Vegas Shooting. An indoor tactical drone was developed over dozens of callouts with the Las Vegas Metro Police Department SWAT team.

The company's 911 response drone responds to calls 24/7/365 and covers 200 square miles. The site says calls for service can be cleared without dispatching a unit, so drones clear non-priority calls while agencies focus elsewhere. Drones can deliver Narcan, AEDs, EpiPens, cell phones and other equipment anywhere in seconds. For tactical use, a drone can enter dangerous places, generate floor plans mid-flight and de-escalate from a distance with two-way audio.

BRINC products are deployed by over 900 public safety agencies globally to initiate contact without force. The company states its drones are designed, supported and made in the USA and are NDAA, CJIS and SOC2 compliant. It offers help across a program's stages, from policy development and Part 107/COA work to training, staffing, maintenance and upgrades. BRINC opened a Seattle, WA headquarters to scale out engineering and manufacturing.

quote.text: BRINC offers a connected ecosystem of tools designed to save lives.

paragraphs: SoundThinking, Inc., listed on Nasdaq as SSTI, sells AI and data-driven public safety technology to law enforcement, civic leadership, and security professionals. Its ShotSpotter system detects and verifies gunfire incidents in near real time to support awareness and response. ShotSpotter is one part of the SafetySmart Platform, which the company says unifies gunfire alerts, vehicle intelligence, investigations, field awareness, and operational context in one place.

Alongside ShotSpotter, the platform includes CrimeTracer, a law enforcement search engine, and CaseBuilder, an investigation management system. ResourceRouter directs patrol and community anti-violence resources to where they will have the most effect. SafePointe screens entry points in high-traffic environments for weapons. PlateRanger connects vehicle sightings across time, location, and related events for investigators.

The company was founded as ShotSpotter in 1996 by physicist Dr. Robert Showen, who was then locating earthquake epicenters at the Stanford Research Institute in Menlo Park, California. After hearing gunshots in a nearby neighborhood, he applied the sound wave principles from his earthquake research to detecting and locating gunfire. Ralph Clark, hired as CEO in 2010, moved the system to a subscription rather than a capital hardware purchase. He also brought the human review of potential gunshots in-house through a centralized Incident Review Center. The gunshot detection service now serves over 170 cities. In 2023 the company rebranded from ShotSpotter to SoundThinking and launched the SafetySmart Platform. It reports more than 300 customers and work with approximately 2,100 agencies.

quote.text: Earn the trust of law enforcement to help them provide equal protection for all and strengthen the police-community relationship, ultimately improving public safety.

paragraphs: LiveView Technologies, known as LVT, sells rapidly deployable security units configured as mobile trailers, wall mounts, or pole mounts. The company says the units are used by DOTs, oil and gas operators, law enforcement, retailers, construction firms, and housing operators. Each mobile unit runs on its own, carrying solar panels, cellular and available satellite connectivity, lighting, a loud speaker, and a configurable selection of cameras. Pole-mounted versions instead take grid power for fixed coverage where infrastructure already exists.

The software side is a cloud platform reached from a phone or desktop, with a forensic search that sorts footage by keywords such as white car or crowd formation. From a mobile device an operator can zoom in, turn on the lights, and start speaker talk downs. A companion app called SafeNow lets employees set off floodlights, strobes, and audio warnings with one swipe.

On the public side, LVT lists remote monitoring of borders, government buildings, parks, school campuses, healthcare facilities, and military sites. The Arcadia Police Department added LVT Units to its operations for surveillance and crime prevention. Prologis put more than 70 LVT Units across industrial real estate properties in multiple states. LVT has been headquartered in Utah since 2005.

quote.text: Protecting critical infrastructure, government facilities, commercial properties, and all Fortune 100 retailers nationwide.

paragraphs: TRULEO sells software to law enforcement agencies that reads the databases a department already has and generates case solvability scores by connecting the dots and surfacing new leads. When a detective runs a name, jail calls, RMS, OSINT, body-worn camera footage and more than 140 sources are cross-referenced automatically. What comes back are investigative next steps, new leads and ranked case solvability scores.

The same platform writes shift and intelligence briefings for patrol and command, drafts policies and recommends resource allocation. Earlier press releases describe TRULEO as body-worn camera review software, adopted by agencies such as the Washtenaw County Sheriff's Office and the Queen Creek Police Department. The company states the platform is 100% made in the USA, FBI CJIS compliant, and included in the FBI National Academy curriculum in Quantico, Virginia.

A 2026 press release describes an on-premise AI agent platform used by hundreds of law enforcement agencies across the US. The CEO and co-founder serves on the board of the FBI National Academy Foundation and has spent his career building COMINT platforms for financial compliance, intelligence and public safety agencies. The CTO and co-founder, Tejas Shastry, holds a PhD from Northwestern University.

paragraphs: Kaiden AI sells AI simulation training software to law enforcement agencies and academies. The product turns an agency's policies and training standards into AI simulations, guided coaching, and evaluations that officers can complete anywhere. Agencies build scenarios, assign practice, and measure officer performance from one platform. The simulations use AI personas meant to cover the full range of people officers encounter in the field.

The company frames the product around the law enforcement training lifecycle. Recruits get more opportunities to practice communication, judgment, articulation, and policy application before the situations evaluated in the FTO program. For serving officers, scenarios cover policy changes, legal updates, emerging threats, and high-risk encounters, with a separate track for interviewing and investigative decision-making. Instructors can assign targeted practice based on documented performance gaps without adding role-player or instructor burden.

Testimonials on the site come from the Baltimore and Atlanta police departments; Lt. Jason Foore of Atlanta says recruits using Kaiden AI felt more confident during practical exercises. A blog post says the Baltimore Police Department has launched a pilot of Kaiden AI at the Baltimore Police Academy for academy and in-service programs. The company reports completing a SOC 2 Type 1 attestation to protect agency and trainee data. A January 2025 post announces a $1M pre-seed round.

Its core product is ePCR software built for how medics actually work, with AI-assisted documentation, configurable workflows, and real-time intelligence for agencies at any scale.

The platform connects scheduling, documentation, compliance, unified analytics, operational readiness, and hospital data exchange in one system. NEMSIS, NERIS, NTDB, and TQIP compliance is built into every workflow, with software filling and validating fields while staff review and confirm before submission. A scheduling product, ImageTrend Slate, addresses the demands of EMS, fire departments, and other critical services. It manages time-off requests, shift trades, and employee availability. Separate pre-plan software digitizes floor plans, hazard locations, water supply points, and utility shutoffs so responders have instant access to tactical data on scene.

The company reports 9,000 agencies, 43 state repositories, and more than a billion records processed. It says its sales engineering team is entirely former fire and EMS. It cites 24/7 US-based support and a 96.5% satisfaction rate, backed by 25 years in the field.

paragraphs: RapidSOS connects public safety agencies, enterprises and large numbers of consumer and corporate devices so emergency information reaches responders. The company states it partners with over 250 enterprise companies and 23,500 public safety agencies.

The premise is that connected systems can share information with responders even before a 911 call is placed. One police department describes adopting a module built around AI-powered live text translation, transcription and call summarization. In an Atlanta deployment, translation covered over 37 languages by voice and over 200 by text. Another center is described using Harmony AI to handle non-emergency calls.

The homepage says agencies and enterprises on the network safeguard over 99% of the country. Published case studies sort customers into categories such as connected vehicles and telematics. organizations.name: Carbyne
organizations.description: Cloud-native 911 call handling with live video, location, and AI triage

paragraphs: Carbyne builds and supports Axon 911 Core, a cloud-native infrastructure layer deployed in agencies across the United States and internationally. Its call-handling product, APEX, pulls call management capabilities into a single user interface for telecommunicators.

Patented live video lets responders see through the eyes of a caller. Location tools pinpoint a caller and track movement as permitted. AI-powered translation arrives directly on the call taker's screen. During call surges, an AI triage tool sorts through calls to identify redundant bystander and onlooker reports, freeing call takers for other emergencies. A continuity option has the AT&T Resolution Center redirect 911 calls and texts to devices running APEX Continuity. That reroute is triggered manually by the center rather than automatically.

The company states 99.999% call-handling uptime in the cloud. It describes the platform as providing the security of AWS GovCloud. Carbyne counts more than 100 partners and over 40 integrations on its open platform. The site names Orleans Parish Communication District as a center using its Emergency Call Triage.

Call-takers can also request a livestream from the caller to see the scene. A separate voice assistant answers non-emergency lines and converses with callers in English or Spanish.

Buyers are public safety answering points, the centers that take 911 calls. Prepared describes the product as a cloud based platform laid over existing systems, with no rip and replace required. Supervisors get automated quality assurance and keyword triggers for visibility into the operation. Its chief executive, Michael Chime, appears in a recorded discussion with three 911 leaders about non-emergency calls.

The company traces its origins to Dr. Paul Zoll, a physician who co-founded it in 1980. The history page lists the co-founders as Dr. Zoll, Leigh Stein and Thomas Claflin. paragraphs: Aurelian builds software for the 911 centers known as public safety answering points. One of its two products answers non-emergency calls instantly, so callers are not left on hold. The other sits with call-takers during emergencies and gives real-time, context-aware guidance without taking control.

The automated line resolves routine calls on its own. It detects and escalates emergencies to a person. During live calls, the guidance tool surfaces the relevant SOP checklist for the incident. It also flags missing information before the call ends. The company says the system learns a center's workflows, SOPs, and systems in order to support the full call flow. Aurelian states that humans remain in control of emergencies and decision-making.

The customers page says PSAPs around the country use Aurelian to cut non-emergency workload and return time to their teams. Published stories include Hamilton County 911 automating more than 300 non-emergency calls a day. The about page says the founders, Max and James, were building call automation technology for hair salons before starting the company. That insight led them to pivot to public safety and build for PSAPs.

organizations.description: AI robotic sorting systems for recycling facilities (MRFs)

paragraphs: AMP designs, builds, and operates facilities that sort single-stream recycling and municipal solid waste using artificial intelligence. The buyers are waste companies and municipalities, offered sortation services and automation at scale.

For municipal solid waste, AMP states that it operates the facility itself and charges a per-ton processing rate with guaranteed diversion. The company puts typical diversion above 60 percent. It says custom plants can be operational in less than a year. Recovery of target materials is put at more than 90 percent.

paragraphs: 120Water sells compliance software to public water utilities and to the state agencies that oversee them. The company describes one shared system that standardizes water data and requirements into reporting and community communications. The argument for it is that utilities and agencies otherwise track assets and water quality across disconnected tools, which hurts data integrity.

The platform gathers the programs and data a team needs to manage compliance from start to finish. That includes asset records and service line inventories, sampling schedules, lab results, resident communications, and program reporting. Programs run on it include service line inventories, monitoring, school and childcare sampling, backflow, consumer request sampling, and statewide 3Ts programs. It is built to fit an existing data ecosystem, with lab integrations and APIs for syncing locations, assets, and records. Most utility and state clients onboard in weeks, with the company handling data migration, configuration, and training.

Public water systems, state drinking water programs, schools, childcare facilities, and local governments are named as the customers. The company states that every module is built with current security standards and role-based permissions meant to meet or exceed state and federal program requirements. Its stated mission is to protect public health by giving communities confidence in their water. The chief executive came from the growth equity firm Edison Partners, which the about page names as the lead investor.

paragraphs: Klir sells compliance and operations software built for drinking water and wastewater utilities. The argument for it is that administration and paperwork take up more than half the working time of utility scientists, engineers and operators. The platform holds that work as centralized, accessible data in one place.

On the drinking water side it manages SDWA permit adherence from start to finish. For wastewater it manages NPDES permit adherence. Pretreatment teams track industrial user details, permits and data. Staff reach it anywhere through a cloud platform with mobile inspections and field data entry. It is described as configurable and compatible with a Microsoft Azure stack alongside LIMS, GIS and SCADA.

Co-founders David Lynch and Elaine Kelly met while working with European drinking water and wastewater utilities and regulators. The company says large water and wastewater organizations in the United States, Canada and Australia now use it to centralize and automate compliance reporting. The team has grown past 60 people across the United States, Canada, Brazil and Ireland. The company lists SOC 2 Type 2, ISO 27001 and NIST compliance, and sells directly, through the Microsoft Azure Marketplace or on cooperative contracts.

organizations.description: AI pipe-failure prediction for main replacement planning - exhibited at AWWA ACE 2026

paragraphs: VODA.ai sells decision support software to water utilities. The point is helping engineers decide which pipes to replace, assess, monitor or investigate next.

Projects start from data a utility already keeps, such as GIS records, pipe attributes, historical break records, work orders and service line information. Machine learning then flags pipes with an elevated likelihood of failure, including ones that have never broken. Utilities do not need clean records to begin. Initial model outputs, risk scores and prioritized watch lists are often available within three to six months. The same approach supports lead service line programs, sorting likely galvanized lines and prioritizing field verification before replacement work.

The company is Boston-based and was founded in 2017. It says it has worked in 31 states and eight countries and analyzed more than a million miles of pipe. Executives from 78 water utilities at the Smart Water Summit picked it as best smart water solution. Published case studies include lead compliance work in Rock Hill, South Carolina.

organizations.name: ASTERRA
organizations.description: Satellite-based leak detection and underground pipe assessment - exhibited at AWWA ACE 2026

paragraphs: ASTERRA sells insight into what lies beneath the ground, produced without breaking ground using patented algorithms and artificial intelligence to detect leaks. Water and wastewater utilities use it for leak detection to reduce non-revenue water and for analysis of potable and wastewater systems. The same approach maps excess soil moisture near or under dams, levees, roads, railways and mining operations.

The company images a customer's system with polarimetric synthetic aperture radar to sense and evaluate soil moisture. The same regions are revisited every few days or weeks as needed to monitor vast expanses. Results land in EO Discover, described as the repository for all insights from a customer's ASTERRA projects. There, detections, hotspots and network risk appear in a single view. MasterPlan scores pipe segments that show non-surfacing leaks and analyzes leak clusters over time. EarthWorks uses synthetic aperture radar to detect soil moisture up to 10 feet below the surface.

Field crews log investigation results, leak location and other data using U-Collect or the Esri ArcGIS Field Maps app. Within five minutes that reporting is available in EO Discover. The company ties EarthWorks, MasterPlan and Recover to the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals. MasterPlan is available in the Advise level of an ASTERRA Recover subscription.

ArcGIS is presented as enterprise technology that integrates and connects data through the context of geography. The premise is that hidden patterns, trends, and relationships emerge once data is visualized and analyzed on a map. Beyond maps and analysis, the company says its technology speeds data sharing and collaboration. For agencies that want to keep everything in house, there is a self-hosted edition for mapping, analytics, and data management.

Esri says it has supported customers with geographic science and geospatial analytics since 1969. Officials working in public safety, transportation, infrastructure, health and human services, and other fields use the technology to support high-level decisions. At the local level, the company says community leaders apply it to economic development, public works, and urban planning. Its cameras pair safety detections with video that managers can pull on demand. The company says the system watches for drowsiness, distraction, tailgating and forward collision risk. It states that these are caught in real time and trigger an in-cab alert before a manager is involved. A multicamera option adds up to four auxiliary HD feeds for visibility around the vehicle. A separate site product brings third-party cameras at facilities into a cloud dashboard for onboarding and troubleshooting.

The camera pages list transportation and logistics, field services, construction, public sector and essential services among the industries served. For school districts the company describes arm-mounted cameras that enforce school bus stop-arm compliance during pickups and drop-offs. paragraphs: Polco sells community engagement and analytics software to city and county governments, with a suite of tools organized around the work of local government departments. The platform is presented as a way to connect residents with the governments that serve them.

Residents use it to weigh in and to see how their own town is doing. On the government side the toolset spans community analytics, simulation and resident engagement. Officials can compare local results against national standards. An assistant called Polly reads survey responses, demographic shifts and economic indicators and pulls out community trends. A second agent, Grace, works on grant applications by finding funding opportunities and helping draft them.

The company puts its user base at more than a thousand communities. Cities, counties and other organizations make up that base. Polco says its AI is built only for local governments and public agencies rather than adapted from a general tool. It describes that work as grounded in decades of public administration research. The company also states that it does not sell user data.

paragraphs: Accela sells software that government agencies use to run permitting, licensing, and asset management from a single system. Its applications are built for individual government service workflows and can operate together or be deployed only where an agency needs them.

For building departments, intake, plan review, inspections, and permit issuance sit in one workflow rather than in separate disconnected steps. Reviewers from different departments work the same record at once, with annotations and approvals tracked as they happen. Planning teams get the same shared review model, plus automated public notice generation, hearing schedules, and agency notifications. Applicants can see where a case stands and receive consolidated feedback from every reviewing department.

The company says it has thirty years of government expertise built into the product. Testimonials on the site are attributed to municipal staff, including a chief building official in McAllen, Texas. Residents and businesses who encounter Accela through a local agency are directed to that agency rather than to the company.

paragraphs: Clariti sells community development software to local governments, pitched at any size and budget. One edition is permitting software for large local governments. A second, Launch, is aimed at small to mid-sized local governments. A third product, CivCheck, uses AI to guide applicants toward a complete and compliant submission and staff through every check.

The software keeps the permit counter online, where applicants apply, pay, and track status. It also tracks code violations from report to resolution, with automatic case assignment and links to local zoning and codes. Staff can build a report, adjust a page layout, or create a new permit type themselves. The large-jurisdiction edition runs on the Salesforce Platform, whose APIs let a government connect its other tools. Launch customers can copy a peer's permitting workflows using a cloning tool. On the AI side, staff have to approve every interpretation the software makes.

The company says the large-jurisdiction product was built with input from government customers over 16 years. Its home page names Los Angeles, Phoenix, and Orange County among the cities and counties using Clariti. Launch pricing is stated as based on population rather than user count.

paragraphs: GovWell sells software that city and county governments use to run permitting, licensing, planning, and code enforcement work. Residents and businesses use the same system to reach services, pay, and get answers outside office hours.

Permits, plan review, and inspections are handled together in one place for staff. Licensing runs online too, with applicants filing, paying, and renewing while staff keep records and approvals on their side. Code enforcement officers track cases, schedule inspections, and follow issues to closure. The company argues that AI can do real work in these processes, reviewing applications against local code, answering resident questions, flagging violations in plans, and routing inspections.

GovWell says it was founded by the son of a general contractor who watched his father struggle to get permits quickly. Its case for existing is that local governments cannot hire software engineers at competitive salaries. Deployment strategists and configuration tooling are meant to shorten implementations against older systems.

organizations.name: City Detect
organizations.description: AI cameras on city fleet vehicles detect blight, graffiti, dumping for code enforcement - exhibited at NLC City Summit 2026

paragraphs: City Detect sells a camera and software service that helps municipalities and counties find and address urban blight before complaints pile up. Cameras ride on a city's existing fleet vehicles and collect images of properties as those vehicles drive their normal routes. The company's PASS AI then detects and maps signs of urban blight and decay from the public right of way.

Roof-mounted data collection units capture street-level imagery during routine city operations. Once the images are processed, each detection is assigned a severity score from 1 to 4 and placed on an interactive map. The conditions it picks up run to illegal dumping, tire accumulations, snipe signs, and graffiti. Staff can export timestamped, image-backed reports in a few clicks.

The company says it was founded in 2021. One published case study describes Cathedral City partnering with City Detect in June 2025. For each municipality the company performs local calibration meant to cut false-positive detections and match local rules.

paragraphs: Holly sells an AI-powered classification and compensation platform for government human resources departments. It is built for HR teams that manage hundreds of classifications, compete for talent and negotiate pay.

The platform scores an existing job spec for clarity, completeness and equity, calling out outdated duties, dense sentences or qualifications that screen out strong candidates. Its similarity scoring compares actual job duties across more than 45,000 public sector roles rather than titles alone. Drafts move through subject matter expert, HR, management and final approval steps, with reviewers commenting the way they would in a shared document. Market data is turned into recommendations for council meetings and union negotiations.

The users are local government HR staff, and one published case study follows Long Beach, California, a port city of about 450,000 residents. Its workforce numbers roughly 6,000 employees across close to 350 civil service classifications. Holly was started by Brendan Hellweg and Cherie Chung, who met as graduate students at Harvard Business School and Harvard Kennedy School. The company says it is supported by J2 Ventures, Roble Ventures, Gaingels and angel investors.

paragraphs: CENTEGIX sells emergency alerting for schools, built around a solution called CrisisAlert that lets any staff member call for help. The alert carries the exact floor, room or hallway rather than just a building name.

When a full alert fires, strobes and intercoms activate across the campus. Arriving responders are shown the precise location of the person who pressed the button. The company is careful to say that most of what it handles is not an active shooter but a medical emergency, a behavioral crisis or a student leaving campus. Around the alerting sit other modules, including visitor management for authenticating and locating people on campus. Reunification is handled the same way, with a guardian verified before any student is handed over. Rollout starts with a short discovery call that maps buildings and looks for gaps in response.

School districts are the core audience, with the product framed as giving staff the confidence to act quickly. The same technology is offered to healthcare organizations facing workplace violence. A third line is aimed at public servants and the staff who work alongside them. The company says the product was built by former educators, law enforcement officers and caregivers. It also convenes an invitation-only customer advisory board drawn from senior safety leaders.

paragraphs: ZeroEyes sells threat detection software that runs on the security cameras a site already has, spotting visible firearms, knives and intruders in real time. The company aims it at schools, businesses and communities.

Once verified, alerts go to designated personnel and law enforcement. Beyond firearms, the platform covers knife detection, intrusion, left-behind objects and obstructed cameras. Analysts staff the operations center around the clock.

The company says it was founded in 2018 by a team of Navy SEALs and technologists after the Marjory Stoneman Douglas school active shooter incident. Its stated mission is to end mass shootings in America. Many of its analysts have law enforcement and military backgrounds. The site says it protects schools, campuses and facilities in U.S. states. It reports over five million images used to train its weapon recognition models.

A therapy service connects students with licensed mental health professionals for weekly teletherapy sessions. A round-the-clock service called ReachOut gives students direct access to confidential care whenever they need support. An archiving product stores files and communications in one searchable, cloud-based system so districts can meet compliance obligations.

It describes itself as the pioneer in helping K-12 districts manage student safety on school-provided technology. The home page puts its reach at over 1,500 K-12 districts, and one case study describes a district choosing the therapy service to meet growing student mental health needs.

Alongside the software, an advisory group takes on the questions districts face away from the keyboard, such as reducing transportation costs. That group is staffed with former district transportation directors and data analysts. Its work covers bell-time optimization, district policy and contract analysis, demographics and redistricting, and operational assessments.

Edulog states that it created the first routing and planning software for school districts more than forty years ago. By its own account, its client districts run from as few as 57 students to as many as 1.8 million. It reports work with districts and transportation providers across 49 US states and four Canadian provinces.

Teaching and learning products sit alongside it, among them a learning management system. For the central office, finance, human resources, and operations are brought into one connected system. A separate data practice centralizes information that would otherwise sit in district silos.

PowerBuddy, the company's AI assistant, is described as built for students, families, teachers, and administrators. It is also pitched at IT staff and data analysts working with district data. PowerSchool states that PowerBuddy won a 2024 GESS Education Award. In districts already using its products, the company says teachers are reclaiming at least 10 hours a week.

Cross-Site Enrollment lets a student take a class at another school in the district, or at another district in the same state that uses the system. Business-side tools help district leaders track key areas so they can understand spending and oversee district resources. District data is monitored around the clock in five physically and geographically secure datacenters in the United States and Canada. organizations.name: Clever Devices
organizations.description: Bus ITS: CAD/AVL, real-time passenger info, and fleet health

paragraphs: Clever Devices builds technology for public transportation providers, meant to help them run more efficiently, spend less and deliver the service riders expect. The company says agencies with anywhere from 50 to 5,000 vehicles have chosen it over more than thirty years.

At the center is CAD/AVL software that gives dispatchers real-time information to monitor and manage the fleet. A vehicle health monitoring product is aimed at cutting repair costs and stretching the mean distance between failures. Onboard, automated passenger announcements are synced with LED signage so riders know where they are. Service planning is handled by the MAIOR scheduling suite, a modular set of planning and optimization tools. For agencies that would rather not run servers, CleverCloud takes on the on-premises hosting burden.

The company tells an unusual origin story, beginning in the early 1980s in the basement of a bar on Long Island. It turned to transit in 1990 when the Americans with Disabilities Act passed. The first product automated the stop announcements bus drivers were required to make. Today the company reports over 600 employees across 12 locations in the United States, Canada, Brazil and Italy. It puts more than 30,000 vehicles on its transportation systems technology. The homepage announces that Hitachi Rail has completed its acquisition of the company.

One platform covers everything from planning and scheduling to real-time depot operations and sharing information with drivers and passengers. Planning tools let a team plan, analyze, and optimize a network to improve service quality and performance. The scheduling side creates optimal crew and vehicle schedules. Optibus Agent runs inside the platform, connected to real operational data and built around real workflows. That agent is included for all customers at no additional cost.

organizations.name: Swiftly
organizations.description: Real-time transit data: arrival predictions and on-time performance

paragraphs: Swiftly sells a cloud platform to public transit agencies for sharing real-time passenger information, running daily operations, and improving service performance. The company puts its customer count above 200 agencies. Those agencies are described as large and small, around the globe.

The platform combines GTFS schedule data with whatever real-time vehicle location feed an agency already has. It then analyzes billions of data points to say where a vehicle was, where it is, and where it will be next. Operations staff use it to make real-time adjustments for on-time performance and headway adherence. Schedulers work from actual run times, vehicle speeds, and dwell times. APIs push the same data out to rider-facing apps, vehicle hardware, and internal tools.

Customer service teams are another audience, answering rider questions from the same information. The site carries comments from transit staff, including an operations technology lead at the MBTA in Boston. Another comes from a transportation planner at MDOT MTA in Baltimore. Jonny Simkin co-founded the company and is its chief executive. Swiftly describes itself as a transit reliability platform meant to keep public transportation a fast and attractive alternative to the private vehicle.

organizations.name: Dimonoff
organizations.description: Streetlight control nodes and SCMS smart-city management platform for municipalities and utilities

paragraphs: Dimonoff sells smart street lighting control, connecting street and commercial lighting to a single platform so teams can monitor every fixture in real time. The site dates its work in smart street lighting control back to 2006.

A controller fits a NEMA or Zhaga socket on any LED fixture, from any manufacturer, and dims over 0-10V or DALI. The nodes network over Wi-SUN, RF mesh or LTE-M, and keep running their schedule if the link drops. In the office, one interface holds groups, schedules, dimming profiles, faults and reports, and pushes work orders into the asset system a city already runs. The platform also manages nodes from third-party manufacturers, so hardware from a previous supplier does not have to be scrapped. One part number covers supply voltages from 110 to 480 Vac nominal at 50/60 Hz. Node firmware is updated over the air rather than by a crew in a truck.

Networks already running on the platform account for more than 219,500 connected endpoints, by the company's count. Dimonoff states that all of its hardware and software is designed, developed, manufactured and supported in North America. The support FAQ names Groupe Vectanor as the parent company and says it joined the Wi-SUN Alliance as a Contributing Member in April 2026.

It puts its accumulated deployment experience at more than 90 million field hours. paragraphs: AiDASH sells software that electric utilities use to find vegetation, asset, wildfire and storm risk before it takes the grid down. The method starts with continuous satellite monitoring, then adds targeted aerial, vehicle-mounted and on-demand inspection.

Very high resolution satellite passes refresh vegetation health data up to twelve times a year. Higher-cadence imagery tracks fuel load, moisture and burnability up to seven times a week. One system covers asset inspection and monitoring. Another handles wildfire situational awareness and risk mitigation. A storm system predicts outages 120 hours ahead so crews can be pre-positioned. The platform exposes REST APIs for automation or for integrating with systems a utility already runs.

The company says it was founded by serial entrepreneurs in 2019. Its about page claims more than 150 customers of every size around the world. The platform page states SOC 2 Type 2 certification. A news item on the site announces that Schneider Electric agreed to acquire AiDASH for $350 million.

It also states that the platform is HIPAA and FERPA compliant. Plans start at $355 per month. Onboarding, training, support and compliance are included in every plan, according to the pricing section. The assistant runs in a closed environment, retrieving verified information only from content the agency has approved. It answers in more than 75 languages and is available around the clock. The company says the platform is meant to sit alongside the software an agency already runs.

Citibot works with local governments from small towns to large cities. The customer page puts the count at more than 200 governments. Much of the use sits with 311 centers and call-heavy departments, where residents can get answers and submit requests without picking up the phone. The company describes over a decade of work behind the platform.

quote.text: For 311 centers and call-heavy departments, Citibot helps residents get answers, submit requests, and connect with the right resources without always needing to pick up the phone.

organizations.name: Indigov
organizations.description: Constituent CRM for elected officials: casework, correspondence, engagement (acquired by Granicus, 2025)

paragraphs: Indigov gives government officials, agencies, and their staff a constituent relations tool for responding and reaching out. It works with officials across the country, at all levels of government. The United States Congress appears among the bodies served.

The platform pulls inquiries from across an office's channels into one place to answer. A separate outreach product supplies resident information along with the tools to contact them. For casework, a team can manage and track activity, give the constituent status updates, and resolve requests. A live dashboard shows how often people reach out, which issues they care about, and how quickly staff respond.

The company says its clients span 35 states and 2 territories. It states that the platform has already cut average response time from months to minutes or hours. Its mission page calls the category an operating system for representative democracy.

Agencies run surveys, voting, mapping and budgeting in one place rather than across separate departmental tools. Input gathered in person can be digitized, and speech can be converted to text. AI features are offered to organize responses and to build reports that can be shared with stakeholders.

The about page describes a global team of more than 50 local experts working with over 500 local governments and organisations across 20 countries. The company was founded in Belgium under the name CitizenLab, and its first pilot project was with the city of Hasselt. It describes itself as a B Corp certified SaaS company. Published case studies cover work with local governments in North America and Europe, including a participatory budgeting programme in Toronto Centre.

The service works by getting large samples of representative residents to answer professionally designed questions. It reaches those residents by email, text and phone. Results are reported 48 hours after a survey launches. To keep outsiders from skewing the numbers, the system filters results by physical addresses.

The company says it works with local governments in more than 30 states. Its customers are described as counties, cities, towns and special districts. FlashVote is the first good-government service offered by the Governance Sciences Group.

paragraphs: EffiGov builds AI phone agents for local government. Every department gets its own agent, trained on that department's own services, hours, and escalation rules. The buyers are cities, counties, and special districts.

Agents hand a call to each other, or to a person, with the conversation carried forward. Before a resident is connected to staff, the agent briefs that staff member out loud. The agents plug into municipal systems of record, so a call resolves against live data instead of a script. A reported problem becomes a tracked record, with a reference number read back on the call. No phone system is replaced: a government forwards its existing lines to a number EffiGov manages.

The company says it is live in production across four states. Its homepage counts more than 12,000 calls in a single month, with 72 percent handled without staff. EffiGov states that a SOC 2 Type II audit is in progress. It claims zero data retention with its AI model provider and US-based data. The site says the company is backed by Y Combinator.

paragraphs: Common Sense sells AI building blocks for local government, aimed at the administrative work that piles up in agencies. The modules cover public records and meeting management, with more beyond those two. Each module is meant to fit an agency's existing setup and account for the policies and laws that apply to it.

On records requests, the software triages, processes, and responds to incoming requests with full audit trails. It searches document management, email, and IT systems to find responsive records instead of asking each department to dig through its own files. Integrations named include Laserfiche, OnBase, Outlook, and Gmail. Redactions are prepared by the software, but staff review and approve them before documents go out. A second module runs the entire council meeting preparation process. After a meeting it drafts a plain summary of what was discussed and decided. A third module, Composer, builds workflow systems from a description written in plain English.

The departments named as users run from police and fire to the city clerk, legal, public works, and finance. The company says it is SOC 2 Type II certified and built for public-sector compliance. It states that the meeting product is co-built with the City of Peachtree Corners, Georgia and Starbase, Texas.

paragraphs: AchieveIt sells software for moving a written plan into measurable progress. It pitches itself to public agencies and other organizations that find performance hard to measure. The idea behind it is connecting people, plans and data in one place.

A plan is structured to match whatever methodology a customer already uses, from pillars and objectives down to initiatives, KPIs and milestones. Update requests then go out on a chosen cadence, asking owners for status, percent complete, commentary and metric values that flow into dashboards and roll-up reports. A tree view shows how each item in a plan lines up with the rest. Custom dashboards can display information drawn from any plan in the organization. A multi-plan view lets a customer filter, segment and drill into progress across everything at once.

AchieveIt says strategy consultants and customer success managers work alongside each customer. Onboarding, training and hands-on help come with the move away from manual tracking. The site sorts prospects by sector so a buyer can see how the software fits their way of working. One page groups its public sector claims under a heading about proven results.

quote.text: Plans look good on paper. AchieveIt makes sure they move forward, with the tools to manage, track, and deliver results.

Plans can be laid out as a cascade, a Gantt chart, tags or scorecards, depending on how the organization works. Staff get scheduled reminders to submit progress and performance updates. Those updates roll up automatically into reports covering actions, projects, measures and narrative. The same material feeds public dashboards a community can read. Every package includes unlimited users.

More than 200 organizations use Envisio, by the company's count. Example dashboards on the site include the City of Rockville's climate action plan, which tracks emissions reduction and renewable energy adoption. The company frames its purpose around a stated decline in trust in public institutions. It points to recognition as a GovTech 100 company. Chief executive Craig Ross was previously interim CEO at Euna Solutions and CEO of eCivis.

paragraphs: SOVRA sells procurement software to public agencies, covering the process from an identified need through the contract lifecycle. The other side of the business serves suppliers looking for government work.

Requests arrive through intelligent forms where AI suggests inputs and asks follow-up questions. Solicitations reach suppliers through automated bid alerts keyed to commodity codes. Evaluation teams score responses with sealed-bid enforcement and audit tracking in place. Awarded work moves into contract drafting from flexible, pre-approved templates.

The contract page says over 7,000 public sector entities across North America use it. Named user types run from cities and counties to school boards and healthcare networks. The homepage claims a network of more than one million suppliers connected to thousands of government buyers. Supplier support is handled by a team the sourcing page puts at more than 100 employees.

paragraphs: Avila sells an AI grant platform aimed at local government. The site says it finds the opportunities an agency qualifies for and writes its proposals. It also says it helps governments, schools and nonprofits discover and apply for funding.

Discovery matches state, local, regional and foundation opportunities to a customer's own projects. For applications, the platform simplifies dense notices of funding opportunity into clearer requirements. It fills in federal forms including SF-424, SF-424A, SF-LLL and program-specific attachments. Once an award lands, it ingests invoices and auto-categorizes expenses against the approved budget. It also flags compliance issues against 2 CFR 200 and the awarding agency's rules.

Users named on the site include the Houston-Galveston Area Council. One case study describes a mid-sized county government in the western U.S. Another describes a statewide public university system in the northeast. The company states that it is SOC 2 compliant. It says all data is encrypted in transit and at rest. The about page says NVIDIA Inception, Microsoft for Startups and MongoDB have welcomed the company into their programs.

A library of more than 60 ready-made reports covers enrollment, engagement and compliance. Self-service enrollment handles active employees, retirees and COBRA participants.

Bentek says it was founded to serve public sector organizations. The company says its story began in 2006. It started when a local school district struggled to manage its benefits. The company puts its experience in the public sector environment at more than 20 years. It says it serves more than 300 employers in the public sector. One story on the site describes helping the Government of the U.S. Virgin Islands transform its benefits administration in four months.

Alerts go out by email, push notification, SMS, text-to-speech, voice call and social media from one place. paragraphs: RollKall sells an off-duty work management platform with separate experiences for law enforcement agencies, officers, and the clients who hire them. Agencies post off-duty jobs with requirements and compliance rules, and officers are matched based on eligibility, availability, and department policy. Invoices are generated from clock-in and clock-out data, payments are routed to officers, and 1099s are handled digitally. An agency can run the platform itself or have RollKall run it as a managed service.

Officers use a mobile app to browse available shifts, view pay rates and locations, accept jobs, and clock in and out from their phones. Payment options include WeeklyPay, PrePay, and InstantPay, which lets officers access earnings immediately after completing a job. Clients and vendors request officers through a branded client portal with approval workflows, automated invoicing, and electronic payment processing. The company reports 85%+ officer adoption within the first 30 days across its deployments.

Published case studies cover the Irving Police Department and the Paulding County Sheriff's Office. Testimonials on the site come from the Cincinnati Police Department, the Prince George's County Police Department, the Randall County Sheriff's Office, and the St. Charles County Police Department.

quote.text: Our mission is to empower the agencies, coordinators, and off-duty public safety professionals who protect and support their communities every day.

paragraphs: Fonroche Lighting America designs and sells off-grid solar lighting for streets and roadways, parking lots, parks, pathways, campuses and other public infrastructure. The range runs from SmartLight solar streetlights to NOWATT solar bollards and solar studs.

Because each system operates independently of the grid, a project can skip underground cabling and utility connections. Pre-wired modular power centers hold the energy storage. The company says a crew can install and activate a lighting system in under an hour. Designs begin with an analysis of ten years of local solar data using the PVsyst software suite and Meteonorm historical irradiation data. Once installed, the lights can be monitored remotely through a wireless network called Fonroche Connect.

The systems are built for municipalities, tribal communities, federal campuses, developers and commercial properties. Case studies describe Augusta, Georgia, which addressed safety and budget problems on Windsor Spring Road by deploying 42 autonomous solar streetlights. In Rowlett, Texas, the city is installing 425 solar-powered SmartLights across a 5.5-mile stretch of three corridors. The American business took its present form when Fonroche Lighting acquired SolarOne Solutions and incorporated Fonroche Lighting America. The site invites visitors to join 1,000+ communities and businesses already using its lighting.

organizations.description: Aerial imagery and property data analytics for county assessors, GIS, and insurers - exhibited at IAAO 2026

paragraphs: EagleView sells aerial imagery and property data drawn from an archive the company puts at more than 3.5 billion high-resolution images. Public agencies are one audience, with the imagery aimed at tax assessment, zoning enforcement, emergency response and infrastructure planning.

The subscription imagery product refreshes annually at 2-inch resolution, with an option to upgrade. The company says its 1-inch imagery carries nine times more detail than 3-inch imagery. Captures include straight-down orthogonal views for mapping and measurement and angled oblique views of building sides. A separate archive holds more than 25 years of imagery covering 96 percent of the United States population. New content is added daily, with annual refreshes across metro areas and high-growth regions. Customers view imagery in a browser tool or pull it through API connections into GIS, CAD, CAMA or analytics systems.
The site states that 20 of the top 20 insurers rely on the company. Governments, insurers, utilities, AEC firms and environmental professionals are named as users of the imagery archive.

paragraphs: three+one sells liquidity analysis to public finance offices, showing them when and for how long their cash can be put to work. The firm presents itself as an operation created by public officials for public officials.

Its cashVest program produces weekly cash balance projections as a complement to traditional cash-flow forecasting. It gives a consolidated view of how much cash is available and how long each dollar can work before it is needed. Banking services and fees are analyzed to keep the relationship equitable. Marketplace and peer-interest benchmarks are offered so an office can gauge the value of its cash. A dedicated team works on liquidity-management strategy as an objective, third-party data provider.

Published case studies describe county and city finance offices, among them Suffolk County, New York, which the site says began using cashVest to complement its cash-management, finance and audit departments. Another says Westmoreland County, Pennsylvania, partnered with the company in 2017. A separate product, the rfpPrep digital portal, is described as a way to issue an investment services RFP. The company also states that it is a national partner of NACo Financial Services Corporation.

quote.text: Created by Public Officials for Public Officials.

organizations.name: GovPilot
organizations.description: Cloud permitting, licensing, code enforcement, and GIS workflows for local governments - exhibited at GFOA 2026

paragraphs: GovPilot sells cloud-based management software to municipal and county government departments. The pitch is to put a government's data and its departments on a single platform. Local governments of all sizes have deployed it.

A government picks the modules it needs, then unifies data across departments and lets residents report concerns, apply, pay and track requests online. The catalog runs to more than 125 templated digital modules, with mobile apps and a GIS map on the same cloud platform. A parcel-level view called PropertyProfile shows records held by different departments about the same property. Two mobile apps, GovAlert and GovInspect, accompany the digital forms and automated workflows.

Case studies on the site cover work such as building and construction permitting. Short-term rental property registration is another documented use. Pricing is set by population and by the number of modules a government selects. The company says it has been named a GovTech 100 company for eight consecutive years. It also points buyers to its Capterra reviews from government users.

quote.text: Say goodbye to paper forms and single-purpose software.

paragraphs: Elation Systems sells labor compliance software to government agencies, non-profits and private organizations. Its core product automates the tracking, monitoring and enforcement of federal Davis-Bacon and local prevailing wage projects.

Certified payroll data collection and prevailing wage certifications are processed automatically, which the company says spares contractors and subcontractors any administrative burden. The same module handles electronic fringe benefits statement reporting. A separate component automates reporting and monitoring for the business utilization programs of federal, state and local municipalities, covering DBE, MWBE and SBE certifications. Another module gives clients a secure, web-based and electronic Section 3 reporting and monitoring process. An OCIP and CCIP component automates on-site payroll reporting and monitoring tied to workers' compensation insurance on applicable projects.

The company says it launched the first SaaS-based Davis-Bacon, labor and contract compliance management system more than ten years ago. It describes support staff with 15 or more years of experience in the industries it now assists. Alongside agencies, the site points to support for the contractors and subcontractor companies doing the building.

quote.text: Whether you’re a government agency, a non-profit, or a private organization, we have the tools you need to fulfill your labor compliance requirements.

organizations.description: Citizen identity and digital service portals (CitizenOne) plus digital trust/signatures (Notarius)

paragraphs: Portage CyberTech sells digital identity, electronic signature and verification software to governments and to organizations working under regulation. The company says its solutions can be used on their own or combined with its own or third-party products to build end-to-end systems.

CitizenOne is the identity and access management product, built for the needs of governments, municipalities and the public sector. From a single account, residents can register for and reach services such as permits, payments, renewals, licenses or benefits. They can also manage how their personal information is shared with different departments. On the signature side, CertifiO certifies a signer's identity, professional affiliation or the existence of an organization. ConsignO Cloud is the web platform that carries internal and external signing projects through the whole cycle.

The company describes 25 years of helping people in regulated professions protect their professional identity online. For CertifiO it cites over 60,000 professionals in Canada. For CitizenOne it says the product today supports millions of citizens, professional associations, and dozens of governments and municipalities. A footnote states that certifications are held by Notarius Solutions Inc., a Portage CyberTech company.

paragraphs: Meridian Knowledge Solutions sells a learning management system built for government and enterprise organizations. The platform supports compliance training, employee onboarding, extended enterprise learning and e-commerce.

Compliance tracking is automated, and learners can view statuses, download certificates and monitor their progress. In-person and virtual learning can be combined so that participants take part together regardless of location. Reporting runs through dashboards, detailed reports and scheduled data exports. Buyers can adjust settings, workflows, branding and user interfaces without altering the underlying code. For more specialized requirements the development team can extend or modify capabilities at the code level.

The named markets are federal, state and local governments alongside healthcare, manufacturing, financial services, associations and public safety. The platform is described as FedRAMP 20x Class C Certified. The company also states that the product is built and supported in the United States. Security controls listed include role-based access controls, data encryption and secure cloud hosting. A customer video on the solutions page features Johnson Controls scaling training across the business.

organizations.description: Recruiting platform translating gov job classifications and matching candidates to state/local roles

paragraphs: GovSkills runs a hiring platform that sits between people who want public service work and the agencies trying to fill those jobs. Applicants pay nothing, and agencies are quoted separately.

The core of the service is translation: dense government postings are turned into wording an ordinary applicant can actually parse. Agencies keep their existing documents, since the platform handles that mapping for them. Matching reads a full resume against a full job description rather than scanning for individual keywords. Listings span city, county, state and federal employers.

The intended audience includes people with no prior government background who find public sector requirements hard to decode. On the hiring side it addresses agencies and associations of any size. The about page lists a small team of founders, a product designer and an engineer, and describes the business as a venture of Citizen Codex.

organizations.name: Bamboo Health
organizations.description: Care coordination and PDMP network software (PMP AWARxE, OpenBeds) for states, counties, and health systems (Appriss lineage)

paragraphs: Bamboo Health sells software that joins behavioral and physical health data into a longitudinal patient record and places it inside the systems clinicians already work in. Its audiences include community and behavioral health providers and federally qualified health centers. Accountable care organizations and other provider groups are addressed separately.

Alerts are driven by admission, discharge and transfer feeds, and care navigation can be started from inside an electronic health record. For people with substance use disorder, prescription drug monitoring program data and alerts are used to flag risk and guide patients toward care. Care navigators also review rosters by hand to find high utilizers whose behavioral health needs have gone unmet. Behavioral health referrals and crisis resource availability sit alongside that history in one place.

The company took its present form in 2021, when Appriss Health acquired PatientPing and rebranded. It claims a footprint across 52 states and territories. Encounters on its network are put at 3 billion a year. Published material points to work with the State of Delaware on crisis care and behavioral health coordination.

quote.text: Bamboo Health now delivers powerful patient clarity during pivotal moments through Real-Time Care Intelligence™ solutions.

paragraphs: Unite Us sells software and data infrastructure for coordinating whole-person care across healthcare, government and community-based organizations. Its named audiences include public health and human services agencies. Managed care and Medicaid plans are also on that list.

The core product is a closed-loop referral system for sending and receiving electronic social care referrals within a network of community partners. Staff can run social needs screenings, after which the platform automatically suggests resources or referrals. A secure chat feature lets users at partner organizations message each other about shared referrals, cases and clients. Integrations let organizations share resources and send referrals without leaving their own system.

Alongside referrals, the company sells predictive analytics meant to predict long-term risks and measure impact. Its Population Insights tool combines social, economic, environmental and health information with modeling to identify at-risk populations. It also automates payments to community-based organizations. The company states that it partnered with Presbyterian Health Plan to create New Mexico's first statewide closed-loop referral system.

organizations.name: ES&S (Election Systems & Software)
organizations.description: The largest US voting systems vendor: tabulators, ballot marking, election management (founded as AIS)

paragraphs: ES&S has supplied election systems since 1979, describing them as secure, accessible and accurate. By its own account the systems are paper based, certified and fully auditable. They are sold to jurisdictions large and small.

The catalog includes ballot marking devices and tabulators. The DS950 handles Election Day, absentee and early vote ballots. On the ExpressVote, voters insert a card to activate the voting session, and the ballot is then dispensed for voter review. That device supports any language in audio and more than 30 languages in text. The ExpressVote XL displays the full ballot on a 32-inch interactive screen and produces an independent voter-verifiable paper record. Paired with an electronic pollbook, a polling place can check in voters and serve up to 15,000 different ballot styles. The ExpressVote 3 uses Secure Boot and application allowlisting to verify that only the certified operating system, software and firmware are on the unit.

ES&S says it has 31 voting systems certified by the U.S. Election Assistance Commission. It describes partnering with the Department of Homeland Security on industry practices. The company presents itself as part of the American Council for Election Technology. Its latest average rating by customers on overall satisfaction is given as 4.63 out of 5.

quote.text: America’s elections are a shared responsibility.

organizations.name: Hart InterCivic
organizations.description: Verity voting systems: tabulation, ballot marking, and election management for counties

paragraphs: Hart InterCivic sells voting systems and election services to the officials who run elections. In one configuration, voters mark a paper ballot with a pen and the ballot is scanned to capture the vote digitally. A hybrid option combines touchscreen voting with a voter-verifiable paper trail. Absentee and mail ballots are handled through central scanning.

On the paper-based products, voter choices are never encoded in a digital seal for tabulation. Products carry role-based controls meant to keep an election transparent end to end. The company announced certification of a newer product line, Vanguard, to the VVSG 2.0 standard by the Election Assistance Commission. Within that line, Flex is a universal ballot marking device. Vault handles the scanning of ballots, whether marked by hand or by machine. Workspace covers end-to-end election management.

Hart says it has worked side by side with election professionals for more than 100 years. Its regional offices span coast to coast. The company also states that Vanguard is the only voting system available in the United States that delivers on both the latest EAC standard and the conditions of the executive order it cites.

quote.text: Election Integrity starts with Hart.
