organizations.name: Aurigo Software
organizations.description: Masterworks capital program and construction management for DOTs, cities, water, and transit

paragraphs: Aurigo Software sells capital program management software to government agencies that plan, build and maintain public infrastructure. It also serves facility owners in areas such as data centers, life sciences, manufacturing, and energy and utilities. The company's platform, Masterworks, brings planning, execution, financials, right of way and analytics together in one system.

On the delivery side it coordinates contracts, schedules, costs and field work so teams can hold to the original plan and keep a complete audit trail. Compliance, funding transparency and governance are meant to sit inside everyday work so public money stays accountable. Agencies can change forms, workflows, business rules and dashboards through configuration rather than code. An AI layer called Lumina supports decision-making with compliance and governance built in, and the company says every insight and recommendation it produces can be audited and traced.

Cities, counties, transit agencies and transportation departments across North America use the platform to manage capital programs, replace legacy systems and automate federal reimbursements. The company claims more than 300 customers and over 20 years of capital program expertise behind the product. It also says the software monitors project signals to catch cost, schedule and delivery risks before they turn critical.

quote.text: Every capital decision carries public consequences.

organizations.name: FASTER (Transit Technologies)
organizations.description: FASTER Web fleet maintenance and management, the government fleet standard

paragraphs: FASTER sells fleet management and asset maintenance software as one platform. The public sector is the core audience, built for municipalities, school systems, transit, and utilities.

Coverage runs from acquisition planning through disposal of an asset. Day to day, that means automated preventive maintenance scheduling, real-time parts tracking, and streamlined work orders. Managers track total cost of ownership, downtime, and utilization by vehicle, department, or fleet. A customer portal lets vehicle users request repairs online, view repair history, and manage appointments.

The company says more than 400 organizations manage over one million assets on FASTER across North America. Those customers include city governments, universities, utilities, public works departments, and private fleet operators. The site claims over 40 years of helping organizations run safer, smarter, and more efficiently. It describes itself as a US-based company with US-based product, engineering, and support teams. The homepage also lists SOC 2 compliant security and data protection. FASTER is part of Transit Technologies.

paragraphs: Motive sells fleet software and hardware as one integrated suite built around AI. The buyers are commercial fleets, which the company describes as ranging from five or ten vehicles up to companies running thousands of them.

On the safety side, cameras and AI flag more than twenty kinds of event on the road. High-confidence events go straight to managers, while a safety team reviews the low-confidence ones to remove false positives. Vehicle tracking uses real-time GPS with traffic updates and weather overlays for route planning. Compliance work such as electronic logs, driver qualification, IFTA and CSA sits in the same platform. Equipment monitoring shows what share of the time an asset is in use and how long it sits dormant. Telematics from various equipment manufacturers is centralized in a single platform.

The company points to operations running from waste services to construction. It says it was named number one in fleet management across every segment. It also cites top rankings for equipment monitoring in G2 asset tracking reports for summer 2026. Its fleet card is issued by Sutton Bank under a license from Mastercard International.

paragraphs: Powerfleet sells software and connected devices that pull fleet and warehouse operations into a single system it calls Unity. Buyers connect the vehicles running on the road along with the equipment moving goods inside a building.

The platform gathers readings from IoT devices, manufacturer systems and outside feeds, then turns them into compliance records for hours of service, inspections, temperature and driver qualifications. On the safety side, cameras watch road conditions while sensors inside the warehouse follow pedestrian proximity, equipment impacts and how operators behave. A separate set of tools collects the fuel and emissions figures a sustainability team has to report. The company points to an open API and packaged integrations rather than a rip-out of what a buyer already runs.

Powerfleet states that its headquarters sit in New Jersey. It describes a partner network and a physical footprint spanning more than a hundred countries. Technical staff are put at 450 people working around the globe.

paragraphs: Forward Thinking Systems sells fleet management technology that puts vehicle tracking, cameras, compliance, routing, driver coaching and asset management on one platform. The product itself is a browser-based console for an entire fleet.

Vehicle and driver data arrives in real time, including location, speed, ignition status and hours-of-service duty status. More than sixty built-in reports break that data down by fleet, vehicle and driver. The camera product saves footage automatically when it detects behavior such as distracted driving, hard braking or texting. A driver-facing app lets drivers watch their own scorecard, review those events, and dispute the ones they consider inaccurate. Routing is handled by a separate optimization tool for building efficient multi-stop routes.

Government and public sector fleets are one of the segments the company addresses. For those buyers it points to real-time GPS built for emergency operations. Asset tracking extends past vehicles to trailers, heavy equipment and containers. The software also integrates with fuel card providers named on the site.

paragraphs: Azuga sells GPS fleet tracking and dual-facing dashcam software meant to keep vehicles, assets and drivers safe. The company argues that such software should improve safety and not only day-to-day operations. It pitches the product as simple to use, affordable, customizable, and easy to install.

The company frames the work as a four-part improvement process folded into daily fleet operations. Driver scoring is meant to show managers and drivers alike how safely they are driving. A mobile app included in the subscription gives administrators and drivers separate views. For tools and small equipment, Bluetooth beacons are picked up by the company's cellular asset trackers. One tracker can detect and report on fifty beacons at a time. Vehicles that leave the factory with built-in telematics can connect to the platform without aftermarket hardware.

Azuga says customers have relied on it since 2013 for GPS fleet tracking and asset tracking. Insurance companies use its telematics data to measure and price risk in commercial vehicle portfolios. The company also says it works with government agencies on how transportation taxes, emissions data and tolls are collected. States and municipalities, it states, use the data to understand traffic patterns and road surface conditions.

paragraphs: AtomAI Solutions sells a suite of software that agencies use to manage assets, work orders, project and utility coordination, permitting, and safety. Its two flagship products are Atom, an asset and maintenance management platform, and Coordinate, formerly dotMaps, a right-of-way and project coordination tool used by state and local agencies across the country.

Work templates can be defined by each agency so that task structures, fields, and workflows match its own operational processes. Forms built inside the platform can include required fields, dropdowns, conditional logic, and photo or video uploads. Every work order records labor hours, equipment usage, and materials consumed, either automatically or through entry in the field. Templated reports are meant to meet compliance and reporting requirements from agencies such as the FHWA, FRA, and EPA.

The company began as an internal startup within SADA Systems Inc. The full team and product suite divested in early 2023 to form AtomAI Solutions, Inc. as an independent company. Since then it has expanded its offerings to include a permitting solution built specifically for state and local governments.

organizations.name: Blyncsy
organizations.description: AI detection of pavement markings and road defects from crowdsourced dashcams (Bentley Systems)

paragraphs: Blyncsy helps cities and state departments of transportation automate their roadway maintenance and asset inventory activities. Rather than sending crews out to look, it works from crowd-sourced dash camera imagery.

Machine learning algorithms and image processing applied to that imagery detect where and when pavement needs maintenance. Condition assessments run from pot holes to paint striping and crosswalk conditions. Paint lines are rated from 1, the worst, to 5, the best. In construction zones the same imagery detects work zone equipment to put those zones on the map. Those detections can also check whether a maintenance of traffic plan matches reality. A further model detects the presence of debris on and beside the road. The AI also estimates the size of the debris it finds.

Results are delivered directly into OpenGIS or another preferred platform. The company claims savings of up to 90% compared to traditional manual inspections. It puts the cost at $10 per centerline mile against $200 or more for a LiDAR scan. News items on the site include a City of Fort Worth partnership on the first phase of automated asset inventory. Another announces a sustainability partner designation in the Google Cloud Partner Advantage Program.

Street Smart, the company's viewer, brings 360 degree imagery, lidar, and map layers into one browser-based workspace. From the desk, users measure distances along facades, pavements, and openings. Automated analysis detects pavement defects, surface types, and deterioration in high-resolution imagery. Property valuation is another stated use, supported by current visual evidence and measurements. Open integrations and APIs connect the data to existing GIS and asset management systems.

The company says it has worked in geospatial capture and visualisation for more than 40 years with public authorities across Europe and beyond. Specialised capture vehicles survey cities and regions throughout the year. Routes are coordinated with local authorities to limit disruption. Its case studies page lists a digital twin created for the London Borough of Harrow from street imagery and lidar.

The flagship EV ARC generates and stores all of its own electricity rather than drawing from a utility connection. It is sized for a standard parking space, so vehicles park on the unit and no spaces are given up. Because it stands apart from the grid, the unit keeps charging through blackouts, and an optional panel can feed electricity to first responders and medical workers. A second product applies the same idea to bicycles, charging up to twelve eBikes on a transportable platform.

Beam Global says it was founded in 2006. The company is publicly traded on Nasdaq under the ticker BEEM. It is headquartered in San Diego with operations in Chicago, Europe and the Middle East, and says it employs combat veterans and individuals with disabilities.

paragraphs: GeoCivix sells cloud-based software that cities, counties and municipalities use to run permitting, licensing, inspections, plan review and citizen services from one system. The pitch is a replacement for paper-based workflows with digital applications, automated routing, electronic plan review, mobile inspections and online payments.

Applicants use a government portal open around the clock, where they manage their projects and pay fees without calling or coming into the office. Staff mark up documents and let the system automate routing. Notifications and comment letters go back out to applicants as reviews move along. Inspectors work from a tablet or smart phone in the field, taking photos, creating reports and managing workloads on site. Permits, inspections, plans, documents, notes and approvals stay organized in one place.

Staff, reviewers, inspectors, citizens and contractors all work from the same project record. An implementation team starts by collecting application forms, communication templates, fee formulas and document workflows for configuration. The company says many agencies launch initial workflows in as little as 6 weeks, with full deployment typically completed within a few months. Every subscription is said to include unlimited technical support for all users. Listed integrations include ESRI ArcGIS, Bluebeam Revu, Cityworks, Infor/Hansen, FireRMS, Laserfiche and payment systems.

quote.text: GeoCivix offers straightforward pricing with free, unlimited support, training, and software upgrades.

That commission serves more than 1.9 million people. Avolve says its plan review is built on insight from more than 350 government customers. Testimonials on its site come from cities and counties, including one crediting ProjectDox with improving operations across Minneapolis.

paragraphs: Chorus Intelligence sells the Chorus Intelligence Suite, software that investigators use to manage every stage of a digital investigation from one dashboard. The suite provides data cleansing, analysis, search, enrichment and evidential reporting tools, and the company sells it to law enforcement, financial and corporate institutions across the globe. The customers page says it is used every day to help combat serious and organised crime, fraud, human trafficking and terrorism.

An investigator starts by dragging in raw digital data such as call data records, handset downloads and ANPR, which the suite cleanses and formats automatically. To attribute an entity, the same dashboard can bulk search a name, phone number, email address or alias across multiple data sources at once. Open-source searches run through an IP-obfuscated environment that hides the identity of the person searching. Anything captured online is hashed to SHA 256 standard so its integrity can be checked.

Case studies on the site describe North Wales Police using the data cleansing and analysis tools to find and convict a crossbow murderer. Another describes West Midlands Police using Chorus on what the company calls the largest modern slavery investigation ever conducted in the UK. The company says its team combines former law enforcement analysts with software developers who specialise in police and financial data.

quote.text: A digital intelligence and investigation suite built for the future

organizations.description: Investigation database: pawn/secondhand transactions plus ballistics ID for agencies - exhibited at Michigan Sheriffs Association 2026

paragraphs: LeadsOnline sells investigative software and forensic tools to law enforcement agencies, aimed at solving crimes faster, recovering stolen property, and building cases that hold up in court. Its two main lines are digital evidence analysis and crime gun intelligence, and the company says the tools are built to work together. The company says it works alongside law enforcement worldwide.

On the digital side, the tools turn raw data, from stolen property records to digital evidence, into answers an agency can act on. Cellular and social media analysis links call records, GPS, and activity data through visualizations meant to identify suspects. When a firearm or cartridge case turns up at a scene, the ballistics products give forensic examiners a way to link firearms to crimes and connect evidence across agencies. Triage tools identify the number of firearms and calibers involved and preserve trace evidence for later steps.

One case study describes a detective at the Plano, TX Police Department recovering a stolen iPhone and obtaining a warrant for the suspect using LeadsOnline. Another, from the Tyler, TX Police Department, credits CellHawk analysis with leading to the arrest of a murder suspect. In the testimonials, Detective Jeff German of the Joliet Police Department says NightHawk helped find evidence in millions of lines of data. The company puts its reach at thousands of agencies and millions of investigations.

quote.text: We exist to help global law enforcement agencies advance cases faster with our unique data, well-designed technology, and exceptional teamwork.

paragraphs: SS8 Networks sells lawful intelligence software used to capture, deliver, visualize and analyze investigative data. Its Xcipio platform gives communication service providers passive and active lawful interception, with data handover, for any type of network, including 5G, so that they can meet regulatory requirements. Xcipio supports CALEA, ETSI and national-specific standards. It can run virtualized or containerized, from on-premises to full cloud environments. For emergency services, law enforcement and mobile network operators, SS8 also sells location-based services that report where a device is.

On the investigative side, the monitoring center product Intellego XT reconstructs and analyzes voice, data, emails and messages in real time and offers access to hundreds of additional data sources. It maps entities, relationships and movements into link charts, then packages the evidence into playlists and galleries for analysts. A second product, MetaHub, is an AI-enabled data intelligence tool that lets analysts import, search, analyze and structure investigative data and enrich it with third-party sources. Analysts drag and drop evidence such as audio, cell phone data, messages, OSINT, photos, social media and video into a single platform, and MetaHub's OSINT software draws on hundreds of third-party data sources.

SS8 says it has delivered lawful interception and mediation solutions worldwide for over two decades. Its home page cites 6 of the world's largest intelligence agencies, 8 of the 14 largest communications providers and 5 of the world's largest systems integrators.

Integrations include access control for managing entry points and license plate recognition for vehicle identification and tracking. Evidence Lock blocks alteration or deletion of selected footage so it holds up as evidence.

XProtect comes in four variants covering installations from single sites to global operations. Milestone releases XProtect updates 2-3 times a year and updated device packs 5-6 times yearly. Licenses are bought through a Milestone Partner.

paragraphs: Verkada sells cloud-managed physical security systems that customers around the world use to operate safer, smarter buildings. The line covers cameras, alarms, and unified cloud physical security software with remote access and AI analytics. Customers control an entire physical security operation from Verkada Command.

The architecture eliminates NVRs and servers by blending the reliability of on-prem with the scalability of the cloud. Onboard camera storage options run 30, 60, 90, 120, or 365 days. Cameras use only 20-50 Kbps of upload bandwidth while recording continuously, even during internet outages.

More than 30,000 organizations worldwide use Verkada, from small and midsize businesses to Fortune 500 leaders. Customer stories include the City of Los Angeles, which uses Verkada to unify physical security and improve public safety. Another story covers the Winston-Salem Police Department, whose real-time crime center solves homicides with LPR and Verkada integrations. A story from Parkersburg, West Virginia describes local government, law enforcement and IT teams keeping citizens safe.

competitors.why: US-built face matching software licensed as an SDK to government identity programs, the alternative engine for the same face-verification integration

paragraphs: FaceTec sells face verification software that organizations use to confirm a remote user is real and physically present, both at account onboarding and on later logins. Its products cover 3D liveness checks, KYC and 3D face verification, running from an ordinary 2D camera rather than infrared hardware. During onboarding the software records a quick video selfie, verifies 3D liveness, matches the resulting 3D FaceMap to the photo on the ID and checks the ID for signs of tampering. When the user returns, a new video selfie is compared with the stored FaceMap, and a high match, which FaceTec rates at 1/125M FAR, can grant account access.

FaceTec has run a Spoof Bounty Program since October 2019 and says it has passed Ingenium, Bixelab, Praetorian and iBeta Testing Lab Level 1-5 PAD and IAD testing with 0% FAR. The bounty currently stands at $600,000. The company's stated best practice is for customers to keep users' biometric data, as 3D FaceMap or 3D FaceVector records, on their own servers, which run FaceTec's software inside the customer's firewall.

A related product, UR Codes, carries digitally signed biometric data so a codeholder can prove legal identity and age both in person and remotely. FaceTec says it trained its 3D algorithms with the help of over half a million volunteer testers from over 180 countries. It lists more than 90 channel partners worldwide.

quote.text: FaceTec proves the Correct User is physically present by Matching them to their ID Photo or 3D FaceMap.

paragraphs: LensLock sells body-worn cameras, in-car video, and CJIS-compliant evidence management to law enforcement agencies. Its pitch to departments is plain: evidence that holds up, upload and redaction that is FBI-compliant, and support staff who answer the phone. The products are designed around how officers work in the field, and a mobile app for iOS and Android handles in-field tagging and review.

The body cameras run a full shift on one battery, start recording on up to 8 auto-activation triggers, and offload video automatically. Docking stations charge up to 20 cameras at a time while pushing footage to LensLocker, the company's cloud evidence system. In the car, the Titan V system pairs a 4-channel mobile DVR with up to 2 terabytes of storage, GPS with geofencing, and cellular or WiFi offloading. Once footage is in LensLocker, officers can share it with the district attorney and redact faces, plates, and IDs.

Storage sits on Microsoft Azure Government Cloud, which the company describes as FBI CJIS-compliant and staffed by screened US citizens only. A license plate recognition feature scans video and flags matches from approved watchlists. The site notes that feature availability varies by device and configuration. Jon Handy founded LensLock in 2015 and now serves as Executive Vice President, Sales and Chairman of the Board of Directors. Chief Conrad Pepperman of the Rockaway Borough Police Department in New Jersey is quoted praising the customer service.

Paladin supplies the drone, the software, the data management platform and the FAA waivers a department needs to operate legally. paragraphs: SkySafe sells a drone detection and airspace intelligence platform that gives businesses the visibility and forensic detail to identify drone activity in real time and build legally sound cases when incidents occur. The company states the platform detects 96% of drone models, including drones flying without active signals. It can pinpoint where a drone took off, where it landed and the location of its controller. Alerts go out through SMS, Microsoft Teams, Slack, CommandCentral Aware or an existing ops stack. The platform produces forensic reports intended for law enforcement or federal agencies.

One case study describes how a near-miss drone flight over a crowd of 10,000 at Fort Adams State Park led Rhode Island toward a statewide drone detection strategy. The University of Illinois Police Department used SkySafe to monitor and respond to drone activity across campus events and facilities, and the University of Louisiana at Monroe uses it to separate authorized university flights from unauthorized activity.

Press releases on its site describe the product as a cloud-based SaaS platform providing real-time and historical drone data to help distinguish unauthorized drones from authorized ones. In November 2025 it launched Forensics as a Service, which the company says lets agencies and organizations respond to and investigate drone incidents on their own. CEO Grant Jordan served as an officer in the US Air Force for four years after graduating from MIT and was President of Somerset Recon.

paragraphs: DroneShield sells counter-drone technology, which it calls counter-UAS, to military, government, law enforcement and critical infrastructure operators around the world. The company describes a portfolio that spans RF intelligence, AI, sensor fusion and software. The stated aim is to help customers detect, understand and defeat increasingly complex drone threats. Engineering, manufacturing and support are spread across Australia, the United States and Europe.

One current product, RfRecon, runs on an AI engine called RfAI-3 and detects, classifies and geolocates AIS/ADS-B signals, unencrypted Remote ID beacons and other RF activity across the spectrum. DroneShield was founded in 2014 with a single focus on countering the threat posed by drones. The company began in Virginia in the United States. DroneShield Limited is publicly listed on the ASX.

paragraphs: Boston Dynamics builds mobile robots that companies use to automate tedious and hazardous work in manufacturing, logistics and other industries. Its product line covers Spot, Stretch, Atlas and Orbit. Spot is a mobile robot that automates sensing and inspection and captures data wherever it is sent. Spot works on factory floors, construction sites and research labs. As a sensing platform it gives teams insight into routine operations, site health or potentially hazardous situations. In energy and natural resources it performs inspections in energized, radioactive or otherwise hazardous areas. Operators can also use it to remotely investigate, assess and de-escalate tense or hazardous situations, reducing the risk to personnel. With the Spot Arm, operators can handle tasks such as nuclear material handling or suspicious package investigation from a safe distance. Standard payload configurations cover inspection, public safety and innovation, including a Government & Public Safety Kit.

Stretch, the company's warehouse robot, handles cases and unloads trailers. Orbit, its fleet management software, manages autonomous tasks, operates robots remotely and analyzes data within the context of a facility map. Atlas, a humanoid robot, is in early field testing with Hyundai on real-world sequencing tasks. The company has announced a new 323,000 square foot facility in Waltham, Massachusetts.

The same cameras can be left in place for persistent observation, with live video and audio over WiFi, 4G and MANET. paragraphs: StarChase makes GPS technology products and services designed for law enforcement, including a vehicle mounted GPS launcher and a tracking app. A Spectrum News story republished on its site explains that once a pursuit begins, a deputy's vehicle launches a dart containing a GPS tracker to tag the fleeing vehicle. Data then goes to the agency's real time intelligence center, allowing officers to track the vehicle without an active chase. The company says the technology de-escalates high-risk events in probable cause and exigent circumstances and supports agencies at every level of law enforcement.

Its home page reports 50,000+ tags deployed, 20,000+ arrests made, and 0 injuries or fatalities. State and local agencies use it for cross-jurisdictional coordination and to bridge case building and real-time apprehensions. Task forces get certified less-lethal options for fugitive, narcotics, trafficking, and other special operations. The company also positions the technology for border security and national defense as well as everyday law enforcement.

The same news story, dated March 13, 2025, reports that the Forsyth County Sheriff's Office in North Carolina had that month added StarChase to its deputies' toolbox. A testimonial from Sgt. C. Robertson of the Lake County Sheriff's office says the agency has tripled its StarChase units over six years. StarChase plans to exhibit at IACP 2026 at booth 1184.

paragraphs: Robin Radar Systems makes 360 degree, 3D radar systems that detect, track and classify small flying objects such as birds, bats and drones. It sells them to aviation, defence, security and ecology teams that want a full view of their airspace. Its two main products are IRIS, a 3D drone radar in a 29 kg package, and MAX, a 3D bird detection radar.

IRIS uses micro-doppler classification and deep neural network technology to distinguish blades and rotating parts. It combines 360 degree views, 60 degree elevation and a 5 km instrumented range. A software-only update, Long-Range Mode, lets operators switch between 5 km and 12 km instrumented ranges in minutes. MAX pairs with two software interfaces, Bird Viewer for live airspace and Report Viewer for historical analysis. Airports, airfields and wind farms use the bird and bat radars to react to hazards as they emerge.

The name comes from a 1980 project by the Dutch research institute TNO to prevent bird strikes on Royal Netherlands Air Force planes. Siete Hamminga, now CEO, spun the technology out of TNO in 2010 to found the company. It reports more than 300 radars deployed worldwide and a staff of 150 or more people. In 2024 its shareholders reached an acquisition agreement with the Dutch investment company Parcom. Scarecrow, a maker of bird dispersal and data logging systems based on bio-acoustic technology, is a Robin company.

paragraphs: Lexipol sells policy manuals, training, wellness resources, performance reporting, and grant support to public safety agencies, delivered through one system. Its buyers are the people running those agencies, from fire and police chiefs to risk managers, dispatch supervisors, and city administrators. An agency can begin with a single product, such as Policy or Wellness, and add others as it goes.

The policy product is the core: state-specific manuals researched and written by policy and legal professionals, then kept current as laws and standards change. Personnel acknowledge each policy electronically, which creates an audit trail for accreditation, audits, or legal reviews. Daily Training Bulletins turn those policies into practice through short scenario-based lessons. The LexOne platform ties training assignments to policy, warns leaders when licenses or credentials are about to expire, and tracks the data agencies need for reporting. Online courses carry accreditation from organizations such as IADLEST, POST, and CAPCE.

Lexipol was created in 2003 by two attorneys who were also former law enforcement officers. Co-founder Gordon Graham still records a weekly two-minute video tip for public safety and local government personnel. The company says its wellness product alone supports more than 1,000 agencies across the U.S. and Canada. Among the chiefs quoted on the site, Edward Delmore of the Gulf Shores (AL) Police Department compares a subscription to having another full-time administrator assigned to policy.

A mobile app is included, so staff can view schedules and submit or handle requests from an iOS or Android device as well as from a PC or tablet. paragraphs: PoliceApp runs an online platform for police recruitment, used by applicants looking for law enforcement jobs and by the police departments hiring them. Job seekers search for openings by location or browse police jobs by region. Police departments and associations request a demo to begin using the service, while applicants create an account or search for a job.

The company says the platform was designed by law enforcement professionals and technology experts to remove redundancies and common frustrations from a hiring process it describes as rigorous for applicants and departments alike. Its stated aims are to publicize current law enforcement openings and match candidates with the police jobs they qualify for. It also aims to allow efficient communication between departments and applicants and to create consistency across police departments. The homepage also carries police recruitment and hiring news.

paragraphs: ForceMetrics sells Velocity, a search and analytics platform for public safety agencies that pulls CAD, RMS and other records systems into one search covering people, locations, vehicles and events. Officers, analysts and command staff get structured records, narratives and unstructured content back in under a second, with filters that surface connections across CAD, RMS, JMS and regional data.

A universal data model links not only an agency's current systems of record but multiple generations of those systems, so historical and current information is searchable together. Flow Static unlocks data from legacy CAD and RMS systems, and Flow Historical adds e-citations, crash reports, court data and EMS records. Flexible Person Merge combines person records from across the agency and multiple jurisdictions into a single enriched profile, and users can merge or unmerge at any time as new information arrives.

For command staff, FMStat replaces rigid CompStat packets with real-time dashboards that show crime trends and what is driving them. Horizon AI summarizes large volumes of reports and spots patterns across related incidents, with every connection pointing back to the records behind it, inside what the company calls a CJIS-compliant environment. Agencies named on the home page include High Point, NC, New Castle County, DE and Beverly Hills, CA. The company describes its team as veteran law enforcement officials who built the tools they wished they had in the field.

quote.text: Drawing on decades of law enforcement experience, we built the tools we wish we had in the field.

paragraphs: Acusensus sells automated traffic enforcement systems to the road authorities and police agencies that are trying to cut deaths and injuries on the road network. Its main product, Heads-Up, detects drivers illegally using a mobile phone and captures evidence intended to stand up in a prosecution.

The same camera pass picks up other behaviours, so one deployment can address seatbelt non-compliance and speed measured at a point or averaged over a distance. A companion product sends live alerts to officers working the roadside. Assessment happens at the roadside, and images of drivers who are not offending are discarded almost immediately. Evidence that is kept is encrypted so that only the customer agency can open it.

The company says the government of New South Wales used its technology in a program enforcing against illegal phone use by drivers. Its list of delivered work includes an Arkansas speed enforcement program covering work zones. Acusensus also reports ISO accreditation for occupational health and safety, quality, environmental and information security management systems.

The company took its current shape after a 2024 merger with TRAXERO and other acquisitions. It says many of its team members are former tow operators, impound managers, law enforcement officers, and telecommunicators. Its stated reason for the work is roadside safety.

organizations.name: Perry Weather
organizations.description: Weather safety platform: WBGT heat monitoring, lightning alerts, stations and sirens for parks and athletics

paragraphs: Perry Weather sells a weather safety platform that pairs monitoring hardware at a customer site with automated alerting, so an entire staff works from the same reading of conditions. The buyers it names are schools, cities, golf clubs, and industrial firms.

Stations at the customer location measure heat stress, lightning, precipitation, wind, and air quality, refreshing every five minutes in the mobile app and dashboard. Each organization writes its own thresholds and decides who gets notified when one is crossed. Alerts can go to phones or to an outdoor siren system. Countdown timers mark the moment it is safe to resume play or work. All-clears go out automatically once the threat has passed.

Colin Perry founded the company in 2013. It reports more than 5,000 organizations nationwide as customers. It also counts over 200 million alerts sent, covering hazards from heat stress to lightning. Arthur Ventures led a $15M Series B. The stated markets run across athletics, golf, parks and recreation, energy, and airports.

quote.text: It shouldn’t be complicated to make weather safety decisions.

paragraphs: EPIC iO sells AI-driven monitoring for physical sites, along with the wireless connectivity that keeps those locations online. Its named settings are utilities, oil and gas, construction, retail and industrial sites. Both sides run on a software platform the company calls EPIC Cortex.

The video analysis is meant to separate security events from environmental activity such as weather or wildlife, which cuts false alarms. License plate recognition adds vehicle awareness at site entrances, along the perimeter and for vehicle activity on site. For police use, the LPR page says the system alerts officers and dispatchers within seconds. On the connectivity side, the company offers primary, backup and failover links across 5G, satellite and fixed networks. The same platform centralizes SIM and device management across multiple carriers with real-time usage monitoring.

For public safety and critical infrastructure customers, EPIC iO frames its role as situational awareness that supports emergency response without replacing established response protocols. Homepage testimonials are attributed anonymously, by role, to bodies such as a municipal public safety agency. The about page names an AI platform called DeepInsights as the cornerstone of its mission.

quote.text: EPIC iO is at the forefront of technology, empowering businesses to thrive in the digital age by harnessing the transformative potential of 5G-ready connectivity and AI + IoT solutions.

organizations.name: B2Gnow
organizations.description: Supplier diversity and DBE compliance tracking SaaS for states, cities, airports, and transit

paragraphs: B2Gnow sells compliance software to public agencies and the contractors on their projects, covering vendor programs, prevailing wage labor compliance and grant management. The company lists states, state DOTs, cities, counties, transit agencies, airports, education, general contractors and healthcare among the kinds of clients it names.

The vendor side is a cloud-based platform covering DBE, MBE, WBE and SBE compliance initiatives. Certification work runs from online applications through agency review to approval. For contract compliance, prime and subcontractor payments are collected, and subcontractors confirm payment directly, monthly or quarterly. Reporting draws on more than 400 standard system reports. A payroll line covers Davis-Bacon and Related Acts, the Service Contract Act, state prevailing wage laws and local living wage ordinances. Grant work runs through BlackCat, from applications to asset management and spend-down tracking.

The company says the software has been implemented at over 400 organizations. It claims one million users regularly access the system to register, prequalify, submit reports, manage grants and review bid solicitations. The site cites over 25 years of vendor program compliance experience. B2Gnow and eComply have joined together into one platform spanning vendor management and labor compliance. Hosting is described as fully redundant, with guaranteed availability of 99.9% and SOC 2 Type 2 certification.

The company states that over 1,300 enterprises worldwide use it to manage $2.9 trillion in annual spend. A customer panel names the State University of New York among higher education users. It says it was the first to bring touchscreen technology to corrections, in 1989.

Its touchscreen system brings door control, CCTV, intercoms and paging, access control, and utility monitoring together as one console. paragraphs: Guard1 sells hardware and software that prove where staff have been and when, working with correctional agencies, behavioral healthcare facilities and security teams. A separate duress system puts a device on staff and visitors that sends a signal once per second. When the button is pressed, the location is shown on a control room monitor.

The company says hundreds of agencies have used The PIPE to document officer rounds and hold defensible logs for inspections and incidents. It puts its corrections figure at over 1400 customers served, including 20+ DOCs, hundreds of county jails, ICE facilities and juvenile facilities. paragraphs: 4Sight Labs sells a biometric monitoring system for correctional facilities, meant to help staff watch over the health of people held in custody. People in custody wear sensors that track heart rate, blood oxygen, skin temperature and motion, along with other indicators of physiological distress. Readings are processed as they arrive, so that anomalies produce structured notifications instead of an after-the-fact review. Thresholds can be set by the facility so staff hear about a pattern that points toward a crisis.

The company says the platform is built for county detention centers, state systems, private facilities and complex housing units. It also states that the technology is designed and manufactured in the United States, with a controlled hardware and firmware supply chain. The site reports that the Harford County Sheriff's Office publicly announced putting OverWatch into its custody and safety strategy.

Staff reach it through a secure browser without installing extra software, and it runs over Power-over-Ethernet.

The company names suicide watch units, medical cells, and high-risk housing as the places the system goes in. Cell-Guardian was developed by Rahm Sensor Development, Inc., the team behind the VetGuardian platform. Its company page lists an address in Orlando, Florida.

paragraphs: DigitalOptometrics is a technology company whose software lets a patient sitting in an optical exam location receive a comprehensive eye examination from a licensed optometrist working somewhere else. The exam and the prescription are meant to be done in under 30 minutes.

The visit starts with preliminary testing carried out on site in the clinical area. A video slit lamp records high-definition footage of the outside structures of the eye for the remote doctor to evaluate. That doctor can control the phoropter remotely and reviews the findings in real time. A comprehensive exam is described as covering ten subject areas, including a vision analysis. At the end the optometrist finalizes and delivers the glasses or contact lens prescription within minutes.

Buyers are optical providers, and the company describes itself as optometrist founded and optometrist driven. Dr. Fried formed the company in 2016 and assembled a team of optical software development specialists. The technology was shown publicly at the Vision Expo in New York City. The company states that its system is used in more than 30 states in the United States and in Canada.

paragraphs: ECINS sells a license-free cloud system for collaborative case management, built for agencies that coordinate support for vulnerable people. Its case management module is used by tens of thousands of users in the UK, including police, health and councils. The central idea is a single shared record, so a client does not repeat the same information to every agency involved. The company reports results across the UK, the United States and Australia.

Work usually begins in the referral module, which replaces paper forms with secure online forms that clients and practitioners fill in themselves. Once a referral is approved, its information can be transferred into the case management module. Within case management, staff receive alerts for significant activity such as child protection interventions. They can also track commonalities between individuals through search fields such as addresses, vehicle license plates and educational institutions. A client engagement module and a MyPortal app let clients receive reminders, respond to messages and tasks, and ask questions from their phones.

Beyond casework, a community collaboration module lets residents, neighbourhood watch groups, business communities, police and local authorities work together on detailed neighbourhood profiles. A staff tasking and oversight module is described as still in development. The homepage claims thousands of users across multiple countries. The system is sold license-free to encourage wide participation at no extra cost.

quote.text: ECINS helps teams provide joined-up support to people in need while empowering those being supported.

Face and biometric matching software for law enforcement: same matching engine decision

paragraphs: Safience sells identity intelligence software that looks only for predefined threats, persons of interest and missing persons, matched against a database built from law enforcement records. The site belongs to Biometrica Systems, Inc., a software and data company that supports federal, state, tribal and local law enforcement and private sector safety teams. Its RTIS and RVIS edge sensors capture a single still image rather than video or audio, and any image that does not match a predefined profile is purged immediately. The company states that an alert follows within 60 seconds of a detection and that database queries return in under 5 seconds.

The database behind the system holds 57.3M+ unique individuals and receives over 50,000 new records per day. Those records come from published law enforcement records, agency JMS/RMS integrations, an OffenderWatch partnership and missing-person records, with no OSINT, social media or consumer data. It also markets the system to airports and mass transit, banks, schools and universities, hospitals, hotels, retailers and stadiums.

A second product, eMotive, turns a one-time criminal background check into a continuous, FCRA-compliant alert system for employers, with written consent required from each monitored individual. Matching for eMotive is performed by a third-party, NIST-approved provider in an isolated environment, and Biometrica staff do not see employee match notifications. Biometrica holds the U.S. patent for System and Method for Continuous Biometric Monitoring.

quote.text: We identify threats or victims in under 60 seconds. Privacy-first. Real-time. Nationwide.

Daycares and schools use it to restrict access and confirm the identity of employees and of parents or other adults who come to pick up a child.

For time and attendance, the IrisTime iT100 combines iris and facial recognition biometrics. It runs on an open Android platform that accommodates hundreds of currently available time and attendance applications. An Android SDK lets developers build and install apps on the iT100. For larger enterprise sites, the web-based iAMS management suite gives administrators a single dashboard for the entire deployment.

organizations.description: Deploy-anywhere MFA including air-gapped and on-prem, sold into CJIS-driven law enforcement IT

paragraphs: SurePassID sells deploy-anywhere multi-factor authentication for IT/OT and critical infrastructure, deployable in the cloud, on-premise, or within air-gapped networks. It covers Windows, MacOS, and Linux logins with offline 2FA and fronts cloud and on-prem apps through SAML2, OIDC, and LDAP identity providers. The company cites 99.999% availability, redundancy, and automatic failover, and markets the product for compliance with OMB M-22-09, CMMC 2.0, and NIS2. It supports phishing-resistant MFA through FIDO2/WebAuthn passkeys and security keys as well as OATH HOTP, TOTP, and OCRA tokens and mobile push.

SurePassID has provided on-premise MFA since its founding in 2012 and says 50% of its customer base, including Fortune 500 companies, uses it on-premise. It also serves financial services, having introduced a private cloud authentication server for online payments licensed by Visa, MasterCard, American Express, First Data, and Discover. About 33% of its install base runs in air-gapped environments, and it provides air-gapped MFA to 11 of 16 critical infrastructure sectors. paragraphs: D-Fend Solutions sells counter-drone systems to military, law enforcement and homeland security agencies. Its core product, EnforceAir, detects a rogue drone, takes control of it through a radio-frequency cyber takeover and brings it to a safe landing. The company describes the approach as non-kinetic and AI-enhanced, built for sensitive and challenging environments.

EnforceAir can operate autonomously or under manual control, and it detects, locates and identifies rogue drones in a protected airspace before taking them over. It is sold in several deployment packages, including a Homeland Security & Law Enforcement Bundle and two tactical configurations, EnforceAir PLUS and EnforceAir2. EnforceAir PLUS, launched in August 2025, adds radar and a jammer to the RF-cyber layer. Beyond agencies, the company says the system has been chosen for large-scale events at stadiums, arenas and open-air venues and for VIP protection.

In an August 2026 press release the company says EnforceAir provided counter-drone security across World Cup host cities and was adopted by more than 20 public safety agencies. Chairman and CEO Zohar Halachmi co-founded the company after founding two mobile and enterprise application start-ups. Its U.S. arm, D-Fend Solutions AD, Inc., is located in McLean, Virginia. In June 2026 the company announced an agreement to be acquired by Motorola Solutions. Its newsroom now states that it has officially joined Motorola Solutions.

paragraphs: Sentrycs makes counter-drone systems that detect, track, identify and mitigate unauthorized drones for defense, homeland security and critical infrastructure environments. Rather than radar, it uses passive RF cyber technology to pick up drone communication signals and locate both the drone and its operator. Detection reports the drone type, serial number and operator position. Mitigation does not jam the drone; the system takes control of it through a cyber takeover. If required, it integrates with other types of effector, including jammers.

The company says a team of communications and radio frequency experts embarked in 2017 on developing modular solutions that could be tailored to each customer's drone environment. The system is built for complex and urban environments, where it aims to minimize interference with surrounding communications. It says its customers include governments, security forces and critical infrastructure operators worldwide. Its blog is aimed partly at law enforcement, with posts on how to legally take down a rogue drone and on lessons from recent UAS attacks.

On November 18th, 2025, Ondas Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ:ONDS) announced it had completed the acquisition of Sentrycs. The announcement describes the company as Sentry CS Ltd., based in Israel. It puts Sentrycs at approximately 200 deployments across six continents in more than 25 countries.

paragraphs: Flash AI builds investigative software in Ohio for law enforcement agencies. Its main product, Flash PD, takes an entire caseload of video, audio, images, documents and phone extractions into one unified system. Flash PD accepts 115+ file types and processes them in parallel. Investigators then ask questions in plain language and get direct answers with linked source evidence and timestamps.

A second product, Flash Signal, connects to a correctional facility's call recording system so recorded inmate calls flow in as they happen, or historical libraries can be uploaded in batch. Each call is transcribed and scored low, medium or high risk from its content, language and behavioral signals, so investigators open the high-risk calls first. The company says a 60-day pilot at a correctional facility identified 33,004 high-risk signals with zero manual review hours required.

A third product, Flash Chat, extends private AI chat and document analysis to the rest of an agency, with a free trial for the standard deployment and CJIS deployments available by demo. Flash AI states that queries, uploads and conversations are never used to train AI models, and that hosting is on AWS infrastructure in the United States. The customers page lists Whitehall Police Department and Perry Township Police Department as active deployments, and Muskingum County and Guernsey County sheriff's offices as previous pilots.

quote.text: From raw evidence to court-ready intelligence, in minutes.

competitors.why: Anonymous citizen tip submission and community alerting feeding an agency portal, the direct alternative for the same PD community engagement budget

paragraphs: nexSOS connects citizens and public safety agencies through real-time incident reporting, location sharing, and NOAA weather alerts, backed by a government portal. Citizens use a mobile app to share their GPS location with emergency contacts and first responders, record video reports with the phone's camera, and call emergency services directly. The company stresses that the app is not a 911 replacement.

Incident reports are stored and routed to a backend portal where public safety agencies filter, review, and monitor incidents across their jurisdiction. Agencies can filter by region, timestamp and category, review video, and see NOAA alerts alongside citizen reports in one view. The page names Emergency Management Offices, County Dispatch Centers and Municipal Safety Agencies as the users it is built for. The pitch to them is early incident context before or alongside 911 calls.

Government access is licensed annually by jurisdiction size, with a base tier of unlimited citizen users, portal access and 12 months of data retention, and larger tiers adding analytics, heat mapping and extended retention. Qualified agencies can start with a 90-day paid pilot that includes full platform access, onboarding support and a usage summary report. nexSOS says the platform originally launched and ran quietly in production and is now being rebuilt as v2, with modernized infrastructure, user experience and government-facing capabilities.

quote.text: nexSOS is a modern emergency reporting and situational awareness platform designed to strengthen the connection between communities and public safety.

paragraphs: Detail Kommander sells software that law enforcement agencies use to run their off-duty, extra duty and overtime detail programs. The company says the software automates over 80% of the task work involved and provides fair job assignments. It is offered to law enforcement agencies at no cost.

Job distribution runs through a fairness engine that applies the agency's own policies so that each officer gets a fair shot at working jobs. Notifications and job reminders go out automatically, in place of the manual emails, texts and calls a coordinator would otherwise send. As a detail runs, the agency and the business that hired the officers can see when officers are en route, on site and finished. Officers record what happens during a detail in a paperless activity log. Agencies, officers and employers can then pull reports on finances and assignments. The homepage also lists a payment platform among the features.

Detail Kommander was founded by a retired Chief, and it says it builds for law enforcement agencies of all sizes. The company says hundreds of agencies have moved to the software. One case study profiles the Lake County Sheriff's Office, where Lt. Mark Stauffer and his team moved their off-duty detail operations onto Detail Kommander. One testimonial on the homepage is attributed to Sebastian Police Department.

paragraphs: DefendEye sells autonomous drones to first responders, emergency services and private security teams. A second product category is aimed at tactical, defense and government buyers. The pitch is situational awareness in seconds, an AI-powered search for people on the ground, and a drone that anyone can operate.

There is no pilot and no joystick: the operator controls the drone from a phone and launches it with a single tap. The company says deployment takes under 20 seconds through a single-button activation. Once airborne, the onboard AI locates and tags people so that officers can concentrate on the rescue. Listed flight times run up to 30 minutes on one model and up to 40 minutes on another. One version launches automatically when motion sensors detect activity and returns to land in its box. Missions can be run remotely from any location through the DefendEye Cloud platform.

The company describes itself as a technology company focused on making aerial intelligence faster, simpler and more accessible. It says its systems can support emergency response, public safety, maritime operations and industrial environments. A media section on the about page lists an August 2026 PR Newswire item about an investment led by NovaCapital to scale production. Another item there announces the integration of Starlink Mini into its tube-launched search drone. Earlier coverage listed on the same page describes the drone as the work of a Polish technology company.

quote.text: DefendEye is a technology company focused on making aerial intelligence faster, simpler and more accessible.

paragraphs: Genfare sells fare collection systems to public transit agencies, and describes itself as a partner to transit agencies of every size across the United States and Canada for more than forty years. Its systems cover fixed route service, microtransit, paratransit, ferries, and light rail.

The company is moving its Genfare Link platform to a fully cloud-based software-as-a-service model. Transaction, ridership, and device monitoring data from fareboxes, mobile apps, e-Fare portals, and retail channels are consolidated in one central location. For riders paying with a contactless bank card or phone, existing Fast Fare fareboxes can be upgraded for open payment, or an Open Link validator can be mounted next to the farebox. The Mobile Link application and the e-Fare online ticketing system use open APIs to work with microtransit and shared ride providers.

Genfare Link is built on Amazon Web Services, with APIs linking agency platforms to each other and to riders. Alongside the hardware and software, the company sells packages for training, maintenance and repair, and technical support.

quote.text: Genfare is the only fare collection provider that works with transit agencies of all sizes, whether your fleet has five buses or more than 500.

organizations.description: Contactless open-loop transit payment infrastructure for 400+ providers in 30+ countries

paragraphs: Littlepay sells payments infrastructure for transit, and public transit providers and vendors of all sizes use it to accept payments in person or online and simplify ticketing for passengers.

Open APIs allow flexible configuration of its capabilities alongside existing AFC and ABT fare collection systems. A single data platform gives operators visibility of passenger behaviour across vehicles, gates, kiosks, mobile apps and web. Risk models optimised across global volumes are meant to minimise losses from fraud and uncollected payments. Advanced PAN and PAR deny lists target card flipping fraud. Multi-operator brokerage services connect operators and agencies in a region under unified customer ticketing.

The company set out in 2016 with a vision to make contactless bank card acceptance faster, cheaper, and less complex for the public transit sector. It now describes working with over 400 transport and mobility providers in over 30 countries, powering payments on local buses, city networks and national public transport systems. One published case study describes Monterey-Salinas Transit deploying a contactless transit fare payment system in May 2021, the first of its kind in California.

Equipment is designed modularly with the transit industry in mind, so an installation can grow both in size and in added functionality. The company describes its fare equipment as the most adaptable on the market and its back-end office application as reliable. A ticketing vending machine also appears among the listed products.

paragraphs: INIT is a supplier of IT solutions for public transport, selling to operators around the world. Its systems cover all operational processes within a fully integrated ITS system.

Planning tools run from timetables through optimizing deployments to managing vehicles and drivers. Fare products handle smartcards, mobile tickets, ID- or account-based ticketing and Open Payment. Operations control covers monitoring the traffic situation, punctuality, disruption handling and passenger information. Transport companies can also use it for electromobility requirements and to set up a single sign-on mobility platform.

The company dates to 1983, when it started as a university spin-off. Its roots are in Karlsruhe, Germany. It reports more than 40 subsidiaries and offices around the globe. More than 1400 transport providers are described as relying on the company. Development and internal processes are stated to comply with IT security standards in accordance with DIN EN ISO/IEC 27001:2022.

organizations.description: myAvail enterprise transit management ITS and CAD/AVL for mid-size US agencies

paragraphs: Avail Technologies sells enterprise transit management software to public transit agencies. The company states that its target market is transit operators with medium-sized fleets.

The myAvail platform covers vehicle location, dispatching, workforce management, reporting, and rider communications, so a team works from one connected system rather than several tools. A single shared database moves data throughout the organization. Dispatchers see where every bus and driver is, and incidents are tracked as they occur. Business intelligence dashboards report metrics in real time, which the company frames as a way to improve efficiency, justify funding requests, and demonstrate compliance. Features can be added to the platform as an agency's needs grow, and the company says myAvail ships multiple platform updates a year.

Founded in 1999, Avail describes a family-oriented staff working hand-in-hand with transit professionals. It says it has stayed a mid-sized company by design. An announcement on the site names Rick Spangler as president and chief executive as the company continues a transition to full employee ownership.

quote.text: myAvail was built on a simple belief: your data should give you answers, not just numbers to interpret.

paragraphs: GIRO makes software for the organizations that run public transport and postal delivery services, covering the work from planning through daily operations. Its two product families, HASTUS and GeoRoute, are in use in more than 30 countries.

The company grounds the work in knowledge of the problems those operators face day to day. GIRO states that more than 30% of its resources go to research and development. New ideas and solutions are developed with clients and validated by groups of users around the world.

GIRO was founded in the 1970s through the work of a Université de Montréal student and his professor. That early work paved the way for the creation of both products. The company counts over 40 years of experience in the field. It also notes a ranking among the 300 largest companies in Quebec.

organizations.name: IVU Traffic Technologies
organizations.description: IVU.suite planning, scheduling, dispatch, and ticketing for transit and rail operators

paragraphs: IVU develops integrated IT systems for public transport, and says it has done so for more than fifty years. The customers are bus and rail operators of any size, from five vehicles to fifty and from two routes to two hundred. Its product, IVU.suite, covers planning, dispatch, fleet management, ticketing, passenger information and the settlement of transport contracts.

Timetabling runs from setting up route networks to publishing services and supplying operation control and passenger information systems. Vehicle scheduling is handled by IVU.run, which supports the entire schedule planning process. Duty scheduling merges thousands of duty elements, crewing guidelines and qualifications through optimisation algorithms. For electric fleets the system weighs charging times, ranges, route lengths and depot or opportunity charging. In daily operation it monitors vehicle status, the timetable situation and the current deployment of vehicles and staff. The whole suite is also offered as a hosted service.

The company says more than 500 customers worldwide use the standard products of the suite. Named deployments include the Lagos Metropolitan Area Transport Authority. It reports as IVU Traffic Technologies AG and has published preliminary results for the first half of 2026.

Dispatch software for police, fire and EMS supports real-time coordination, incident management and control room operations. A contact center and interactive voice response product carries passenger updates on schedules, fares and disruptions across voice and digital channels. The company says its systems are used by organisations across transportation and public safety, with deployments in Europe and North America. The transit offering is modular, covering electromobility for electric fleet monitoring and smart charging as well as traffic control and monitoring for real-time fleet oversight and incident management. Passenger information delivers accurate, real-time updates to riders both onboard and offboard. Every part is described as multivendor and multimodal compatible, deployable in cloud, on-premise, or data centre environments. Support runs end to end, from installation and integration through maintenance and training.

The hardware and software are installed on more than 40,000 vehicles globally. Named customers include Skyss in Norway, Tide Buss in Sweden, Ventura Bus Lines in Australia, and Din Tur in Sweden. paragraphs: TransTrack Systems writes software for public transit agencies that pulls scattered operating data into one place so performance can be watched and reported. The main application collects data from across an agency so teams can follow trends and produce the reports decisions rest on.

Much of the appeal is federal reporting: agency data is applied automatically to the required National Transit Database forms, which the company says turns most of the annual filing from weeks of work into days. A companion analytics product presents the same operating data as dashboards, reports and metrics an agency can adjust. The point of it, in the company's framing, is to replace manual spreadsheets and disconnected systems and keep the numbers behind federal funding accurate.

The firm was formed in 2002 by transit management professionals. More than twenty years on, it describes its business as helping agencies turn operating data into better decisions. Alongside the software it lists consulting work such as transit financial planning and cost analyses. The platform itself was built with transit professionals involved.

paragraphs: CSched sells scheduling services and software tools to public transit agencies, private operators, and school boards, whatever their size or mode of transportation. The company is the exclusive authorized reseller of GIRO's HASTUS software in North America.

Its scheduling and operations modules are built on the HASTUS platform. When an agency is short of schedulers, its Rent-a-Scheduler service supplies coverage from the short term to the long term. Training runs from foundational courses to advanced HASTUS workshops. Consulting work covers efficiency audits, labor negotiations, and tender bids. The firm also advises agencies adapting their scheduling practices for the shift to electric buses.

Transit agencies worldwide have relied on CSched since 2008. The site says more than 4,650 buses run every day on schedules developed with its software or services. CSched calls itself the only consulting firm fully dedicated to public transit scheduling. It operates globally with a strong presence in North America, serving agencies, school boards, and private operators. Its experts are described as bringing over 100 years of combined hands-on experience.

quote.text: As the only consulting firm fully dedicated to public transit scheduling, CSched understands scheduling better than any other company.

paragraphs: Connixt sells iMarq, a mobile-first application built for field crews, technicians and mechanics to digitize and automate data collection, paperwork, processes and workflows. The company aims it at fleets, rail, transit, manufacturing, heavy engineering and facilities.

There are native apps for iOS and Android. They run on phones and tablets, both online and offline. Crews record asset details in the organization's own forms, on their own devices, in real time. An assistant called iBot puts institutional knowledge, troubleshooting guidance and compliance support in front of frontline teams, while reporting lets users reach their data on any device and track asset status.

Public agency case studies include a transportation department whose traffic signal division used the customizable mobile app to digitize work orders and improve transparency. Another covers Metrolink, which automated the train delay reporting its conductors had been doing on paper. The company reports winning two Progressive Railroading Reader's Choice Awards for a second consecutive year. It is run by two co-founders, Satish and Prabhu, described as industry veterans, and the site cites a 4.8 rating on Capterra.

organizations.name: Cylus
organizations.description: CylusOne rail OT cybersecurity: threat detection for signaling, trackside, and onboard networks

paragraphs: Cylus makes cybersecurity software for railways, built to continuously monitor, detect, and protect every layer of rail operational technology. Its product, CylusOne, covers mainline, urban, and freight rail operations.

The system integrates passively into an operator's network and existing monitoring tools. It automatically discovers and classifies all assets in the operational networks. Vulnerabilities are prioritized and scored by analyzing their severity in the rail environment. Detection runs continuously using deep packet inspection and machine learning to identify and classify threats across railway and IT protocols. Coverage reaches trackside and wayside networks, train-to-ground communications, operational control and maintenance centers, and station networks.

The company says the product lets operators prove compliance with frameworks including IEC 62443-3-2, NIST 800-82, and EN TS 50701. It describes CylusOne as the first rail cybersecurity solution certified to IEC 62443-4-2 at Security Level 3. Cylus says it works with technology providers, integrators, and rail experts worldwide. For passenger rail, detection is tuned to separate expected supervision and control traffic in ERTMS environments from anomalous behavior.

quote.text: CylusOne enables teams to investigate and contain threats without disrupting service, integrates with existing SOC processes, and keeps freight rail operations at the center of decision-making.

organizations.name: Citiri
organizations.description: CitiriOS owner scope management and operational readiness (ORAT) for transit, airports, and utilities

paragraphs: Citiri sells CitiriOS, a system owners use to define readiness, assign accountability, collect accepted evidence, and govern gate decisions. The company aims it at organizations launching complex infrastructure and services.

The premise is that finishing construction is not the same as being ready to operate. The discipline the company calls Owner Scope Management runs as a chain in which the owner defines what must be true to operate, evidence proves it, and gates authorize it. The output is a Ready Score along with accepted evidence and gate decisions. An agent named Opti surfaces false greens, aging blockers, and the decisions that still need an owner. People, not the software, approve every evidence and gate decision.

The company is direct about the boundary, saying CitiriOS is not a PMIS, commissioning tool, EAM/CMMS, document repository, or BI replacement. Citiri says it is helping the ATL team manage a $13B capital program that includes more than 114 distinct projects. It also describes the SFO team using CitiriOS to keep the Harvey Milk Terminal One project on track. A companion layer, OpsCenter, is listed as generally available, while an ecosystem orchestrator called Struxis is listed as limited access.

paragraphs: AngelTrax sells mobile video surveillance systems built for transportation safety. The company describes its customers as student transportation, mass transit, fleet, locomotive, and waste operations.

On a school bus, interior, exterior, stop-arm, and windshield views cover students, drivers, and transportation staff. Footage leaves the vehicle two ways, and a cellular link carries live view, active tracking, and instant notifications. Wi-Fi handles automated downloads once vehicles return to range. Video and data can be hosted by AngelTrax at its secure U.S. data center rather than handed to a third party. Its online software covers live view, downloads, vehicle location, health reporting, stop-arm workflows, and driver behavior. Driver behavior events arrive with video meant to support coaching, claims response, and accountability.

The company page dates the business to 2006. It reports 250,000 active systems operating worldwide. It also states $2.5M spent on research and development yearly. The same page describes a SOC 2 Type II-compliant data center for data security.

paragraphs: Gatekeeper Systems sells video recording and data systems for transportation, meant to make travel safer for children, passengers, and public safety personnel across several modes. The company says it uses AI, video analytics, thermal cameras, and mobile data collectors to inter-connect public transit assets within intelligent transportation systems.

Its mobile data collectors gather video and audio along with GPS tracking and door open and close events, analyzing the data on the bus itself. Those units are ruggedized and crashworthy, serving as black boxes that hold data for accident investigations. Recorders take analog and IP channels at up to 1080P and 30 frames per second, with independently selectable resolutions. Drive caddies have passed MIL SPEC 810F for shock and vibration, and a thermal system warms the hard drive to its prescribed operating temperature before writing or reading in cold weather.

Fleet software called G4 Vision centralizes system health checks, driver behavior analysis, video management, live streaming, GPS, routing and mapping, and student tracking. An Automated Lane Enforcement product for transit buses is named on the home page. The company describes a Platform-as-a-Service business model. Testimonials on that page are attributed to school district transportation directors.

quote.text: Smart video and data solutions for transit and rail safety and effeciency.

organizations.description: TRACC travel-time and accessibility analysis plus transport datasets for government transport agencies

paragraphs: Basemap describes itself as an expert in transport software and data for accurate travel analysis. Its main product, TRACC, analyses travel times, optimises transit routes, and identifies accessibility gaps to key destinations. Government departments, city planners, transport operators, and consultants are named as the people who rely on those products.

Alongside the software, the company produces public transport timetables, average speed, and speed limit data for government agencies. DataCutter handles data management, with extraction tailored to a specific project. An electric vehicle routing product plans routes and forecasts energy consumption using more than 12 factors. Highways Analyst covers traffic data visualisation and analysis.

The case studies list the UK Department for Transport, which has been developing and publishing journey time statistics for over 10 years. Another describes OC Transpo, the municipal transit provider in Ottawa, starting to use TRACC for route and level of service planning. Leicestershire Tri-Service Fire and Rescue is described using Basemap speed datasets in its command and control system. An NHS case study covers a travel time analysis spanning emergency vehicles and private and public transport.
