paragraphs: SWARCO supplies road marking systems, traffic technology and industrial glass products to the people who build and operate roads. The group is headquartered in Wattens near Innsbruck, Austria, and runs an international network of plants, offices and partners. Its portfolio reaches across road marking, signage, urban traffic management, parking, highway and tunnel management, public transport and street lighting.

For cycling infrastructure the company offers coloured area markings, using green for general lanes and red to flag spots where the risk is higher. Pictograms are made from preformed thermoplastics so they sit in a rider's line of sight. Choosing a system means weighing location, traffic intensity, cost and environmental compatibility. A separate line covers runways, taxiways and aprons, where markings have to hold up against fuels, deicers, engine oils and hydraulic fluids.

Airfield marking systems have been tested and approved by the German Federal Institute for Material Research and Testing. Airport paints and marking products are made in compliance with FAA and Federal specifications as well as EASA. The company counts 5,300 transportation experts and traces its outlook to founder Manfred Swarovski.

paragraphs: The business sells a traffic signal priority control platform, marketed as Opticom, to cities that want essential vehicles moving through intersections without delay. It covers two jobs: preemption that clears a path for fire, police and ambulance crews, and signal priority that keeps buses and light rail closer to schedule.

Whichever communication method a city uses, the steps are the same. When a crew activates lights and siren, equipment on the vehicle sends a request ahead to equipped intersections, which then sequence the lights to green on the approach being used. As soon as the vehicle is through, the intersection goes back to its normal cycle. Agencies can run cloud, satellite positioning and infrared deployments side by side rather than replacing everything at once.

The buyers are the people who run those services: fire and police leadership, ambulance directors, transit operations staff and fleet managers. The site dates the technology back close to six decades. Fleets can be connected through integrations with a number of vehicle and telematics vendors.

Its 3D Land Cover product delivers planimetric vector layers for buildings, roads, driveways, sidewalks, water bodies, sports fields and overlapping tree canopy, with height attribution for buildings. The company states that features are extracted from high-resolution imagery with greater than 95% geometric accuracy. Partner imagery providers capture fresh imagery every year, which lets the company detect change and deliver annual updates. A separate transportation product covers sidewalks, crosswalks, medians, bike lanes, turning lanes, paint striping and intersections. Those layers carry attributes such as width, material and feature type, distinguishing a left turn lane from a right turn lane.

The transportation data is aimed at AEC firms, MPOs and DOTs. Stated uses include assessing sidewalk width and curb characteristics against ADA regulations. Another stated use is emergency services and dispatch planning, drawing on 3D maps of buildings, roads and driveways. Ecopia says it produces millions of square kilometers of vector data per month. It also announced a self-serve platform for high-precision geospatial data downloads.

An operations module manages work orders, service requests, crew scheduling, inventory, and day-to-day maintenance activities. A field-ready app handles inspections and work execution online or offline, keeping condition records current. An environmental module scores maintenance strategies using Global Warming Potential metrics. Agencies of any size can run it in the cloud or on premises.

The company says the dTIMS suite has been used by agencies in more than 40 countries over four decades. It gives its headquarters as Canada and Ireland, with implementations across North America, Europe, Asia-Pacific, Africa, and the Middle East. organizations.description: Safety Cloud digital alerting for DOT, fire and public works fleets

paragraphs: HAAS Alert sells a collision prevention service that sends real-time digital alerts warning drivers about nearby emergency vehicles and roadway hazards. Its customers are fleets that work at the roadside, including tow trucks, utility vehicles, waste management trucks, school buses and snowplows.

The system is wired to a vehicle's warning light bar or master switch, so alerting begins when crews turn on their lights and stops when they turn them off. Motorists install nothing, because alerts are broadcast directly to the navigation platforms they already use. Fleets can activate the service through three primary methods, depending on their existing setup. The company says drivers get up to 30 seconds of advance warning to slow down and move over.

The company traces its start to 2015, when co-founder and CEO Cory Hohs was almost struck by an ambulance on the road. He co-founded the business with Noah Levens and Jigar Patel. paragraphs: Compass IoT sells connected vehicle data for road networks, taken from the cars themselves rather than roadside equipment or phones. The company says more than 3,000 users globally use its connected vehicle data to understand traffic across their road networks. Its Road Intelligence platform presents that network-wide vehicle data in a browser.

The data comes from cloud-connected vehicles that have an internet connection. Compass says it receives over a billion connected vehicle data points every day from 64 different car manufacturers. Each record can carry location, timestamp, speed, acceleration, make and model, plus road attributes such as the speed limit and pavement type. Published case studies show clients using the tools for road safety, city planning, and infrastructure questions. One covers Sunshine Coast Council measuring how speed cushions retrofitted at a pedestrian crossing changed driver behaviour. Afterwards, average speed in both directions dropped to 22km/h. organizations.description: Cloud CMMS for municipal facilities, water plants and public works

paragraphs: Limble sells a computerized maintenance management system for the teams that keep equipment and facilities running. The pitch is simpler work orders, assets that keep running and more productivity across every site. The company says it is rated number one by more than 50,000 maintenance professionals.

A work order can start from a dashboard, an asset record or a vendor, with details and photos added from a phone. Anyone in the organization can submit a request by scanning a QR code or visiting a URL, with no account required. Preventive maintenance is scheduled automatically on time, usage or condition. Parts inventory triggers push and email alerts when stock runs low. The mobile app keeps working without a signal and syncs once the device reconnects. Listed integrations include SAP S/4HANA, Oracle NetSuite, Microsoft Dynamics 365 Business Central and QuickBooks Online.

Public sector users shown include a city water treatment plant in Lompoc. The company says a team at the City of Albuquerque was confidently using the mobile app after one day of training. It reports a 4.8 out of 5 rating on G2 and Capterra from well over 1,400 combined verified reviews. It also says customers typically see value in about three weeks.

quote.text: Simplify work orders, keep assets running smoothly, and increase productivity across every site.

paragraphs: Fulcrum sells a field operations platform that organizations use to run, record and close out work done away from an office. The pitch is aimed at teams still working from paper forms and a scatter of separate point tools.

Crews are given location-enabled apps on ordinary mobile devices in place of paperwork. They capture points, lines and polygons using the device's own GPS or a Bluetooth receiver. The collected records move into ArcGIS or other systems through APIs and formats such as shapefiles and GeoJSON. The company treats working without a signal as a baseline rather than an add-on.

State and local government is one of the named audiences, alongside utilities, construction and public works, with inspections and documentation for community projects. The home page states nearly 3,000 companies and 50,000 users in over 100 countries. On security, the company points to SCIM and SOC 2 compliance, and its timeline records an independent SOC 2 Type 1 certification. Spatial Networks Inc. is named as the maker of Fulcrum, and the company reports acquiring Wildnote to deepen environmental compliance work.

paragraphs: E.J. Ward sells automated fuel management systems to fleet operators. One platform covers fuel access, real-time monitoring, tank management, telematics, EV charging and reporting.

Access to the pump is controlled and every transaction accounted for, with reports meant to reveal anomalies. Storage tanks are watched from the same software that runs the fuel islands. Warnings for low levels and alarms for leaks or moisture can go out by text and email. EV chargers can be added to an existing installation as a fleet electrifies. There is also a fleet card for fuel and non-fuel transactions.

The about page dates the company to 1974. Its founder built the first fuel management system at the request of the City of San Antonio. The company describes itself as still family-owned and managed. paragraphs: Handtevy sells clinical workflow software for emergency medicine, pairing precision dosing and protocol access for clinicians with control and reporting for the administrators who oversee them. The buyers are agencies and hospitals looking to raise their standard of emergency care.

Handtevy Mobile puts precision dosing, real-time protocols, and clinical decision support directly in clinicians' hands. Weight-based calculations are cross-checked against clinical thresholds and customized to local protocols. An admin portal lets administrators manage pharmacology, protocols, order sets, and checklists across an organization and control exactly what clinicians see at the point of care. The software connects directly with ePCR and EHR platforms, which the company says involves no PHI exposure and no IT infrastructure.

The company says it is used by more than 200,000 clinicians in all 50 states. Pediatric Emergency Standards, Inc. has operated under the name Handtevy since 2010, offering evidence-based software to healthcare providers domestically and internationally. Its founder, Dr. Peter Antevy, is a practicing pediatric emergency medicine physician and EMS Medical Director. The company started in pediatrics and now describes its goal as improving emergency care for adults as well.

Maps carry pre-plans and custom layers for hydrants, hospitals, landing zones, flood hazards and fire trails. The app is native and designed to run entirely independent of internet connectivity. It connects to CAD systems and integrates Esri GIS map layers, pre-plans, FireMapper and AVL.

The site reports over 250,000 incidents managed, covering everyday calls and multi-agency coordination. The product is also positioned as a complete replacement for mobile data terminals in the fire service. San Bernardino County Fire is named as using it in every front line response unit. A case study describes Stockton Fire Department turning to it as an MDT replacement and fire ground accountability tool.

Allerium, formerly the Terrestrial and Wireless Networks segment, sells what the company calls dependable, life-saving solutions to public safety professionals.

On the public safety side, its equipment connects originating service providers and public safety answering points, the centers known as PSAPs. The company has announced Allerium Mira, a cloud-native call handling platform for NG9-1-1. It also offers Global Navigation Satellite Systems reference data feeds for location-based products and services. Its wireless portfolio includes end-to-end SMSC and Wireless Emergency Alerts solutions.

The business began as Comtech Laboratories, Inc., founded in 1967 in Smithtown, New York. It is now headquartered in Chandler, Arizona. Everything runs on one model delivered through four capabilities: speech to text, text generation, medical coding, and a framework for building agents. A single API call returns structured predictions along with supporting evidence and an audit trail. Common builds include an ambient scribe that captures a visit as it happens and turns it into a structured note. For electronic health record vendors, the same components are pitched as AI embedded in the core of the record system. Pricing is usage based and metered in credits.

Corti says more than a million patients receive care each week from providers using it. The about page describes a team spread across nine countries. The company states that every capability ships with HIPAA, GDPR, SOC 2, ISO 27001 and ISO 42001 built in. It also says its research is published at NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR, ACL and npj Digital Medicine.

Groups that need to stand something up quickly can order deployable kits, which ship with devices already carrying Advanced licenses.

Beyond the fire service, the company points to campus security teams and the organizers of large events such as marathons. 3AM says it belongs to purchasing vehicles including GSA and SAVVIK, which can let a buyer skip the RFP process. Deployments span retail, smart city, entertainment, education and transportation settings. Airports are one target, where the pitch is winning back customers from off-airport parking.

Digital signage placed at each intersection and parking aisle entrance keeps drivers from circling or driving into fully occupied areas. The displays are meant to blend into the existing streetscape, wrapping around lampposts. Occupancy data can be published to any other system through a REST API. Rather than launching another app, availability, search and guidance components can be built into an app visitors already use. Fully digital 360 degree displays can push updated messaging visible from all directions.

Cleverciti was founded in 2012 by Thomas Hohenacker and Konrad Prinz-Dreher. It reports deployments at over 200 locations in over 20 countries. Offices include European headquarters in Munich, Germany, and North American headquarters in Atlanta. Among the projects it describes, the company says it led an on-street guidance deployment in Cologne and supplied the hardware and software to RheinEnergie, the city utility company.

quote.text: The average driver spends 20 minutes looking for a parking space.

paragraphs: Gainwell sells the systems that run state Medicaid programs, tying together claims and encounter management, provider contracts, capitation and member benefits. Pharmacy is a separate line aimed at medication management and the total cost of care. Another line helps payers avoid and recover improper payments while detecting fraud.

The claims, encounters and financials module is presented as a modernization step built on automation and interoperability. An EDI gateway lets providers submit all their claims centrally, which the company says simplifies Medicaid billing. Its analytics platform is shaped around Medicaid data and federal compliance requirements. Provider management can be modernized in phases with Provider Flex, replaced outright with Provider+, or extended across state lines through a cross-state provider network.

The analytics page cites 52 state Medicaid programs. A case study on the home page covers provider enrollment in Vermont. That case study claims an 87.5% reduction in enrollment processing time. Its centralized credentialing platform is described as NCQA accredited. The company points to longstanding experience keeping Medicaid programs running with accurate data for decision making.

An automated adjudication engine sends processed claims on for payment and flags the ones that need further review. A separate provider management module handles enrollment through a configurable intake application. Before a provider is enrolled, a credentialing service verifies licensing and looks for sanctions. External Quality Review services sit alongside the software.

The company claims more than 30 years of public sector health experience. Its claims platform, it says, has earned CMS certification back to day one of operations with zero CMS findings. The provider module is described as CMS certified and compliant with National Institute of Standards and Technology requirements. A federal claims product is described as carrying an Authority to Operate in secure federal data centers.

Foothold was formed by Marlowe Greenberg, Tom Mitchell and Nick Scharlatt to take software developed at Community Access and make it available to other human services agencies. The company says it now supports hundreds of agencies across the nation, in Guam, and in Puerto Rico. It is a Certified B Corporation and states that it operates to standards of verified social and environmental performance. It also states that it is part of the global Pledge 1% movement, donating 1% of profits. Its timeline notes that Foothold joined Exym and KaleidaCare as part of Alpine Software Group.

Intake captures client data, settles eligibility in real time and connects people to services. The feature list runs from configurable workflows, encryption and role-based access to reporting, mobile access, client and partner portals, document management and case notes. Agencies can adapt forms, workflows and assessments themselves through a builder tool without writing code. An assistant called Cara is described as cutting documentation time and surfacing insights.

Users are nonprofits, government agencies and community organizations running programs such as aging services, behavioral health, homelessness and HMIS, workforce development and veterans services. The site claims more than 1,000 nonprofit organizations and local and state governments as users.

paragraphs: Bitfocus builds Clarity Human Services, the case record system a community uses to coordinate housing and services for people who are homeless. The pitch is aimed at continuums of care that need to move people into housing and show funders what happened.

The system covers coordinated entry, case planning, and outreach work done in the field on a phone. It joins up records from across the continuum so agencies stop keeping separate copies of the same client. Reports can be generated against HUD, SOC, HIPAA and local standards, and access is scoped by role. There is a separate configuration for domestic violence providers, where client safety and privacy are treated differently.

Alongside the software the company sells services: system design, health evaluation, training, and taking over day-to-day administration of the system. Bitfocus describes itself as founder-led and says it talks regularly with HUD, USICH, NAEH and Community Solutions.

paragraphs: CaseWorthy sells a software platform for case and program management in human services. Its buyers are nonprofit organizations and local and state governments that deliver social care programs.

The platform pulls programs, people, data and workflows together in one system rather than scattering them across separate tools. Agencies configure their own workflows, forms, assessments and service plans to match how each program operates. Reporting for funders is built into the platform instead of assembled in spreadsheets. Underneath sits a data lakehouse called CORE that consolidates information from CaseWorthy applications and outside sources. CORE ships baseline data models for particular sectors, including HMIS for homeless services, aging services and workforce development metrics.

Beyond case management there are applications for HCBS and I/DD providers covering care coordination, scheduling and Medicaid-supported service delivery. Another handles scheduling, documentation and billing for Home and Community-Based Services agencies. An AI copilot named Cara is embedded in the platform to reduce documentation time and surface insights. The company states that the organizations it serves touch more than 41% of the US population.

paragraphs: AidKit sells software that governments and nonprofits use to get cash aid and benefits into people's hands. The company says its work runs from local relief up to statewide and national programs. Among the listed uses is giving disaster survivors immediate relief through pre-positioned aid infrastructure.

Programs begin with application forms, which the company calls the first touchpoint between recipients and staff. Reviewers get application fraud detection tools built into the eligibility step. When digital checks do not fit a case, there are in-person verification fallbacks. Money moves by RTP, ACH, FedNow, or prepaid debit cards. Reporting arrives through preconfigured dashboards and one-click reports.

AidKit states that its platform is HIPAA-aligned, SOC 2 Type 2 compliant, and mapped to NIST practices. It also claims conformance with Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.1 AA. The City of Boulder partnered with AidKit to administer a guaranteed income program. A second case study covers a basic income pilot for people living in the Amazon.

organizations.name: Fortuna Health
organizations.description: Medicaid enrollment and renewal navigation for states and plans

paragraphs: Fortuna Health runs a digital service that helps people apply for and keep Medicaid and other government health coverage. It reaches consumers through providers and insurers rather than being offered directly to the public.

A person starts with a screening rather than a long form, and the site says an eligibility check can take as little as 30 seconds. From there the service guides the person through enrollment and renewal for the Medicaid programs that fit their circumstances. Status notifications follow each important administrative action, so deadlines are less likely to slip past unnoticed. The company states that every one of its navigators is certified and licensed to enroll. Live navigation is offered in more than one language.

Fortuna describes itself as modernizing the infrastructure for Medicaid and government health programs. Case studies on the site include Alomere Health System, described as cutting uncompensated care after working with Fortuna. The company says it is expanding nationwide.

quote.text: Everything you need for government coverage from enrollment to renewal.

paragraphs: Bark sells digital safety products for children, used at home and in schools. Schools set up their account through Google Workspace or Microsoft 365. For families there is a parental control app plus hardware, including a watch for children not yet ready for a phone.

The software looks for threats to physical and mental well-being and sends real-time alerts to caregivers or educators. Alerts span 26 categories including self-harm, suicidal ideation, disordered eating, cyberbullying, grooming, drugs and alcohol, violence, and sextortion. On the Bark Phone, caregivers can also manage app or website access, set contact permissions for calls and texts, and use location tracking. Beyond the software, the company offers on-site and virtual digital citizenship training.

The site credits CEO Brian Bason, a father of two, with founding the company. After the Parkland tragedy, it began offering free monitoring to all K-12 schools in the United States. The company says Bark for Schools now helps protect students in thousands of districts. A community partners program extends the same work to nonprofits, funders, treatment centers, and state agencies.

paragraphs: Deledao sells web filtering to K-12 schools, built on patented technology the company says analyzes each webpage as a human would. The product line later grew to cover student safety and classroom management.

The filter blurs, mutes, and screens inappropriate images and video frame by frame. It detects gaming behavior from keyboard and mouse activity without logging keystrokes. Proxy sites students use to bypass filtering are caught automatically. Teachers get visibility into student tabs or screens. Websites can be allowed or blocked by group or by individual student. The wellness product looks for cyberbullying, self-harm, and toxic language across platforms. High-risk alerts receive human review and escalation to the district.

The company names Shuang Ji as its chief executive. Its first product, a web filter using real-time AI, launched in 2019. It says it now supports schools in the United States, Canada, Europe, New Zealand, and Australia. Case studies on the site describe schools adopting the filter for CIPA compliance and student safety.

organizations.description: AI-based weapons screening gateways for schools, venues and public buildings

paragraphs: Xtract One makes AI-powered concealed weapons detection systems for building entrances. The company sells them for schools, hospitals, and other public venues.

The premise is that the systems flag actual threats while ignoring laptops, phones, keys, and everyday items. SmartGateway uses AI-powered passive magnetic field sensor arrays to identify firearms and bladed weapons. It is rated to screen up to 4,000 individuals per hour per lane. A second system, Xtract One Gateway, is built for places where people carry a medium volume of personal belongings, with no conveyor belts or divestment bins. Multiple units are managed centrally through Xtract One View.

On privacy, the company states that SmartGateway collects no personally identifiable information and does not use facial recognition. It also says the magnetic field sits well below safety limits set by the IEEE, FCC, and international health organizations. Among the deployments it publicizes is Manor ISD, which it says put Gateway across its high school campuses as one of the first Texas districts to do so at scale. Another cites Community Health Network preventing 6,007 weapons across 9 entry points in 6 months.

paragraphs: Anonymous Alerts sells a reporting platform that gives students, staff and community members a way to raise concerns before they turn into serious incidents. It is used by K-12 schools, districts, colleges and public safety organizations nationwide.

Students can anonymously report bullying, behavioral concerns, threats of violence or mental health risks through a mobile or web interface designed for use across age groups. Designated school administrators receive the information immediately. From a centralized dashboard they can review, manage and investigate reports. Staff can hold real-time conversations with tip submitters while the submitter keeps anonymity. Reporting categories, workflows, notification settings and response protocols can be configured for each organization. A companion panic escalation app lets staff instantly alert administrators and safety personnel.

The company says the system helps schools comply with state laws requiring anonymous reporting systems for school safety and violence prevention. A dedicated page covers Alyssas Law compliance in New York. Newtown Public School District is named on the site as one district that chose the reporting app. The company lists United States patents on the technology, with additional US and non-US patents pending. Anonymous 2-way Communications is registered with the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office.

quote.text: Give students, staff, and community members a safe way to report concerns before they turn into serious incidents.

The company positions itself as a single source for mass emergency notification systems and critical communication needs. Its stated goal is to help colleges and universities, K-12 schools, corporations and government organizations solve unified mass notification problems.

The approach is network based, using an organization's existing IP network to turn VoIP phones into alerting devices. Hardware fills the gaps, including a wall-mounted alerting device meant for places with no existing notification endpoints. Outdoor coverage is handled by high power speaker arrays.

The company traces its origin to 2001, when an F3 tornado ripped through the University of Maryland campus. Alertus was founded the following year. It reports serving more than 2,500 organizations across more than 40 countries. Those customers are described as spanning higher education, K-12, industrial, corporate, healthcare, government and military sectors.

paragraphs: Senstar makes security systems for protecting infrastructure and facilities. The portfolio runs across video management, video analytics, access control and perimeter intrusion detection sensors. Products are designed, manufactured and tested in North America.

Perimeter sensors mount on the fence, sit above ground or lie buried, and are meant to locate intruders before they enter a secure area. The MultiSensor unit packs short-range radar, an image sensor, dual PIR, an accelerometer and a high frequency sensor into one device. An embedded engine weighs the data from each of those sensors to decide whether an event is a threat. On the software side, Senstar Symphony is a modular platform for security management and data intelligence. It works with analog and IP cameras, encoders, DVRs and other video devices from many manufacturers.

The company organizes its work by sector, pointing to electrical utility assets exposed to service interruptions from vandalism, theft and targeted attacks. Water treatment plants, pumping stations and storage tanks are another market it names. It states over 40 years of experience working with correctional institutions. paragraphs: Dedrone by Axon sells counter-drone systems that secure fixed locations such as airports, correctional facilities and critical infrastructure from unauthorized drones. Law enforcement, military and public safety organizations are named as the buyers for its mobile unit.

A fixed installation combines radio-frequency sensors, radar and pan-tilt-zoom cameras over the airspace at a site. The radio-frequency sensors analyse signals to detect and locate both the drone and its pilot. Cameras add visual verification of a drone incursion. Command and control software called DedroneTracker.AI fuses those tracks and reports drone and pilot location. A towable trailer packages the same mix for temporary sites and is described as set up in less than twenty minutes. A city-wide option skips installed equipment altogether, letting users mark alert zones and get notified when drones enter them.

The company states that its fixed-site product is deployed at over 829 sites globally. It says its customers include military organizations, airports, correctional facilities, stadiums and critical infrastructure sites. The city-wide app is described as available in over 50 cities.

paragraphs: Hidden Level sells radio-frequency sensing hardware and data services to government, defense and commercial security teams. The sensing is passive, which the company says leaves the equipment undetected and hard to jam.

The Breaker sensor is built for fixed sites and is meant to coexist with infrastructure and telecom equipment already there. The Surge mounts to land and water vehicles and is made to withstand harsh conditions. Customers who would rather not run hardware can buy data from a global sensor network the company owns, operates and maintains. That service pinpoints drone operator location and lets users define zones so alerts arrive only for activity in chosen areas. Data reaches other systems through an open API secured with FIPS 140-2 compliant cryptography, or through a web interface.

Stated uses include protecting airspace around stadiums, airports and buildings, and preventing contraband drone deliveries to correctional facilities. The hardware page cites FCC compliance along with TRL9 and MIL-STD-810 testing. The company says its sensors analyze the physical characteristics of signals without decoding private information. Researchers can reach the collected captures through APIs for training and benchmarking work.

organizations.description: Access control and perimeter security for airports and critical government sites

paragraphs: Gallagher Security designs and manufactures integrated security products across access control, perimeter security, intruder alarms, and cybersecurity. Its customers range from small businesses to enterprise organizations and critical infrastructure sites. Systems are sized from a single door to thousands across multiple sites.

Access control runs on card readers, mobile credentials, and biometric devices that verify permissions. Controllers act as the central hub, processing access requests and communicating with connected systems. Roles, schedules, and activity are managed in Command Centre, the company's centralized platform, with customizable dashboards and reporting. On the perimeter, high-tensile pulse fences form a visual barrier and deliver safe, short pulses that deter intruders. Sensors alert a team the moment a fence is touched. Perimeter protection is a native part of Command Centre, the same software that runs access control and intruder detection. It works with most existing fence types, so a site can add detection without replacing its fencing.

The company says it has been doing this work for over 35 years. Listed uses include safeguarding energy plants, utilities, airports, and seaports with multi-layered systems. Another is securing classified areas and complying with defense standards. Published case studies include one on the Indiana Department of Corrections. A featured project spans campus life for students and staff across 143 buildings and 150 research centres.

paragraphs: UVeye builds automated inspection systems that scan the full exterior, undercarriage, and tires of a vehicle in seconds. Dealerships use the scans to document pre-existing damage and avoid unnecessary claims. Seaports and logistics hubs use touchless inspections to speed vehicle handoffs and settle disputes. Bus and truck operators run standardized inspections to improve compliance.

A scan combines high-resolution imaging, sensors, and patented AI to surface problems the eye cannot catch. Findings run from tire wear and misalignment to leaks, rust, and underbody damage. Output arrives as images and measurements of dents, scratches, and undercarriage issues. Automatic notifications flag critical issues that need immediate attention.

Brothers Amir and Ohad Hever founded UVeye in 2016. The first application was undercarriage security screening, which grew into a platform that scans whole vehicles. Systems are now deployed across hundreds of dealerships, fleets, rental agencies, and manufacturing lines worldwide. The company names Amazon, General Motors, Volvo, and CarMax among the companies using it. It reports over $380 million raised.

Its buyers are criminal justice agencies that supervise people in the community rather than behind bars. The company claims more than 30 years of field experience in over 30 countries, supporting hundreds of programs.

Caseloads span GPS tracking, radio frequency monitoring and alcohol testing, all watched from a single platform. One home curfew unit connects over an LTE network, Wi-Fi or a landline and includes a handset for voice communication. The command center for a monitoring program is EM Manager, and a mobile version lets staff perform essential monitoring functions in the field. The monitoring centers operate around the clock, every day of the week. Customizable services on offer include alert triage, outbound alert resolution calls and officer notifications.

Corrections agencies and probation services worldwide are named as the customers, whether they are starting new programs or expanding existing ones. The pitch to those agencies is an alternative to incarceration that lowers recidivism, improves reintegration and reduces prison overcrowding. Boaz Raviv was appointed chief executive of Attenti in 2017.

paragraphs: Overstory sells vegetation intelligence to electric utilities, from investor-owned utilities to municipalities and cooperatives. The analysis rests on satellite imagery, which in one European project was used to identify 37 species of vegetation.

The company notes that vegetation management is typically a utility's greatest operations budget item. Its pitch is spending less on unnecessary trimming and more on riskier areas. Utilities can see strike trees, declining trees and hazard trees individually or aggregated. Encroachment risk, hazard trees and species identification can be laid over wildfire risk maps to show where trimming matters most. The same data lets a utility verify and document risk reduction from work that contractors completed.

Risk reports are meant to support data-driven conversations with regulators, insurers and executives. Indra den Bakker and Anniek Schouten founded the company in Lisbon in 2018. The company says it has worked with more than 50 investor-owned utilities and cooperatives across the Americas and Europe.

organizations.name: E-ONE
organizations.description: Fire trucks, aerials and rescue apparatus for fire departments

paragraphs: E-ONE manufactures custom, heavy-duty fire trucks. The line covers pumpers, tankers, aerial ladders and platforms, rescues, industrial units and aircraft rescue and firefighting vehicles. Those trucks reach fire departments through a dealer network.

The company was founded in 1974 by an industrial engineer and says it designed and manufactured the first modular, extruded aluminum fire truck and body. A company timeline runs from that first modular all-aluminum body through decades of chassis, ladders and platforms. The same timeline records testing cabs in excess of the European ECE-R29 crash worthiness standard. Recent entries include an all-electric fire truck called the Vector.

E-ONE writes that first responders and the communities they serve have relied on it for 50 years. The timeline notes that American Industrial Partners purchased the company. Company news reports an order from the Chicago Fire Department for 120 emergency vehicles from E-ONE and Wheeled Coach. Another post describes a $23.5 million expansion expected to increase aerial production by 35 percent and add 100 new jobs in Ocala.

organizations.name: Ferrara Fire Apparatus
organizations.description: Custom fire apparatus and aerials for municipal fire departments

paragraphs: Ferrara Fire Apparatus manufactures custom, heavy-duty fire trucks. Its line covers pumpers, aerials, industrial, wildland, and rescue apparatus. The company works hands-on with municipal and industrial fire departments.

It offers a custom chassis line that it says has exceeded all safety and strength tests. Those chassis use Domex steel frame rails, with optional full-length liners. They are combined with extruded aluminum fire bodies. Welds are made with a root pass and two filler passes rather than tack welds.

Ferrara describes itself as the only apparatus manufacturer using marine-grade aluminum. Trucks are built at the company facility in Holden, Louisiana. The company states that over 6,000 of its fire trucks have been delivered around the world. It also points to more than 30 years of work in the Louisiana oil and gas region behind its industrial pump expertise. Many of its team members serve as volunteer firefighters.

organizations.name: Fybr
organizations.description: IoT parking sensors and smart city occupancy data for municipalities

paragraphs: Fybr sells parking technology and an operations platform built on privacy by design. It turns anonymous, real-time parking activity into the tools that run an operation and the insights to improve it. The range covers every space, facility, and curb.

The foundation is the FybrPuck, the company's own fourth-generation occupancy sensor, a compact, self-powered, wireless edge device. It covers on-street and off-street spaces, loading zones, no parking zones, ADA spaces, and EV charging stations. Occupancy status feeds real-time guidance through a mobile application, web browsers, and dynamic wayfinding signage. For enforcement, officers can be directed to potential violations rather than running continuous sweeps. Where an ordinance requires vehicle identification, license plate recognition scans vehicles for compliance. Payment is pay-per-use inside the mobile application. A dashboard tracks turnover, session duration, dwell times, rule compliance, peak demand, and utilization trends.

The homepage carries testimonials from municipal staff, one crediting the real-time enforcement app with helping officers identify issues and respond to violations. Another says the sensor technology improved parking enforcement operations in Marysville. A third says that after the parking system was implemented, spots could be found easily through the app.

organizations.name: eleven-x
organizations.description: Smart parking sensors and LoRaWAN networks for cities

paragraphs: eleven-x sells a smart parking system to cities, campuses, and private organizations. The product, eXactpark, monitors occupancy in real time and turns it into data for whoever manages the spaces.

Occupancy readings come from a sensor the company says is designed to withstand even the harshest climates. Drivers are told where available spaces are. Operators get real-time overstay alerts to support enforcement. The platform is also aimed at performance parking, dynamic pricing, and curbside management.

Buyers are municipalities, campuses, and other organizations. For public agencies and schools, the company lists cooperative purchasing through Sourcewell. eleven-x was founded in 2014 as a wireless solution provider. It is headquartered in Waterloo, Ontario. Since 2020 its focus has been parking.

organizations.name: CurbIQ
organizations.description: Curb inventory, regulation digitization and curb management for cities

paragraphs: CurbIQ sells curb management software to cities, universities and airports, giving them one place to keep curb regulations and usage data. The problem it addresses is balancing curb access among pedestrians, parking, deliveries, rideshares and vendors.

The platform pulls curb regulation and usage data from multiple sources into a single database. Records are held in curb data standards including CDS, D-TRO and CurbLR. Map overlays show when and where regulations are in effect, and the tool models what a proposed policy change would do. Data sharing runs through APIs so couriers, ride-hailing companies and navigation platforms can see the current rules.

CurbIQ was founded by Peter Richards, formerly chair of the Institute of Transportation Engineers Parking Standing Committee. The team managed the Southern California Association of Governments Curb Space Management Study. The company belongs to the Open Mobility Foundation, a nonprofit that builds open-source tools for cities. CurbIQ itself is a product of the design firm Arcadis.

quote.text: We digitize curbside regulations, empowering cities and businesses to create a planet-positive future.

organizations.name: AIMS Parking (EDC Corporation)
organizations.description: Parking citation, permit and enforcement management software for agencies

paragraphs: AIMS is parking management software from EDC Corporation, built to handle citations, permits and field enforcement for whoever runs the parking operation. The company writes that the system is meant to scale whether the buyer runs a city, a university, a hospital campus or an airport.

Citations are entered in real time from the field, with photos, GPS coordinates and notes attached to each one. Permits can be virtual or physical, and the software carries waitlists, renewals and permit prioritization. Fixed and mobile plate recognition cameras push reads, hits and occupancy data back into the system as they happen. A self-service portal gives the public round-the-clock access to payments, permits and appeals.

The site states that more than 300 clients in the United States and Canada use the software. A move onto the platform is described as taking twelve to sixteen weeks. The company describes the system as PCI and SOC 2 compliant. It also says the developers who write the software are the ones who support it.

quote.text: Whether you manage a city, a university, a hospital campus or an airport, AIMS is designed to scale.

organizations.name: BusBoss (Orbit Software)
organizations.description: School bus routing and scheduling software for K-12 districts

paragraphs: BusBoss is a school bus routing and transportation management platform for districts that need accurate planning, real-time visibility, and dependable daily operations. The software is aimed at transportation directors, school administrators, and bus contractors.

Districts can create efficient routes, track buses live, verify student boarding, and respond to changes without paper routes or disconnected systems. A fleet optimization tool automatically generates routes for individual or combined schools while adhering to load counts, bell times, and travel constraints. Route planning shows bus stops and house locations on integrated GIS maps with satellite view underlays. Two GPS applications, TRIPpatrol and STUDENTpatrol, integrate with the transportation software system.

The company says its routing software is built on more than 25 years of experience. It describes an affordable system that allows for unlimited users without a per-user annual fee. Implementation comes with data conversions meant to maintain the integrity of current student, driver, and routing information. A SuccessRoute training program helps customers learn and get more out of the software.

quote.text: You can create efficient routes, track buses live, verify student boarding, and respond quickly to changes without relying on paper routes or disconnected systems.

organizations.name: Bytecurve
organizations.description: School bus operations, driver pay and dispatch software for districts

paragraphs: Bytecurve sells operations software for school bus fleets, tying routing and GPS data into driver management, dispatching and payroll. The company pitches its payroll application as one that catches pay inconsistencies, and says it was built by people who worked in K12 transportation. Private student transportation contractors are one audience for it, and school districts are the other.

Real-time integration with routing systems and GPS lets dispatchers reassign drivers on the fly and break routes apart. Time and attendance removes manual calculation of employee guarantees, contracts and overtime, and runs through a mobile app or a garage-based tablet. Drivers check in and out remotely, view schedules and receive messages on their phones. Dispatchers get immediate alerts for late or missing drivers, and access to the driver app is limited to authorized employees through a customer-specific code.

The company says dozens of districts use the system across more than 40,000 buses and 50,000 drivers. Its founders claim over 30 years of combined transportation experience, with a focus on student transportation. One case study states that Rome Public Schools reduced payroll by $30,000 per month.

paragraphs: First Student moves students to and from school, with a stated mission of the safest, most reliable and most efficient ride. School districts are its partners, in communities big and small.

The company reports more than 48,000 vehicles, including electric buses. It lists over 530 locations across two countries. By its own count, those buses carry 4.8 million student journeys a day. A technology platform called HALO oversees the transportation journey. One piece of it, First View, is a vehicle tracker app for parents and caregivers. Buses can also be rented for events and field trips through a charter quote.

The company says it has provided a safe and reliable experience for nearly half a century. In one award citation it was recognized in a transportation category for HALO's safety tools, predictive maintenance and real-time visibility. A mascot named Safety Dog teaches students about safe school bus behavior. The mascot travels a coast-to-coast, back-to-school tour. Its leadership team spans transportation management, technology and electrification.

organizations.name: Durham School Services
organizations.description: Contracted school bus transportation for K-12 districts nationwide

paragraphs: Durham School Services runs contracted student transportation for school districts across the country. The company describes itself as part of a network that carries more than a million students every day.

A district that contracts with Durham hands over routing, fleet, staffing and maintenance. Beyond daily routes, the company offers specialized service designed around student-specific needs and IEP requirements. It also covers field trips, athletics and special events. Support can extend to driver recruiting, screening and training. Fleet procurement, maintenance and lifecycle planning can sit with the company as well.

Durham has worked with school districts since 1917. It began as a three-bus operation in California's San Gabriel Valley, with early expertise in transporting students with specialized needs. Local operating teams are backed by the broader Summit School Services network for safety, recruiting, maintenance and technology.

quote.text: Getting students to school safely, on time and ready to learn

organizations.name: 247Security
organizations.description: School bus camera and DVR surveillance systems for districts

paragraphs: 247Security sells video recording systems for vehicle fleets, and school bus video is the product it puts at the front of its site. Its school bus offering pairs on-vehicle cameras with cloud fleet management software. Public transit and motor coach operators are a second market listed on the site.

Video comes off the vehicle wirelessly over cellular or wi-fi rather than by pulling hard drives, and is retrieved from cloud servers. Staff can watch a bus live over a cellular link while recording continues uninterrupted. The lineup also includes a compact sensor that detects smoking and vaping devices on board. The company says its storage device carries a lifetime warranty and keeps recorded video encrypted.

Products are designed, assembled and packaged in Canada and the United States. Installation is handled by the company's own teams, which it says work on more than 3000 buses a year. Feature decisions draw on transportation directors, shop leaders and mechanics, according to the about page. Support is pitched around reaching a person on the phone rather than a call centre.

quote.text: Fleet video, made easy.

paragraphs: GreenPower Motor Company builds battery-electric buses and trucks for schools, public transit, delivery work, vanpools, micro-transit and shuttles. It began in 2010 with the goal of making battery-electric buses and trucks affordable, durable and easy to deploy.

Vehicles are built from the ground up to be electric rather than converted from existing diesel platforms. The BEAST school bus comes with air ride suspension, pass-through storage and seating for up to 90 students. The EV Star line is offered in configurations holding up to 19 passengers, with ADA wheelchair provisions or cargo delivery setups.

The first BEAST buses went to Rialto Unified School District after clearing 292 certifications from the California Highway Patrol. Corporate headquarters is in Vancouver, Canada. A sales and administration office sits in Rancho Cucamonga, California, and United States assembly takes place in Porterville. The company trades on Nasdaq under the ticker GP. Leasing options are offered to help buyers put a fleet together.

quote.text: The GreenPower chassis has been engineered to be the strongest, safest, and most durable product on the market

organizations.name: Highland Electric Fleets
organizations.description: Electric school bus fleet-as-a-service subscriptions for districts

paragraphs: Highland Electric Fleets sells fleet electrification as a service to school districts, municipalities and fleet operators. The company was founded in 2019.

Customers hand over the whole job, and Highland plans, procures, implements and optimizes the electric fleet on their behalf. A performance guarantee reimburses customers for down time if the fleet is not charged and route-ready. The commercial pitch is that an electric fleet can be operated at or below the cost of running a diesel one. Highland also secures grants and incentives on behalf of the agencies it works with.

The company serves as the Official Electric School Bus Provider of the LA28 Olympic and Paralympic Games and Team USA. It points to vehicle-to-grid work and to managing some of the largest electric school bus fleets in the country. Maintenance figures cited on the site come from Twin Rivers Unified School District, which operates 58 EV buses. The site also counts the states where it has operational and contracted projects.

quote.text: mission is to make electric fleets accessible and affordable for all.

organizations.name: Skedda
organizations.description: Space and facility booking platform used by municipal and campus facilities

paragraphs: Skedda sells booking software for shared workplace space, giving staff self-serve booking of desks, rooms and other resources. The company frames it as one platform to book space and manage operations, backed by data about how the square footage is used.

People browse desks by neighborhood on an interactive floor plan and see where colleagues are sitting. A desk takes three clicks to reserve from a desktop, a phone or Microsoft Teams. Check-in by QR code or automatic Wi-Fi connection frees desks that nobody claims. Administrators set approvals, quotas, priority windows and check-in rules that govern when and where people book. Room bookings sync with Outlook or Google calendar events, and release automatically when the calendar event is declined. Reporting covers desk and room usage, peak hours and booking patterns over time.

The company says it has 8,000 global customers across 28 countries and 3m active users. For campuses it describes cleaning buffers between sessions and approval workflows for spaces in high demand. Customers named on the desk booking page include Toyota Connected EU, PVH Corp, Columbia University, Aon, and Pella Windows & Doors. The site states SOC 2 Type 2 certification with independently audited controls. It also states GDPR compliance, with data processing agreements available.

quote.text: Skedda replaces the daily scramble of calendar conflicts, room hoarding, and manual admin with a conference room booking system that runs itself.

paragraphs: Campminder makes management software for summer camps of every shape, from day camps to sleepaway programs and from twenty campers to two thousand. It is sold by role, with separate material pitched to camp owners and directors and to registrars and administrators.

Families register from their own devices, and the forms they fill out land in one organized place. Payments are collected and tracked inside the enrollment hub. A transportation planner lets staff drag and drop buses, routes, schedules and shuttles. Messaging tools pull camp data to send specific emails and texts to campers, parents, staff and alumni. An API distributes report data instantly to other departments. A companion app gives parents a photo feed that finds their child using facial recognition.

The company describes itself as a customer-centric business 22 years strong. Both product suites are tiered on the number of enrolled campers in the camp. Onboarding covers website integrations, historic data import and merchant account setup in fewer than three weeks. Camps across North America are described as using the platform to coordinate the logistics of running their programs.

quote.text: Campminder is made for all kinds of camps. We mean it.

organizations.description: Campground reservation and management software for public and private campgrounds

paragraphs: Campspot sells campground management and reservation software to park owners and operators. It also runs a consumer booking site where campers search campgrounds, RV parks, cabins, and glamping stays.

On the operations side the software reaches from the front desk to housekeeping. Dashboards and reports track a park's health metrics. The platform connects to dozens of third-party applications. Software customers can show real-time availability on the consumer site for guests to search, discover, and book. Listing on that marketplace is not sold separately from the software.

Campspot serves more than 3,500 parks across the U.S. and Canada, including private RV parks and campgrounds, public parks, franchises, multi-park groups, and investment groups. The company was founded in 2015 to bring a modern booking experience to the camping industry. The marketplace itself launched in the winter of 2020. Campspot is headquartered in Grand Rapids, Michigan.

quote.text: Founded in 2015, Campspot was created to bring a modern booking experience to the camping industry.

organizations.name: Camis
organizations.description: Reservation and park operations systems for state, provincial and federal parks

paragraphs: Camis sells reservation and park management software to government-operated parks, marinas and harbors, work the company says it has done for more than 46 years. Visitors use it to book a camping trip, a day-use pass, a harbor stay or a ticketed event.

Bookings can come in ahead of time, at the gate, or through a call center. Payment runs through the same platform, whether the visitor is online or standing at a park office. A combined on-site and webstore system handles merchandise sales with real-time inventory tracking, and the company describes it as fully PCI and SOC compliant. Field staff get a separate enforcement app called Sidekick, built for the job assignments of wardens and rangers. On the back end, staff work from real-time data and customizable reports.

The company describes its origin as outdoor enthusiasts who saw a better way to connect people to parks. Its own timeline starts with a first park contract at Craigleith Provincial Park. The same timeline records that the business was acquired by Banyan Software. It also claims continued expansion across more than 30 national, provincial and state parks.

quote.text: Connecting People to a World of Memorable Experiences

organizations.name: ROLLER
organizations.description: Venue management, ticketing and POS for aquatic centers and attractions

paragraphs: ROLLER sells venue management software to attractions businesses, pulling bookings, point of sale, memberships and reporting into a single platform. It is cloud-based and built for growing attractions businesses, meant to stand in for the several tools a venue would otherwise run. The company describes the platform as powering more than 3,000 attractions.

Ticketing is built around flexible bookings and add-on sales for both staff and guests. Operators running more than one site can hold branding consistent across locations and publish changes from a single headquarters account. Plans are tiered, with an entry level covering online and in-venue selling and day-to-day operations. Higher tiers are aimed at established venues wanting more customization and support.

One franchise operator, We Rock the Spectrum, put the platform into more than 120 locations over six months. Another customer, Area 51, is described on the site as an Australian family entertainment center operator running venues across multiple states. The company also publishes a guest survey it says covers 1,500 people.

organizations.name: Aquarius Spectrum
organizations.description: Fixed acoustic leak monitoring sensors for municipal water networks

paragraphs: Aquarius Spectrum sells acoustic leak detection systems that let water utilities find and prevent leaks. The stated aim is cutting non-revenue water and putting resources where they matter. The products are meant to suit water networks of any pipe material and size.

Sensors take a daily audio sample and send it to a cloud server for analysis. Every two coupled sensors are then correlated, and when the same noise turns up in the same location an alert gives the exact position of the leak. The AQS-SYS platform pairs those sensors with algorithms, big data analytics and CAT-M or NB-IoT connectivity. Accelerometers fit externally on hydrants above ground and on pressure and air valves below. A hydrophone covers large transmission lines of 24 inches and above, plus plastic and PVC pipe. Where continuous monitoring is not wanted, mobile products let a utility survey large areas instead.

Alongside the hardware the company sells what it calls Human-as-a-Service, described as ongoing human support, expertise and system updates. AQS states that it is a company of the Aliaxis Group. It reports receiving ISO/IEC 27001:2022 certification. Published case studies include the national agency that manages Singapore's water loop.

organizations.name: Electro Scan
organizations.description: Machine-based pipe defect and leak assessment for municipal sewer and water - exhibited at AWWA ACE 2026

paragraphs: Electro Scan sells leak detection and lead pipe location work for water and sewer systems. The company says municipal sewer utilities and sewer contractors use it to pin down the location, measurement and flow of defects inside a pipe before a repair or replacement job.

The method rests on a simple claim: pipe defects that leak water also leak electricity, so a defect shows up whether or not it happens to be leaking during the inspection. A low voltage conductivity probe travels through the pipe at 45 to 60 feet per minute, locating and measuring defects as it goes. Crews can then create summary and detail level reports for a team to review. The flagship probe is built for gravity mains between 6 and 30 inches in diameter, and the company says agencies and contractors use it worldwide.

Electro Scan lists ISO 9001:2015 certification for quality management systems. Its case studies page includes a North American benchmark study comparing closed-circuit television inspection with focused electrode leak location on gravity sewer mains. Other write-ups describe a Florida utility dealing with excessive inflow and infiltration in its gravity collection system.

paragraphs: InfoSense sells the equipment, software and services that let a city work out which sewer pipes actually need cleaning before crews are sent out. The centrepiece is a handheld acoustic device that scores blockage conditions in small diameter gravity sewer lines.

A transmitter goes on one open manhole and a receiver on the next. Within a few minutes the display returns a rating from zero to ten showing whether the pipe is clear or obstructed. Nothing touches the flow and nobody has to enter a confined space. The company reports that two people can cover fifty to sixty segments in a day. Readings feed a companion platform that records, organises and maps the results. Data can be pushed out to mapping and spreadsheet tools already in use.

Buyers are public works departments and utilities moving away from cleaning on a fixed calendar toward cleaning based on measured condition. The company states that more than 1,350 utilities have used the tool. One published case study covers a small town serving just under ten thousand people. That town is reported to have cut its cleaning workload by more than half.

paragraphs: BlueConduit sells predictive modeling tools to water systems that need to manage risk and make data-driven decisions about their distribution assets. The customers are municipalities and water utilities.

One product builds community-specific models that pinpoint high-risk lead and galvanized service lines, which lets a utility classify its inventory and prioritize replacements. Another scores every main segment in a network for likelihood and consequence of failure. A third uses statistical models to confirm the absence of lead in a water system. The company says model processes, important features, and performance metrics are always shared with customers. Output is integrated with Esri ArcGIS.

The work started at the University of Michigan, where faculty and student researchers saw a use for data science in removing toxic lead from the water supply. In Flint the company used predictive analytics to identify where to dig for lead service lines. A published case study describes Des Moines Water Works classifying unknown service lines and reducing uncertainty by 75% in six months. BlueConduit cites ongoing relationships with EPA and state regulators. Its stated mission is to empower communities to prioritize health and sustainability through data science.

paragraphs: 2NDNATURE sells stormwater software built on GIS, aimed at streamlining compliance, asset tracking and reporting. Buyers fall into two camps, those tackling MS4 permit requirements and those advancing corporate water stewardship. Two products carry that work, 2NFORM and Rainsteward, both pitched at streamlining compliance and showing measurable results.

2NFORM is organized around municipal permit programs, covering post-construction, industrial and commercial, and illicit discharge detection and elimination. In Oceanside it was connected to the city's existing Esri-based GIS and met local security and IT standards. For longer-range planning the company built a Stormwater Asset Management Model that serves as a decision-making tool. Fed with the storm sewer system and local costs, it lets a city explore how twenty years of asset management would affect the health of that system. Rainsteward points the other way, at owners trying to cut costs and get more value out of stormwater investments.

The customers shown are city stormwater programs; Oceanside had nine separate systems tracking inspections and compliance tasks before it changed course. Salinas is described as a Phase I MS4 with a population exceeding 150,000. That city worked with 2NDNATURE to develop a comprehensive Asset Improvement Plan. Private owners appear too: a real estate company called Reveler implemented Rainsteward in a series of six steps.

organizations.description: Touchless self-service check-in and bag drop technology for airports

paragraphs: Elenium Automation makes self-service check-in kiosks and bag drops for airports and airlines. The company describes bag drops that cut queues and keep passengers moving through the terminal. It pitches the same equipment to airlines as a way of activating their services instantly at any airport.

The product suite is called VYGR, short for Voyager, and covers self-service steps of the passenger journey. Elenium says it is built on computer vision, AI, modern UX, and a cloud backbone. The company reports achieving over 97% first-time read rates and sub-15 second processing speeds on its bag drop. In 2020 it launched HealthGate, described as an automated, touchless fever detection device approved by both the Australian Therapeutic Goods Administration and the European Medicines Agency. The company also says it achieved ISO 13485 certification.

Elenium was founded in 2015 by Aaron Hornlimann, Fred Melki, and Heinz Corona. It says it now operates in over 35 airports, serving more than 45 airlines and 250 million passengers annually across Australasia, Asia, Central Asia, the Middle East, Europe, and the UK. For service, the company describes partnering with Unisys to provide global 24 by 7, remote and onsite support coverage.

organizations.description: Indoor wayfinding and blue-dot mapping for airports and public venues

paragraphs: Pointr sells indoor mapping and wayfinding software that turns a venue, office or campus into interactive digital maps. Customers put those maps into their own apps, on the web, or on kiosks, using dedicated mobile and web SDKs. One stated use is guiding travelers to their gate with turn-by-turn updates and estimated arrival times.

Maps are generated from CAD files by an AI tool called MapScale. Blue dot positioning indoors runs on Bluetooth Low Energy rather than a satellite signal. The site says accuracy holds without fingerprinting or geomagnetism, so the system needs less ongoing maintenance. Geofences drawn on the map trigger actions when visitors enter or leave a zone.

The company describes itself as the top choice for Fortune 100 companies. Its homepage names product wayfinding work at The Home Depot. It states that its positioning technology is patented, with more than ten years of testing and development behind it. On privacy, the geofencing page says visitor location data is collected anonymously and aligned with GDPR.

organizations.name: Oracle Utilities
organizations.description: Metering, CIS, billing and grid analytics for public power utilities

paragraphs: Oracle Utilities sells software to energy and water providers for serving customers and for managing networks and assets. Billing is presented as one place holding the data, processes and insights a utility needs.

Billing workflows use AI anomaly detection intended to cut errors on complex accounts. The outage management system is deployed for electric, gas, water or wastewater networks and coordinates restoration with field, mutual aid and asset management teams. Field crews record network updates straight into the network management system rather than relaying them verbally to control room staff. Analytics tools look for trends among customers and pick out electric vehicle owners for targeted recommendations and service. A commercial account product pulls billing history, consumption, appointment scheduling and service interruptions into a single dashboard.

The outage page states more than 60 million meters in production worldwide. The industry page counts 3.8 trillion AMI data reads managed annually. Those figures carry a footnote saying they are calculated from client deployments from 2009 through 2024. Oracle also cites recognition as a leader in the 2025 IDC MarketScape for utility meter data management.

quote.text: Master your data with tools built for utilities

organizations.name: Survalent Technology
organizations.description: SCADA, ADMS and outage management for municipal utilities and co-ops

paragraphs: Survalent sells control room software to utilities, bringing SCADA, outage management and distribution management into one system. The company describes its buyers as electric, water and wastewater, oil and gas, renewable energy and transit utilities around the world. It argues that running a distribution network well is hard without a modern, centralized supervisory control and data acquisition system.

One network model and one database sit under every application, so a change made once carries across the platform. Operators work from real-time equipment status, metering data, alarming and control, with the aim of catching problems before outages start. A utility can start with a limited set of feeders, substations and applications and add more over time. A metering interface pulls readings from the AMI system using the MultiSpeak protocol, and a lightning interface fetches strike data and filters it by the utility's area of interest.

MultiSpeak itself is described as an initiative for rural electric co-ops and municipal utilities. The site says more than 700 utilities worldwide use its SCADA product. It reports 800+ customers around the world and 97.6% customer retention. The company also says it puts 20.3% of revenue into research and development.

quote.text: SurvalentONE ADMS is a fully integrated SCADA, OMS, and DMS solution, delivering real-time operational intelligence to proactively respond to issues and take corrective action when necessary.

paragraphs: Tantalus is a technology company selling grid modernization systems to public power and electric cooperative utilities. It has been delivering data-centric products to that market for more than 35 years.

The products sit on the Tantalus Grid Modernization Platform, a modular architecture meant to move data across devices, systems and vendors. One piece is edge-computing metering infrastructure aimed at resiliency, reliability and lower total cost of ownership. Another handles load management and distributed energy resources sitting behind the meter. A gateway device fits any ANSI meter socket and adds visibility and control behind the meter without replacing the meter itself.

Utilities across North America partner with the company on distribution grid work, with published case studies including one in Bolivar, Tennessee. Tantalus Systems trades on the TSX under the symbol GRID and on OTCQX. It is based in Burnaby, British Columbia. Recent announcements include a debt restructuring and an annual survey of how utilities view grid modernization.

organizations.name: Camus Energy
organizations.description: Grid orchestration and DER management for municipal utilities and co-ops

paragraphs: Camus Energy sells software that electric utilities use to interconnect data centers and local generation. What it sells is the flexible grid connection, in which the utility guarantees firm capacity for most of a site's demand and applies conditional limits to the rest.

Camus uses real utility data to map how much additional load each conductor and substation can safely serve in every hour of the year. Utilities then decide what portion of the load is served firmly and set operating limits for the conditional portion. Day-ahead operating forecasts show when those conditional limits will apply, alongside closed loop controls. The platform pulls SCADA data, GIS assets, network models, AMI, and DER telemetry into one consistent system model. Two applications sit on it: FlexConnect for interconnections and ODMS, which gives utilities a unified view of the distribution grid.

The company says it supports investor-owned and public power utilities. It counts 12 or more utility partners across the United States. It states that joint studies with Google, AES, and Princeton's ZERO Lab set the benchmark for how utilities and developers evaluate flexibility and grid capacity. On security, it says OAuth authentication, MFA, role-based access, audit logging, and continuous monitoring protect the platform.

paragraphs: GridUnity sells software for transmission and distribution interconnection, aimed at making energy project approvals faster. It is built for the parties on both sides of an interconnection request, including ISOs, RTOs, utilities, developers and transmission owners.

The platform runs the life cycle from application intake to commissioning in one place. It is delivered as configurable software as a service, which the company says lets customers meet federal and state orders as those evolve. Near real-time data sharing among developers, utilities and regulators is offered as a way to cut disputes and speed studies. The company states compliance with NIST 800-171 and SOC 2 Type II standards.

Products are broken out for transmission, for large load and for distribution. On its own record the company cites a five-year research and development strategy focused on AI, automation and predictive analytics. It also cites $45 million in matching Department of Energy funding and GRIP award recognition. Collaboration with research institutions and government agencies is described as part of that work.

paragraphs: EnergyHub sells utilities software for building virtual power plants, helping them scale VPPs to manage load growth and renewables. The resources involved are customer-side devices such as connected thermostats, solar and storage systems, and electric vehicles.

A single platform holds all of a utility's distributed energy resources. Control runs year-round and across resource types, based on price signals and customer rates. The stated aims are to relieve congestion, protect assets, and defer infrastructure investments. The company also points to a deep partner ecosystem behind the platform.

EnergyHub says it has been delivering load control programs since 2009. One customer story describes work with National Grid on a pay-for-performance residential battery program in Massachusetts. Another describes a thermostat demand response program with Ontario's Independent Electricity System Operator to reduce peak summer load. That program enrolled more than 100,000 homes within six months. EnergyHub is an independent subsidiary of Alarm.com, listed on Nasdaq as ALRM. A newsroom item reports its acquisition of Resideo Grid Services.

organizations.name: Virtual Peaker
organizations.description: Cloud DERMS and demand flexibility software for municipal utilities and co-ops

paragraphs: Virtual Peaker sells cloud software that lets an electric utility reach the smart devices already sitting in homes and businesses and use them to shave peak load and cost. The buyers are utilities standing up demand response programs.

Three suites make up the product, and the company presents them together as a virtual power plant platform that aggregates distributed energy resources at the edge of the grid. The Shift suite is the dispatch side, aggregating resources at homes and at commercial and industrial sites to hold down peak market costs and defer new construction. The Relay suite handles the customer side, signing people up and paying out the incentives. A utility can run several program types at once across electric vehicles, thermostats, water heaters and batteries.

The company describes partnerships with more than thirty device types, from thermostats to electric vehicle chargers. It states that the platform is SOC 2 Type 2 certified. Municipal energy providers are named as one audience, using demand response to meet grid goals and engage customers. One published case study covers Sacramento Municipal Utility District optimizing hot water heater efficiency on the platform.

quote.text: Modern utilities use Virtual Peaker to launch demand response programs.

paragraphs: Heimdall Power sells sensors and software to electric utilities, with capacity tools meant to help them safely adjust transmission limits, improve operational planning and stay compliant with industry standards. The company was founded in Norway in 2016.

Its dynamic line rating offering combines physical and virtual Neurons to take real-time, on-line measurements. The sensors report temperature, current and inclination on the conductor. Deployment is handled by an autonomous drone installation system that the company says places Neurons in remote or hard-to-reach areas. A facility ratings module consolidates all ratings into one unified system and is aimed at simplifying NERC FAC-008 compliance. Further tools give grid operators real-time visibility into threats like icing, line movement, electrical faults and wildfire risks.

The about page states that the company has grown 10x in two years, raised a $25M Series B and expanded with a North American headquarters in Charlotte, NC. A news item on the site reports that Heimdall Power was selected by Statnett for a new Dynamic Line Rating project.
