organizations.name: Neara
organizations.description: Physics-based digital twin modeling of grid networks for utilities

paragraphs: Neara sells physics-based digital twin software to electric utilities, which use it to model their networks. The pitch is to unify assets, surroundings and workflows in a single physics-accurate view.

The model is built from a utility's existing LiDAR, imagery, GIS and asset records. Teams then simulate wind, ice, thermal, flood, vegetation, reconductoring and new builds on the real network geometry. Outputs include prioritized hardening plans, regulator-ready reports and field-ready work orders. Solution areas cover resiliency and reliability, wildfire mitigation, asset management, risk and value optimization, and design and construction.

On the asset side, replacement candidates are ranked by measured load rather than by install date. Wildfire work pulls pole loading, asset condition, vegetation, GIS accuracy, weather and consequence into one physics-backed model. Resiliency work prioritizes mitigation by how asset condition, vegetation proximity and environmental conditions interact across the network. Case study quotes on the site are attributed to the chief executive of Essential Energy. Another comes from a general manager of network management at SA Power Networks.

quote.text: Utilities on four continents run their networks on Neara, from ambitious regional co-ops to national grid operators.

organizations.name: Anterix
organizations.description: 900 MHz private LTE spectrum and networks for utilities and public power

paragraphs: Anterix provides private 900 MHz spectrum to utilities so they can run their own wireless networks instead of leaning on commercial carriers. The company frames that as operational control, with the utility owning the communications infrastructure behind essential services. Licensed spectrum is sold together with deployment solutions and ecosystem partners so utilities can get networks running faster.

The deployment accelerators are described as simplifying site access, device onboarding, and connectivity management. Two of them, TowerX and CatalyX, are named on the solutions page. A partner program helps utilities integrate devices, applications, and network components so deployments move faster. That program spans over 150 technology providers, from rugged device manufacturers to software companies, with solutions validated for 900 MHz networks.

Eleven utility customers are deploying its 900 MHz solutions, the company states. It describes itself as the largest holder of licensed 900 MHz spectrum in the United States, counting the contiguous states plus Hawaii, Alaska, and Puerto Rico. The about page also claims over 93% of Texas counties served. The same page traces the founders back to Nextel.

quote.text: Anterix is the market leader in providing mission-critical private 900 MHz spectrum to the utility sector.

organizations.name: Copperleaf Technologies (IFS)
organizations.description: Asset investment planning and decision analytics for utilities and public agencies

paragraphs: Copperleaf sells decision analytics software that helps large organizations decide how to spend limited money on the infrastructure they own. The buyers are agencies and companies running critical infrastructure, where choices about maintenance, sustainment, or growth projects always involve a trade-off. The site groups the work by industry, among them electric utilities, government, rail and transit, roads and highways, and water and wastewater.

The method puts every proposed investment on a common footing so dissimilar options can be compared objectively. A single collaborative repository stores all asset and investment data, with proposals entered in one format and common financial metrics. Analytics then weigh hundreds of thousands of possible investments and return an optimal plan, with what-if scenarios for different budgets, timing, and constraints. A companion product, Copperleaf Asset, forecasts the long-term risk exposure of an entire asset population and bundles planned interventions to reduce service outages.

The company says its decision analytics is used to manage over $2.9 trillion of assets globally. Copperleaf is now paired with IFS, aimed at asset-intensive organizations allocating capital and operating expenditure. Its planning approach is described as embodying the key principles of ISO 55000. The enterprise software also connects to existing EAM, APM, ERP, and GIS systems.

quote.text: Decision-making needs to be rigorous, agile, and defensible.

The company page traces the software to 1982, when it digitized manual energy management processes. In 2022 the company acquired an energy monitoring software business. The same timeline cites SOC 2 compliance and FedRAMP Certification. The company claims over 45 years of experience. The homepage puts its user count at 26,000 energy and utility professionals.

paragraphs: Everspot sells cemetery software meant to hold all the tools you need to manage your cemetery in one system. It comes from a team of prior cemetery operators redefining cemetery software after finding the existing options wanting. New customers can join hundreds of cemeteries already using Everspot with no credit card required.

Maps are GPS-enabled, with walk-to-site directions and public access for visitors looking for a grave. A global search finds any burial, customer, or document in milliseconds. Deeds and certificates are generated from built-in or custom templates. Work orders can be created, assigned, and tracked for grounds maintenance and other operations. Bookkeeping syncs with QuickBooks Online or exports journal entries. Paid tiers add memorial (monument) tracking.

The company says hundreds of cemeteries across the United States and Canada use it to manage their operations. Before starting the company, the team ran cemeteries spread across Pennsylvania and Ohio. One founder, Cash, managed multiple cemeteries prior to founding Everspot.

organizations.description: Cemetery record management and public search tools for municipal cemeteries

paragraphs: Grave Discover Software sells a web-based cemetery management system that cemetery managers use to maintain burial information and grave locations. The same system lets a cemetery grant the public access to that data along with a searchable map.

Records are digitized into an inventory of burials, occupants, plot owners, deeds, grave types, grave locations and headstone images. The information sits on cloud-based servers that the company says are backed up daily. That is offered in contrast to desktop software, where backups depend on the cemetery's own computer environment. The interactive map can be viewed in four different ways. Public users can search grave occupant information by name, date of birth, date of burial, date of death and type of veteran. A visitor standing in the cemetery can pull the software up on a mobile device through a custom cemetery URL to find the grave they are seeking.

Cemeteries shown on the site include Mica Hill Cemetery, which is located in Durham, CT and operated by Durham Cemetery Company. A cemetery board uses the software to manage one cemetery along with other small cemeteries in its care. The company describes a team made up of designers, developers and usability specialists. It says it aims for software that is user-friendly and affordable.

quote.text: Cemeteries contain decades and sometimes centuries of historical information documenting beloved people; maintaining accurate records is essential.

organizations.name: Computronix
organizations.description: POSSE permitting, licensing and regulatory platform for state and local agencies

paragraphs: Computronix sells off-the-shelf software solutions for permitting, licensing, alcoholic beverage control, and gaming control. Those products run on POSSE, a web-based platform for automating permitting, licensing, enforcement and compliance workflows.

The permitting product automates workflows for building, planning, engineering, permitting, inspections and code enforcement. The alcoholic beverage control product manages the business and data behind liquor licensing, compliance and enforcement. The gaming product is aimed at agencies seeking a risk-based regulatory model for the gaming industry. The company says the software is engineered to comply with high security and regulatory compliance standards, including NIST, FedRAMP and ISO. Newer offerings include AI-powered portal assistance that helps applicants find answers and navigate permitting processes.

Computronix was founded in 1979 by Herman Leusink. It describes growing from a single employee to nearly two hundred employees and dozens of clients in major population centers across North America. One case study covers the Nebraska Liquor Control Commission, which regulates and controls that state's alcoholic beverage industry. The same alcohol system is used in nine other states and two provinces for alcohol industry regulation. Another case study describes the Alcohol and Gaming Commission of Ontario using POSSE ABC for liquor control, gaming, horse racing and recreational cannabis.

organizations.description: Cloud permitting, licensing and code enforcement software for small and mid-size municipalities

paragraphs: Citizenserve sells cloud software for community development, pulling permitting, inspections, code enforcement, planning and zoning, and licensing into a single system. Its buyers range from small towns and growing cities to large counties, departments inside major cities, and specialized agencies.

The company says the platform matches an agency's existing workflows without custom coding. It connects to GIS and financial systems among others. Applications, processing, and tracking sit in one secure system that the company says runs at 99.999% uptime. The licensing side covers online applications, automated renewals, payments, contractor tracking, and compliance. A published case describes work with Lawrence, Massachusetts to create a dedicated food permit type and a custom food establishment inspection form. On completion, the system generates an inspection report formatted for state submission.

The company says many of its clients have stayed with it for over twenty years. It reports that 99% of users give its support team a thumbs up. It also claims 99.999% uptime and zero data losses over more than 20 years.

organizations.name: Bitco Software
organizations.description: PermitTrax permit tracking and inspection suite for small government agencies

paragraphs: Bitco Software sells PermitTrax, hosted software for governments and agencies. It follows a permit from application through to final inspection.

Building permits are accepted and issued online, with mobile inspections carried out in the field. A planning module circulates applications, keeps up communication with applicants, and issues land use permits. A licensing module renews and issues business licenses and takes payments online or over the counter. Code enforcement staff track complaint cases, run in-field inspections, and issue violation letters and notices. A public portal called Citizens Connect lets residents track permit progress, request inspections, upload files, apply for permits, and pay online. Inspectors work from a companion application on an Apple iPad.

The company was established in December 2002. Cory Jorgensen is listed as founder and president. The suite is now described as a land management system covering permit, license, and code case tracking, reporting, GIS integration, and electronic plan review. Pricing is a flat fee for the license and maintenance. That fee is said to cover implementation, data conversion, training, and unlimited users.

quote.text: Bitco Software is dedicated to delivering simplicity, automation, and efficiency.

organizations.name: Symbium
organizations.description: Instant automated permitting and zoning compliance checks for building departments

paragraphs: Symbium runs an instant permitting service that lets homeowners and contractors see what a property allows, scope a project such as solar panels or a heat pump, and then file and manage the permit application. The company is based in San Francisco and puts its initial focus on permitting for residential decarbonization projects.

Compliance checks run against the applicable building, zoning, and energy codes while the applicant is still scoping the work. The technology underneath, called Complaw, is described as a TurboTax-like mechanization of regulatory analysis first built by the founding team at Stanford AI Lab. It layers onto the permitting workflows a building department already has, with contractors getting issuance within seconds of applying.

Contractors use it to accelerate permit issuance across a range of project types. The company says it has saved contractors and city staff time, and puts the running total at 3,500,000 project hours so far. It names Elemental Impact, Third Derivative, Uptake Alliance, and IMPEL among its backers. It was founded by Leila Banijamali, Abhijeet Mohapatra and Michael Genesereth during work at Stanford University. Recognition it lists includes a California Building Officials industry achievement award and a United States Conference of Mayors Civic Challenge.

quote.text: Symbium performs compliance checks against applicable building, zoning, and energy codes as a permit applicant is scoping out a project.

paragraphs: GovBuilt sells community development software to local government agencies, covering plan review, code enforcement, licensing and compliance in a single platform. On the site the product is presented under the MCCi name, with a claim that an agency can process permits up to 80% faster. The company also builds government websites that it describes as ADA-compliant and mobile-friendly.

Guided digital forms walk applicants through each requirement and flag missing information before submission. Applicants then get automatic status updates at every stage of the process. Inspectors complete reviews, log photos and update permit statuses from the job site. License records connect to supporting documents, inspection records, correspondence and approval history through a Laserfiche integration. As a license approaches expiration, automated renewal notices go out with what the business owner needs to finish online. For code enforcement, community members submit complaints and track case status through a public-facing portal. Officers document violations with photos and update case records directly from the property.

The company describes the platform as a browser-based SaaS product hosted on Microsoft Azure. An Android and iOS mobile application is offered for staff and inspectors. Agency staff are said to configure forms, requirements and workflows without submitting IT tickets or calling a vendor. A county planner in Pottawatomie County, KS is quoted saying permits that used to take 10 to 12 days now go out the same day in most cases.

organizations.description: Zoning code automation and development capacity analysis for cities

paragraphs: Gridics converts municipal zoning code text into parcel-level data that people can look at visually. The work is aimed at two audiences, developers choosing sites and cities trying to make their zoning easier to understand.

A patented zoning rules engine processes the data and powers the applications. Underneath it sits a mix of public property data, GIS shapes, and transit data. CodeHUB handles code publishing, letting staff collaborate on, manage, and publish zoning code changes. ZoneCheck is offered as a way to virtualize the zoning and planning front counter. ZoneIQ analyzes development potential and capacity scenarios in real-time 3D.

In Miami, the company built and implemented CodeHUB with the city's planning and zoning departments. It reports that over 60,000 users a year visit that instance for zoning information. For a study commissioned by the Wynwood Business Improvement District, the team modeled over 200,000,000 gsf of maximum buildable area across two proposed transit sites. The company says a city's code text can be digitized in as little as four weeks.

organizations.description: Community development, permitting and inspections software for municipalities

paragraphs: CityView sells community development software to municipalities, giving them one integrated system for permitting, inspections, planning, code enforcement and licensing. The company describes the platform as purpose-built for local government.

Permits run their full lifecycle in one system, with electronic plans review, mobile field access and automated workflows configured to a jurisdiction's own rules rather than a generic template. Planning teams track rezoning, subdivision, variance and development applications through review, referral and public hearing. Complaints and enforcement cases connect to the same permits and property data. Licensing covers business licenses, cannabis permits, short-term rentals and animal licenses, with online applications, automated renewals and fee calculation. Residents and contractors submit applications, schedule inspections and pay online at any hour.

The company has focused on software for local governments since 1982. It calls that platform one of the first community development and permitting software platforms in North America. The about page says the business was founded by former local government employees for local government. CityView is part of Harris Computer Systems and Constellation Software Inc. One customer story describes the Town of Bradford West Gwillimbury, Ontario, moving to a fully electronic plan review process while upgrading its CityView technology.

paragraphs: The software on this site is sold under the name Neumo, and it handles transactions and interactions between government agencies and the communities they serve. The catalog spans revenue compliance, court management, DMV services and integrated payments.

On the revenue side, the products listed are tax and licensing, short-term rental compliance, auditing and unclaimed property. Court, jury and probation systems sit under the justice line. Public administration covers land records, vitals, records search and pension. A shared platform layer adds reporting and analytics, forms, digital processing, ID verification, eSignatures, alerts and managed IT services.

The company claims 4,500+ state and local agencies across North America as customers. Those buyers are described as city, county, state and federal agencies. One published case study describes how Oregon DMV extended access beyond office hours with self-service kiosks.

It says thousands of public sector organizations use its software for developing policies with impact and accelerating processes. One of its stated aims is to streamline the building assessment and consent process.

Objective Trapeze is electronic plan review software that helps planning and building departments review plans quickly and accurately while checking compliance with ICC codes and amendments. Stamping is digital, and a 100-page application can be stamped in a few mouse clicks, with the software finding white space to place the stamp. Objective Connect is an IRAP assessed external file sharing product that gives control over information shared outside a council. Objective RegWorks centralises, tracks and administers the compliance process, including education and engagement. A separate product keeps disclosure document management production, review, verification and publication in one central system.

The company states that more than 500 local governments in the UK, Australia and New Zealand rely on Objective Trapeze to conduct plan reviews faster. It puts the file sharing product at more than 200 organisations worldwide.

paragraphs: Archistar sells AI plan review software to local governments, with a product called AI PreCheck that speeds building code and zoning compliance checks so permits can be issued faster. The same platform is offered to developers, architects and certifiers, who can check compliance before submitting to a municipality or council.

Submitters drag and drop design files onto the platform, which accepts PDF, CAD or BIM formats and reviews them in 2D or 3D. The software then evaluates each submission against the city's local codes and regulations. It is built on generative AI, computer vision and machine learning. Applicants receive standardized reports. For municipalities and councils with particular zoning, planning and compliance requirements, tailored and white-labeled versions are offered.

The company says Archistar was founded by Dr. Benjamin Coorey in 2010 and began life as an education portal. It grew from a university research project into a platform that could read planning rules, run feasibility tests and generate compliant designs in minutes. The site states that Archistar powers digital planning for over 30 cities and governments across Australia, Canada and the United States. Among the municipalities it names supporting are LA County, the City of Los Angeles, the City of Austin and the City of New York. Offices are listed across Los Angeles, Vancouver and Sydney.

paragraphs: Civica makes software that public bodies use to deliver critical services to citizens around the world. It says over 6,000 public bodies use that software to help provide critical services to over 100 million citizens.

Its solutions span local and central government, health and community care, housing and social care, libraries and education, and regulatory and compliance services. The company describes integrated cloud platforms that automate workflows, support data-driven decision-making and reduce operational costs. Named products include Spydus, a library management system. Civica also sells master data management for state and local government. It says it is an approved supplier on major government frameworks.

Civica was established in 2001 and describes itself as one of the UK's largest software companies. Its team has grown to 5,500 colleagues, one-third of whom have worked in the sectors it serves. Acquisitions are part of the strategy, with more than 37 completed in the last 10 years. The company reports delivery in the UK, Australia, New Zealand, India, North America and Europe. organizations.name: Ecolane
organizations.description: Paratransit and microtransit scheduling software for public transit agencies

paragraphs: Ecolane sells scheduling and dispatch software designed for public transit agencies that operate paratransit, non-emergency medical transportation, and microtransit services. Whichever way a trip is booked, the optimization that follows is autonomous and does not require manual intervention from a human.

The software optimizes service at the individual trip level and updates schedules as conditions change during the service day. That lets agencies account for no-shows, cancellations, delays, and staffing changes without rebuilding schedules manually. Eligibility rules, reporting, and compliance are integrated into daily operations. Managers can capture data for every vehicle, including rides per hour, run utilization, on-time performance, and deadhead. For medical trips, the platform helps agencies locate providers, verify rider eligibility, and schedule trips with vehicles equipped to accommodate rider needs.

Agencies supported by city, county, state, or federal funds are the intended buyers. The company says it is a U.S.-based company with U.S.-based product, engineering, and support teams. It states that its self-service applications are compliant with the Americans with Disabilities Act and Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.1 Level AA. It also says it holds three clean Voluntary Product Accessibility Templates. The hosted service is described as providing significant cost savings for transit agencies.

organizations.description: Demand-responsive transit dispatch and booking software for transit agencies

paragraphs: Blaise Transit sells software for running transit without a fixed route or a fixed schedule. It was built to equip municipalities, cities, transit agencies, and transit operators. One platform covers demand-responsive service, paratransit, fixed-route integrations, and private shuttles.

The system comes in three parts. Blaise Engine lets operators set the vehicles, drivers, stops, and payment options that make up a transit system. A passenger app is available on Android, iOS, and as a website, where riders book, pay, and follow live vehicle locations. A driver app supplies turn-by-turn navigation on optimized routes and a passenger manifest at each stop. A separate simulations service recommends which transit models to implement and the parameters for each service.

Blaise was started in 2018 by a small group of transit-loving engineers. The site says more than 70 communities have chosen it to optimize their transit services. It reports working with agencies serving a few hundred rides a month up to a few million. Its optimization models are described as patent pending and customizable.

paragraphs: EasyMile makes autonomous driving software for vehicles working at airports, logistics sites and industrial sites around the world. The company supplies the autonomous driving intelligence, a CE-marked stack handling perception, path planning and safety. The vehicles it powers are distributed by TractEasy.

One of them is a heavy-duty autonomous tow tractor built for airports, factories and logistics hubs. It is described as running around the clock with a single operator overseeing an entire fleet. The other is a cargo dolly for air cargo and ground handling operations. It carries up to 7 metric tonnes while navigating around personnel and ground equipment. The software is meant to be modular enough to power other kinds of heavy-duty vehicles as well.

EasyMile says it was founded in 2014 between Singapore and Toulouse. Its timeline starts with a first passenger fleet on the road in Lausanne, Switzerland. The same timeline names Alstom, Bpifrance and Continental as investors backing the company. It records driving in autonomous mode in more than 300 locations worldwide. The company also claims to be the first autonomous technology provider to obtain ISO 9001:2015 certification.

paragraphs: Auve Tech develops and manufactures autonomous transportation systems. What it sells is more than the vehicle: the offer covers integration of the vehicles into a given environment and fleet management alongside them. The stated aim is to extend public transport with a weatherproof first and last mile link running from a bus, tram or train stop to the doorstep.

The current shuttle, MiCa, is electronically limited to 25 km/h. The specification lists operating time of up to twenty hours a day. Sensing hardware named on the product page includes lidar, radar, GNSS and an inertial measurement unit. Teleoperation and remote monitoring are offered as options. A later software version added dynamic reaction to objects, detection of overtaking vehicles and side detection.

The company traces its origin to a 2018 project run in cooperation with Tallinn University of Technology. Testing of the earlier Iseauto shuttle on Estonian public streets began in the summer of 2020. One case study describes a scheduled last mile service in Takamatsu, Japan, with the shuttle operated by Boldly. That route ran 2.6 kilometres between a car park and a viewpoint.

paragraphs: CP Group designs, manufactures, installs, and services sorting machinery for the waste and recycling industry. It sells turnkey systems for both new material recovery facilities and retrofits of existing ones. A project management team handles third parties, scheduling, shipping, and installation.

Designing a facility begins with collaborative design meetings, cost reviews, and civil and electrical considerations. The equipment itself is engineered and manufactured in the United States. The shop has 115,000 sq. ft. of manufacturing space and 435,600 sq. ft. of storage on 9 acres. At startup and commissioning, the team goes over compliance, operations, and safety with the customer. Support afterward covers spare parts, process upgrades, and troubleshooting.

The company dates its machinery to the invention of the first commercial aluminum can flattener in 1977, and its name to Can Pac. It later acquired Krause Manufacturing, which makes construction and demolition separation equipment, and Advanced MRF, a specialist in intelligent motor controls and data acquisition. It says it owned and operated a material recovery facility for over 25 years, processing half of the city of San Diego's curbside recycling. That adds up to nearly 50 years of hands-on experience by its own account.

paragraphs: EverestLabs sells vision AI, software agents and robotics meant to digitize and automate material processing plants. The company frames the work as transforming recycled and virgin material processing. Its stated buyers are operators in recycling, resource recovery, metals, e-waste, packaging, and mining.

The software side, Navigator, is described as a vision and agentic AI platform that gives every operator a process engineer, an equipment expert, and a data analyst in one chat. EverestLabs states that Navigator never acts autonomously. Equipment presets are applied only once an operator approves them. On the hardware side, the robotic sorting cell has a compact 3x3 ft footprint and works over existing conveyor belts without expensive retrofit. Those cells are presented as fully turnkey and remotely managed, delivered by a 24/7 staffed Remote Operations Center.

The company says its vision system covers 65 or more material classes at over 95% detection accuracy. On commercial terms, the site says payback lands in under 12 months, guaranteed by SLA. EverestLabs is headquartered in Fremont, California.

organizations.description: Camera and telematics systems for refuse fleets used by municipal sanitation departments

paragraphs: 3rd Eye sells modular, subscription-based software that runs on top of its own heavy-duty truck camera systems. Its buyers are waste hauling companies that have to manage collection fleets safely and stay connected to their customers. A truck can carry up to eight cameras for a full view around the vehicle.

Video and telematics data upload to the cloud, where they become safety events that a review team turns into driver coaching material. A maintenance module watches the chassis, body and equipment continuously. It hands mechanics a list of repairs ranked by severity or by how long remains before failure. Other modules take on tax paperwork, recording the data behind IFTA reporting and excise fuel tax recovery.

Contamination detection spots recycling contamination and other non-conforming refuse at the point of collection. Adding the route review module helps haulers plan and report the annual reviews that California State Bill 1383 requires. Container quality reviews photograph and geolocate each collection event to find carts needing repair or replacement. The company presents itself as part of Environmental Solutions Group alongside Soft-Pak and Heil, under the Connected Collections banner. Equipment can be taken monthly rather than bought outright, on what the company calls a Hardware as a Service model.

paragraphs: Heil designs and manufactures the bodies that go on garbage trucks, selling to the fleets that collect refuse. The range runs from front loaders and automated front loaders to rear loaders, automated side loaders, and multi-compartment rear loaders.

The bodies are made in the United States, at a plant in Fort Payne, Alabama, that the company calls home. The product the site leads with is the RevAMP, a fully electric automated side loader. It is described as running with an auger compactor and no hydraulics on route. A training programme called Nexteligence is built for service technicians working on the Heil product line.

The company dates itself to 1901 and says it has built its reputation in the solid waste industry since then. It began as the Heil Railjoint Welding Company, founded by Julius P. Heil. Heil was later acquired and became a subsidiary within Dover Corporation. Dover then combined Heil Environmental, Marathon Equipment Company, and Bayne Machine Works into Environmental Solutions Group. Terex Corporation acquired Environmental Solutions Group on October 8, 2024.

paragraphs: Balancing Act sells simulation-based public engagement tools to government. The company describes an online simulation that draws stakeholders in so that leaders can make hard choices with public input behind them. The suite is aimed at budget, housing, climate and planning work.

In a budget simulation, residents see a model of the budget and their input is collected. A companion tool asks a few questions, estimates the taxes a household pays and shows where those dollars go. A mode for meetings turns the simulation into a facilitation tool for in-person and online sessions. There is also a research version for use with representative samples. The Prioritize product goes past a survey by having users pick items and then rank their picks. Its consensus analysis reports how many stakeholders end up with at least one of their choices included.

The housing product addresses cities and counties that struggle with public participation as they try to meet demand for new housing. Those simulations put residents in the shoes of decisionmakers and ask them to help solve the problem, with an interactive map showing where housing would be placed. Prioritize has been offered for input on stimulus funds such as ARPA and ESSER. A testimonial on the site is attributed to a village administrator in Germantown, Wisconsin.

paragraphs: For The Record makes recording technology for courts, capturing what is said in a proceeding and turning it into text that can be searched. One audience is court administrators trying to keep operations running at lower cost. Judges are a second audience, able to pull up audio, video, and speech-to-text without leaving the bench.

Recording runs on multiple audio channels, so individual speakers stay distinct even when they talk over one another. Courts that need local infrastructure can run the FTR Gold software in the courthouse rather than in the cloud. The cloud option is described as centralized storage built to NIST 800-53 Rev. 5 with more than a thousand security and privacy controls. Access is governed by role-based permissions, audit trails, and encryption of both transmission and storage.

The company says it supports courts in more than 80 countries. Its software is API-ready and meant to sit alongside the case management and evidence systems a court already runs. The work extends past software into specifying equipment and installing courtroom hardware.

Appearances run over video, audio or telephone. Attorneys use it to appear for routine matters in civil, family, criminal, probate and bankruptcy cases. Participants schedule, continue or cancel an appearance before the hearing. Before doing so, the site asks users to check its list of participating courts.

CourtCall states that it was established in 1995 to make remote court appearances simple, accessible and affordable for all parties. It describes providing supported remote legal collaboration services throughout the United States, Canada and worldwide. A home page announcement says the company was the successful bidder on the Colorado Judicial Department solicitation RFP #25005 and entered into an agreement with the department.

Connectors pull data straight from platforms such as Slack, Microsoft 365, and Teams. The processing engine supports over 600 file types. A separate FOIA product is built around how agencies respond to public records requests. Requesters use a portal to file requests and pay for them through pay.gov. For Canada, ATIPXpress carries access and privacy requests from submission through search, review, redaction, exemption analysis, and delivery.

The company describes the platform as purpose-built for corporations and government entities. It states that Casepoint holds FedRAMP Moderate and High authorizations, ISO 27001 certification, and Department of Defense Impact Level 5 and Impact Level 6 authorizations. It also claims to be one of only six SaaS companies globally with DOD IL6 authorization. Its AI is described as built for legal and regulatory work.

paragraphs: Assaia sells software that gives airports, airlines, and ground handlers real-time visibility into aircraft turnaround operations. The problem it names is that missing visibility on the ramp produces costly delays, underutilized capacity, miscommunication, accidents, missed service level agreements, and excess emissions.

Cameras placed across aircraft stands, aerobridges, and the apron generate accurate timestamps for turnaround events in real time. Machine-learning models turn those timestamps into predictions for aircraft off-block and departure readiness. The company says the system can use a wide range of cameras already installed at airports around the world. It runs in the cloud and on premise.

Beyond the core product, SafetyControl detects unsafe situations on the ramp for airports, airlines, and ground handlers. EmissionsControl gives airports real-time monitoring of auxiliary power unit engine usage. A separate interface is designed for airline users, ground handlers, departure coordinators, and gate managers. The company names JFKIAT and Seattle-Tacoma among the airports where its apron product has been deployed. It also states that the solution is fully compliant with the General Data Protection Regulation.

paragraphs: BondLink sells a platform to municipal bond issuers, aimed at making their bond sales go better. It gathers printing, distribution, deal pages, analytics and support into one place. The company describes itself as a single source for investor relations and debt management for issuers.

On the investor relations side, an issuer gets a website where investors find the finance team, five years of annual reports, project updates and required disclosure documents. Investors who follow a site are alerted when new documents or events are posted to it. An outreach tool lets an issuer filter investors by what they did on the site and email them from inside the product. A debt profile keeps a current view of every outstanding bond, payment and call date so reports and board presentations start from the same data. Exports are meant to line up with what continuing disclosure filings require on EMMA.

It is pitched at debt professionals working with limited time and resources. The debt management page reports the total amount of debt the platform currently tracks. The company says issuer websites built on it have been viewed more than two million times. A news item on the home page announces being named to the GovTech 100 for an eighth consecutive year.

quote.text: BondLink is the sole-source provider of IR and debt management solutions for municipal bond issuers looking for an edge.

paragraphs: Actionfigure sells real time transportation information to employers, operators and transportation professionals, delivered through live screens, mobile apps and custom integrations. The products are built around transportation demand management.

Screen puts real time transportation information and managed communications on displays. Journey is a trip planner a customer can brand and customize. Insight, an add on to those subscriptions, reports how deployments are used, from a scanned QR code through to a trip that gets started. The company also creates and maintains GTFS transit data as a service. MobilityScore is its metric for how much transportation access a location has.

The business started as TransitScreen, described as the first display to combine real time public transit, bikeshare, carshare and other modes in one place. Matt Caywood incorporated it and was soon joined by co-founder Ryan Croft. The company says it now works with over 1,000 customers in more than 50 cities across ten countries. Its own AI is said to drive trip recommendations and insights for transportation and real estate.

paragraphs: D4H makes cloud software that helps businesses, organizations and public safety agencies plan for, respond to and recover from incidents.

Its incident management product builds a common operating picture out of forms, tasks, logs, maps and status boards. Customers configure the system themselves without code, including on the fly during an incident. The company says it has been awarded ISO 27001:2022 for information security standards. Data residency is offered in the region the customer picks.

D4H states that responders use its software across many hundreds of organizations. The founder writes that he started D4H in 2008 based on his own experience in the Coast Guard. The company says it is now part of EcoOnline, and that its headquarters occupies a former lightkeeper training college in Ireland.

organizations.description: AI decision support and disaster analytics for emergency management agencies

paragraphs: Disaster Tech builds PRATUS, a platform for AI-driven emergency management aimed at organizations and communities. The product provides AI-powered real-time data insights. The company frames the work as protecting lives and property, from extreme weather to critical infrastructure failures.

PRATUS integrates live weather data, critical infrastructure impact models and analytics for near-instant situational awareness. One view brings together objectives, assets and operational tasks. Its AI lets users generate SITREPs, access real-time updates and produce after-action reports in seconds. The platform also supports training and exercises, from tabletop drills to full-scale deployments. It is available for purchase through the Microsoft Teams App Store.

The company describes itself as a certified Veteran-Owned Business committed to advancing public safety and resilience. It is headquartered in Alexandria, VA. Contract vehicles are offered so government, defense, energy and public safety organizations can reach the platform. Sean Griffin is CEO and co-founder, and previously served as Director for Incident Management Integration Policy on the U.S. National Security Council at the White House.

paragraphs: IQGeo gives telecom and utility operators a single platform to plan, design, build, and operate their physical network infrastructure. It is aimed at telecom, fiber, and utility network operators, including planners, engineers, and construction teams.

Network Manager Telecom is built to plan, build, and operate fiber and coax networks with accurate data, simple field tools, and automated AI quality checks. Field staff can download their work area, update records offline, and sync changes back automatically. Construction photos are audited with real-time visual AI to verify quality, completeness, and compliance at scale. A companion product, Network Manager Electric, is described as built for geospatial work execution, combining geospatial intelligence with AI-powered workflows across the full lifecycle.

Buyers choose between two deployment options, an IQGeo SaaS deployment or a private cloud deployment they host themselves. The hosted option is listed with ISO/IEC 27001:2013 certification. The private cloud option is pitched at operators needing bespoke integration with legacy GIS and OSS/BSS systems. The company says electric and gas utilities rely on it for asset management, grid modernization, inspection and field operations. On the telecom side it describes its customers as reaching some of the largest and fastest-growing global telecom operators, managing highly complex, rapidly scaling networks.

paragraphs: CostQuest Associates is a broadband consulting, data, and technology firm that collaborates with businesses and governments of all sizes. Its work covers network cost, economics, asset valuation, planning, policy, program support, mapping, and data science.

The data side of the business builds broadband-specific geographic information system data and applications for service providers, government entities, engineers, and consultants. It begins by pinpointing Broadband Serviceable Locations at the coordinate and address level across the United States. Essential broadband insights are then layered onto each serviceable location, including service availability, competition, funding details, and cost to serve. A consulting services team builds custom cost, business case, valuation, and appraisal models detailing the economics of broadband infrastructure for service providers, engineers, and governments.

The founders left the corporate telecom world to set out on their own. Over twenty years later, in 2023, the company transitioned to employee ownership. It is headquartered in Cincinnati, Ohio, with a team in Seattle, Washington, and a presence in Washington, D.C. Clients include service providers, engineers, consultants, and governments at the federal, state, and local levels. The company states that it serves as the Broadband Serviceable Location Fabric data provider for the FCC's Broadband Data Collection and for NTIA's BEAD program.

organizations.name: Adtran
organizations.description: Fiber access and broadband network equipment for municipal and rural providers

paragraphs: Adtran builds broadband access equipment and software for service providers that are extending fiber across different technologies and deployment settings. Its access platforms are meant to fit several architectures, from disaggregated designs to integrated systems. The company also sells a pluggable optics module aimed at operators of data centers working under power, cooling, space and latency limits.

Deployments run from small sites carrying a few hundred subscribers up to locations serving more than 100,000. Open APIs and OSS/BSS integration connect the equipment to systems an operator already runs, while the Mosaic software suite supplies visibility from end to end. A shared operational layer correlates signals and alarms across areas that were traditionally kept apart, so a team can see how a fault affects subscriber service before tracing where it began. Fiber monitoring runs while the fiber is in service, looking for degradation before subscribers feel it.

Customer stories on the broadband access page name a rural electric cooperative bringing fiber to parts of Indiana. Another names a municipal power and light utility building a multigigabit fiber-to-the-home network. For buyers who want to talk to someone, the contact page sets out regional office details.

quote.text: Broadband networks must scale to support higher speeds and more subscribers while adapting to different deployment models and existing infrastructure.

paragraphs: Cambium Networks sells Wi-Fi, broadband and security equipment to organizations building and running their own networks. Named markets include residential broadband and managed Wi-Fi for multifamily buildings, senior living, student housing and affordable housing.

The wireless line runs from Wi-Fi 5 access points through indoor and outdoor Wi-Fi 7 models. Service providers can also offer subscribers a managed home mesh router with cloud visibility and self-service setup. On the wired side, the switches come in indoor and ruggedized versions with Layer 2 and Layer 3 features and Power over Ethernet options for enterprise, industrial and campus sites. Devices are profiled without manual setup, and a switch configures itself as equipment is deployed, disconnected or moved. Management runs from public cloud, private cloud or a customer's own premises. Planning software models a fixed wireless link before anything is bought, weighing geography, distance, antenna height and transmit power.

Customers quoted on the homepage include a technology infrastructure manager at a county public school system. Another is an IT communications manager at a city government. The company courts school buyers directly, promoting a webinar on E-Rate funding.

paragraphs: Alden Systems sells Alden ONE, a platform that automates the business processes behind utility joint use and real estate. It sits between electric utilities, the companies attaching equipment to their poles, and the service firms working in between. The company also names communications and broadband providers and their engineering and construction partners.

Alden ONE is a centralized database holding more than 60 million utility joint use assets and activities. Its stated purpose is getting the right data to the right project partners at the right time by automating processes. Alden says its customers quantify the net gains they have seen.

organizations.name: 3-GIS
organizations.description: Fiber network design and asset management for public and municipal broadband

paragraphs: 3-GIS is an enterprise software company whose customers are telecom, electric, and gas organizations that plan, build, manage, and maintain complex infrastructure networks. The software is built for telecom and utility networks, turning spatial, asset, and operational data into a more accurate view of critical infrastructure.

For telecommunications customers it keeps a connected network record for planning, designing, building, documenting, and managing fiber and copper networks. On the utility side it drives Esri Utility Network workflows with tools for editing, tracing, validation, versioning, map production, and data quality. Separate tooling handles third-party pole attachment requests, permits, make-ready coordination, records, communications, compliance support, and billing inputs.

The about page dates the company's combination of GIS expertise and industry software to 2006. Staff are described as software developers, GIS specialists, telecom and utility experts, implementation consultants, support professionals, and customer success leaders. A published case study describes Oman Broadband needing to move to a modern, GIS-based asset management solution as its previous system neared end of life. organizations.description: Automated fiber network design software for broadband programs and operators

paragraphs: Biarri Networks sells fiber network planning and design, producing construction-ready designs for network operators and engineering teams. The company says its designs arrive up to 25 times faster than traditional methods. Cost estimates and planning insights are aimed at Tier 2 and Tier 3 service providers preparing bids.

The platform is GIS-based and fits its designs into systems and workflows a customer already runs. Plans can be tailored to a customer's own rules, architectures, and deployment environment. Teams can weigh deployment options such as underground against aerial. GIS data can be exported in formats including TAB, SHP, GEOJSON, and KML. Demand forecasting is offered for rural and low-density areas, where operators must justify the build. A standalone software-as-a-service product called FOND Planner lets customers design their own network plans.

The company was founded in Australia to change a traditional and time-consuming planning and design process. Its team now spans Australia, the Philippines, Vietnam, the UK, and the United States, and the Denver office serves as its American headquarters. Its information security management system is certified to ISO/IEC 27001. The company takes part in the Fiber Broadband Association and INCA.

paragraphs: Celona sells enterprise wireless that puts private 5G and Wi-Fi on one subscription, with Wi-Fi access points included at no additional cost. The company says the product is designed for the teams building the AI-native enterprise. Robotics and AI device makers are a second audience, able to embed multi-wireless connectivity into their products.

Celona Orion is deployed as an overlay that runs on existing physical infrastructure, the same cabling, switches, and network elements. Microsegmentation isolates IT and OT traffic across both Wi-Fi and private 5G. SIM-based authentication can be used on Wi-Fi as well as cellular. The platform delivers deterministic per-device, per-application quality of service on 5G.

The company says it began from the belief that enterprises deserved wireless purpose-built for their most mission-critical operations. Celona reports more than $135 million in funding. Its resources include published research, among them a study of OT and IT traffic separation in refinery and petrochemical industries.

paragraphs: Cayenta makes enterprise software for utilities, covering customer management, billing, financials, work management, and human capital management. Its customers are utilities across the United States, Canada, and the Caribbean.

The customer information system sits at the center, supporting utilities of every size from standard billing through highly complex rate structures. It is built to run the complete meter-to-cash lifecycle inside one system. Work management ties planning, work orders, and cost tracking to that customer and financial data. A financial module handles accounting, budgeting, reporting, and internal controls for utilities and municipalities. An AI layer called Cayla fields customer inquiries across voice and digital channels and answers staff questions inside the application. CayentaCloud provides single-tenant hosting in dedicated environments, and on-premises options remain for utilities not yet ready for the cloud.

The company dates its founding to 1983. It began as Solutions for Government, created to serve the needs of local governments and utilities. Cayenta later joined Harris Computer, which it describes as a global software organization. Its hosting infrastructure carries SOC 2 certification.

The company reports injuries and incidents falling 20 percent for one client over a twelve-month period. It also claims at least six times return on investment across sectors. FYLD announced a $41 million Series B round aimed at infrastructure field work. Amey has deployed the platform for highways operations, according to a company announcement.

It then gathers the EBT balance and transaction history, makes that easier to read, and displays it in the app. That spares people from calling a 1-800 number or logging in to a state website. Balance checking works in 49 states, the District of Columbia, and several U.S. territories. Iowa is the exception. The app also carries card security features such as suspicious activity monitoring and out of state transaction blocking.

The company says it was founded to make government benefits better at the speed and scale recipients deserve. The company points to more than a million 5-star reviews of the app. Money comes from advertising. Most of the promotions are free or discounted services available only to EBT cardholders. Propel also runs surveys that reach millions of users nationwide. It says those findings give insight to policymakers working to improve state and federal benefits programs.

People using it make daily quick check ins and can draw on a self-management library informed by cognitive behavioural therapy. The system learns a personal baseline in 28 days and then watches for change against it. When something significant shows up, a key worker gets an email notification. Clinical teams work from a real-time panel of their caseload. The company states that early warning signs appear just 3-10 days before relapse.

CareLoop Health says the tool is built on a decade of NHS-led research. Its home page states the approach is validated by five randomised controlled trials. The platform was co-designed with patients, clinicians, researchers and software engineers. Its co-founders hold academic posts, including a professor of health informatics at the University of Manchester. Another co-founder is described as a psychiatrist for over 30 years.

paragraphs: Halda sells an enrollment platform to colleges, universities and K-12 independent schools. It is pitched at enrollment teams asked to improve outcomes and lower cost per enrollment without extra budget or staff. AI agents individualize each interaction across a school's site, calls, texts and emails.

On the website, AI search and individualized content aim to earn an inquiry from students who would otherwise read a few pages and leave. An Engagement Score flags which anonymous visitors deserve staff attention. Behavioral emails and SMS react to what a student does, and an SMS and voice agent answers after hours. Yield surveys try to surface what is holding admitted students back before the deposit deadline. Conversion analytics tie each touchpoint to an enrolled student.

Halda connects to Slate, Salesforce and analytics tools with two-way sync, so it runs alongside a CRM rather than replacing it. The company says student data is fully FERPA and SOC 2 Type II compliant. It states that most institutions are fully live within 90 days. The platform is said to work in more than 40 languages. Halda says it was founded in 2021, starting from a question about enrollment.

paragraphs: Meadow makes software that handles the student financial experience at colleges, from application to graduation. The company says more than 300 higher education institutions use it.

One product is a net price calculator that gives prospective students a cost estimate in under three minutes. A billing product aims to cut manual work for staff and resolve balances sooner. A pre-collections product goes after unpaid tuition balances without punitive action. A checkout product collects non-tuition payments such as parking passes, lab fees, event costs and ID replacements.

One case study follows Tulsa Community College, which implemented the pre-collections product. The gap it addressed was the six-month period between the end of a semester and referral to traditional collections. Text messaging proved especially effective there for the college's dual enrollment population. Meadow also joined a Foundation for California Community Colleges procurement program to widen access to its tools among California community colleges and independent institutions. The founders trace the idea back to a bad higher education financial experience of their own.

paragraphs: Ativion sells software that K-12 school districts use to filter what students can reach online and to watch for signs that a student is at risk. The StudentKeeper side of the product handles classroom management and digital safety together, reporting into one place.

Filtering under the ContentKeeper name runs partly on district hardware and partly in the cloud, with one console covering both. Because it filters at the network layer, it reaches district-managed endpoints, personal devices, guest access and connected equipment alike. Districts can run it in the cloud, on premises, or as a mix, and set rules down to the level of individual sites.

The company says it has been in technology since 2002, serving education and enterprise customers with remote access and security products as well. Its lineup came together through acquisitions that included Netop and ContentKeeper, and the Ativion name itself dates to a 2024 rebrand.

paragraphs: CredibleMind partners with health plans, health systems, employers, and communities to break down the barriers of stigma, navigation, and cost that keep people from mental health care. Its platform blends evidence-based self-care, early intervention, and screening-based navigation into one integrated experience.

People start with validated assessments, and each customer configures referral rules and custom questions that triage higher-acuity needs to in-network care. The catalog runs to over a dozen assessments and more than 100 content topic centers. Behind those sit more than 10,000 evidence-rated resources that the company describes as grounded in science. The experience is designed for accessibility and available in 38 languages. APIs and EHR integrations tie the platform into clinical workflows.

Deryk Van Brunt is a co-founder of the company and serves as its chief executive. Marcos Athanasoulis, also a co-founder, serves as chief technology officer.

paragraphs: Gimlet is hosted software for keeping track of what happens at a service desk. It is sold to libraries and other organizations that want to see the trends and patterns behind the questions their desks field.

Staff log each interaction on a form the organization configures with its own category values. Entries can be tagged, and the full text of a question and its answer is kept so it can be searched later. A search can cover every entry or narrow to a single building or desk. Reports can show which desks are busiest at which hours of the week and which staff field the hardest questions. Data can be moved out to spreadsheet or reporting tools such as Excel, Google Sheets or Tableau. A web browser is all a desk needs to use it, and there is no cap on the number of staff or computers on an account.

Gimlet was founded by Eric Larson, a librarian, and Nate Vack, a library web application developer. The site puts the running total at more than 106,929,217 questions answered. The service is monitored around the clock for uptime, performance and security, with data mirrored, encrypted and backed up. Customers keep ownership of the data they enter. A 30-day free trial is offered.

paragraphs: FeedbackFruits sells teaching activities that run inside a university's own learning management system, so neither instructors nor students need a second login. The activities pull assessment, collaboration and feedback into a course in a few clicks.

Peer Review carries the whole process from assignment submission through to graded feedback. An instructor decides whether students review each other individually or as teams. They also decide whether feedback is anonymous or attributed. An AI companion called Acai offers coaching, grading and content creation to cut the work faculty carry. It can generate discussion prompts and quiz questions to speed up course design. A newer activity, Oral Practice, has students talk through their reasoning with that AI or with a peer, around work they submitted or a skill. Every session is recorded and stored without extra admin.

The site claims use at more than 200 institutions worldwide. It also counts over 5,000 educators. Testimonials on the peer review page are attributed to staff such as a director of academic technology at a school of public health. An institution can start with a supported pilot before committing further. Psychology and counseling programs use it to observe students in live or simulated sessions with real patients or in role-playing scenarios. A separate configuration is aimed at law enforcement and child advocacy interview recording. The company reports more than 50,000 active users across over 770 locations.

organizations.name: Cirrus Identity
organizations.description: Managed SAML and CAS identity federation, SSO, and guest-identity services for higher education institutions - exhibited at EDUCAUSE 2026

paragraphs: Cirrus Identity sells hosted sign-on services to colleges and universities of all sizes, university systems, research institutions, and medical centers. The problem it addresses is that campus identity systems were never designed to work together. Instead of replacing what a school already runs, Cirrus proxies authentication across identity providers, federations, and legacy systems.

The Bridge solution provides multilateral SAML and CAS for Entra ID, Okta, Duo SSO, and others. That lets a school meet the multilateral federation requirements of eduGAIN federations such as InCommon, CAF, and GakuNin without running Shibboleth, ADFS, or SSP. The Proxy solution handles people outside the enterprise directory, so guests, collaborators, alumni, and lifelong learners sign in without being given enterprise identities. Those users can bring credentials from Google, Microsoft, LinkedIn, Amazon, Apple, an ORCID iD, or a Cirrus Identity OrgBrandedID. Applicants can sign in to selected applications with their existing Slate credentials.

The buyers named on the site are identity and access management, security and privacy, systems architect, and enterprise application teams. Administrators get a console for reaching log events and configuring the products. The service is fully cloud hosted with 24x365 production support. Pricing is an annual subscription plus a one-time implementation fee, quoted for each use case. The company calls itself an InCommon Catalyst community partner.

quote.text: Cirrus connects identity systems that were never designed to work together.

paragraphs: Autoagent sells payment software to local government offices, built around the work of collecting public revenue. The company says its payment products work together or independently, to fit how a government office operates.

EscrowCloud handles bulk property tax payments by holding current tax data that mass payers must pay against, so they cannot submit a different amount or pay on an invalid property ID. A tax office adds its start and due dates to the system, and payers are notified of the collection cycle in real time. On the payer side, each parcel is validated and the amounts and exceptions are displayed before payment. The company states that it works with data files from all major tax administration systems. A second product, MuniciPay, brings online, in-person, IVR, eCheck, bankcard and mobile wallet payments into one platform. A third lets residents split an annual property tax bill into monthly payments.

The company describes county and municipal tax offices across 48 states as its users. It states that the platform integrates directly with more than 900 tax offices nationwide. EscrowCloud is free for property tax offices, with mortgage lenders, tax servicers and property managers paying a per-property fee. The company says the product is PCI DSS Level 1 certified and SOC 2 Type 2 compliant.

organizations.description: Natural language processing software that surfaces risks and insights from caseworker case notes for child welfare and behavioral health agencies - exhibited at APHSA 2026

paragraphs: Augintel builds software for health and social services agencies whose staff are buried in paperwork. The product pulls narrative data out of case notes, forms, and records and centralizes it. The pitch is that a worker can review an entire case history in minutes instead of reading the file page by page.

Natural language processing identifies the critical content inside those notes. A case dashboard reveals clinical risks described within notes and maps how those risks progress over the life of the case. Supervisors, quality specialists, and executives can customize a dashboard of quality indicators and alerts across an agency. Frontline staff see risks, strengths, and social determinants surfaced automatically. Alerts for early warning can be customized by the agency.

Caseworkers, clinicians, supervisors, and executives are the intended users. The company describes its team as specialists in natural language processing, a subdiscipline of artificial intelligence that uses computers to understand the written word. Its algorithms were trained with the help of partner agencies to understand the context of social services. Marty Elisco is listed as CEO and chairman of the board.

paragraphs: CampusIQ sells colleges and universities real-time space analytics meant to improve utilization, right-size facilities, and optimize occupancy. Its customers are institutions using the product for space utilization and campus planning.

Occupancy is read from the campus wireless network, so coverage scales as far as WiFi is available, with additional hardware sensors placed where it is not. Monitored spaces include classrooms, libraries, dining halls, recreation centers, residence halls, research facilities, and outdoor areas. The company says the system captures occupancy data without identifying individuals. It claims compliance with FERPA and other educational privacy regulations. Full implementation typically ranges from two to eight weeks. Field tests are reported at 95%+ accuracy in occupancy detection.

A published case study describes the University of Kentucky launching a pilot with CampusIQ in the fall of 2024. In that account, a 5% reduction in planned space translated to approximately $8M in avoided construction costs. Core pricing is based on gross square footage. Subscription models include software licensing, installation, and ongoing support.

Rather than coming into an office with a paper check, filers submit electronic payments through the platform. Alongside the software, the firm runs revenue reviews covering utility taxes, cable franchise fees, sales taxes, telecom taxes, hotel-motel taxes, and short-term rental taxes. Jason Perry founded Azavar in 1996. A technologist by training, he is described as the son of a midwestern city manager. The company added a full revenue-analysis arm in 2006 and a tax remittance and licensing platform in 2016. It says it has served local governments for more than 30 years.

paragraphs: Craft Education sells software for running registered apprenticeships and work-based learning programs. The platform, called Craft Connect, is built for employers, education partners, and intermediaries. Healthcare and education are the fields it is designed around first, though the company says the platform itself is field-agnostic.

A program administrator configures the program to registered-apprenticeship standards and invites learners, employers, and evaluators. Learners then log on-the-job hours against the work-process schedule from any browser. Mentors and reviewers work a queue rather than an inbox, approving hours, submissions, and competencies or sending them back, with every action time-stamped. Sign-offs roll into competency records, and one data model produces the WIOA, Perkins, RAPIDS, and Workforce Pell exports funders and accreditors accept.

The company describes itself as an essential part of WGU and puts mission before margin. Its stated purpose is to change lives for the better by creating pathways to opportunity. For buyers in IT, security, and procurement, the company states SOC2 compliance, invitation-gated access, and audit-ready records by default. It also cites WCAG 2.2 accessibility with a VPAT available and reporting to USDOL and RAPIDS.

paragraphs: AWE Learning sells self-contained childrens learning workstations to public libraries and community organizations across the United States and Canada, aimed at learners ages 2 to 12. The stations arrive turnkey, meant to support school readiness and early literacy and to extend programming without adding staff time.

The current release, Platinum Version 4 of the Early Literacy Station and AfterSchool Edge, carries more than 250 titles and runs without an internet connection or ads. Modules span literacy, math, STEM, and creativity. Rather than tap-and-swipe alone, each station combines touchscreen, mouse, and keyboard so children practice navigation, coordination, and early typing. The environment is closed and child-safe, built around structured, play-based learning children can work through on their own.

The company was founded in the mid-1990s as a remote network technology company. Work with the Free Library of Philadelphia exposed how hard it was for libraries to manage educational software for young patrons, and the Early Literacy Station grew out of that. It says its products are used by over 49% of U.S. public libraries. More than 40,000 workstations have been sold, according to the same page. The product is the Program Evaluation System, which the company calls the only complete one for higher education. It is meant to help institutions make decisions that increase revenue, reduce cost and save time.

One part of the system tracks revenue, cost and margin by college, department, program and course. Another reports student demand, competition, wages, skills and jobs across more than 1,500 academic programs and six award levels. Dashboards give a snapshot of program indicators for budget allocation and management. Written reports are generated automatically, distilling more than 50 metrics into short summaries for over 1,500 IPEDS programs. A facilitated workshop puts course data in front of faculty and administrators, who use their own judgment to find efficiencies in the courses and sections offered.

Case studies describe Utah Valley University evaluating program economics down to the course level. Another describes Tiffin University streamlining its review process and reaching 25 percent year-over-year growth in eight programs. A third credits the software with helping Jessup University avoid launching low-demand programs.

quote.text: My message to other universities is that if you are committed to having a process of ongoing program evaluation based on internal and external data analysis, you need Gray PES.

paragraphs: Beanstack is reading challenge software for public libraries. Schools and districts use it to run reading programs built on choice rather than quizzes.

Readers join a challenge, track progress, earn badges and mark milestones from any device. Libraries can start from ready-made challenge templates or build custom programs for their community. Logging tools include a reading timer, an ISBN scanner and progress bars for individual titles. Reporting goes down to the specific badges an individual reader earned. A feature called Beanstack Tandems links a reader's library and school accounts.

Challenge templates are developed with public library system partners including CSLP, iREAD, Page Turner Adventures and TD Bank. Client success managers help launch a site and stay on for ongoing support. The company describes thousands of libraries, schools, readers and students using the Beanstack app. A measure called the Reading Motivation Index is meant to show educators what drives students to read beyond minutes logged.

organizations.description: Teller enterprise cashiering, receipting and online payment software for city, county and state finance and treasury departments - exhibited at GFOA 2026

paragraphs: Can/Am Technologies sells Teller, a cashiering and point-of-sale package made for local and state government agencies across North America. More than 80 state and local governments use it for cashiering, payment technology, and credit processing. The idea is a single hub that centralizes revenue collection, credit processing, and reconciliation.

Residents pay through web and mobile portals, which clear through a processor cloud. Departments that collect revenue submit structured batches directly instead of handing paper to a cashier to re-key. Lockbox files, third-party systems, and online application payments import automatically on a schedule the agency sets. At the close of business Teller posts a single organized general ledger entry while accounts receivable stays in sync. It also produces the ICL file carrying scanned check images and MICR data so checks clear electronically.

The stated audience is state and local governments, education, and utilities. The company cites over 20 years of experience in those markets. Teller integrates with financials, accounts receivable, tax, parking, and records systems. Every modification to a payment, session, or batch is recorded and shown as an audit timeline.

quote.text: Achieving excellence in government cashiering

paragraphs: Harris provides mission critical software and service solutions for the public sector. The same page names utilities, private sector and insurance markets globally alongside healthcare.

It operates less as a single product line than as a group whose focus is to acquire businesses with growth potential, manage them well and then build them for the future. The solutions page describes an expanding portfolio of software businesses operating across diverse industries worldwide. That structure grew from an early bet on writing one product for the shared needs of many customers in a single industry, what the company history calls vertical market software.

In July of 1976, LEBS became the N. Harris Computer Corporation, and Nigel Harris became its first CEO. Research pointed to the utility industry as the right first target for that new way of writing and charging for software. In 1996, twenty years after the founding of N. Harris Computer Corporation, Nigel sold to Constellation Software Inc.

quote.text: All these years later, I’m grateful for the job that Constellation and the Harris leadership team have done with my baby.

organizations.description: Network data analytics software for water utilities covering leakage, infiltration, energy use and capital planning - exhibited at AWWA ACE 2026

paragraphs: Baseform makes software for networked water infrastructures, sold to utilities as analytics and planning tools. The product is presented as end-to-end software for the operational management of a water or wastewater system.

It continuously tracks and reconciles utility SCADA, GIS, billing, AMI and other data sources. One module handles event detection, DMA management, component analysis, non-revenue water reporting and infiltration tracking. Another covers failure and condition prediction, risk exposure, renewal planning and capital project generation. A billing module manages meters, consumption, revenue, under-registration and meter changeout. Network hydraulics are factored in continuously rather than treated as an afterthought.

The results are meant to reach everyone from the technicians who generate the analyses to field crews and top level executives. The stated approach is making better use of data that utilities and cities already collect daily. The company dates its inception to January 2015. It states that it is 100% owned and managed by its founders. One example given on the product page is a Texas public utility using the predictive analytics against a yearly rise in pipe breaks.

quote.text: Baseform is proud to be 100% owned and managed by its founders.

The company has broadened beyond field crews into GIS data synchronization and Esri Utility Network migration.

Epoch Solutions Group was founded in 2006. It says it serves utilities across North America, Australia, New Zealand, and the UK. It says client data is stored in Canada. Every account is described as including a dedicated implementation specialist who walks the team through setup.
